- input-dispatch: an input of workflow_dispatch (inputs, github.event.inputs): whoever dispatches the workflow chooses the value of the input. A credential whose only write access is to the permission Actions can dispatch the workflow, and the credential premise keeps the holder of such a credential as a possible attacker; the linter does not know whether such a credential exists or who holds it. The rule reports the value in a job with an environment that has required reviewers too, where a required reviewer of the environment can stop the run
  - disposition: limitation (decided by: dispatcher)
  - example: input-dispatch.yml (workflow, inconclusive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the workflow runs on workflow_dispatch with the input x, and a
    #   step writes inputs.x and github.event.inputs.x into its run script by
    #   ${{ }}.
    # reason: whoever dispatches the workflow chooses the value, and the
    #   workflow does not tell who that is, so whether an attacker controls it
    #   is not known; nothing the rule could read is expected to tell it.
    # attack-value: inputs.x = "\"; echo PWNED; echo \""
    # attack-run-behavior: when the one who dispatches the workflow gives the
    #   value as x, which inputs.x and github.event.inputs.x both hold, the
    #   script becomes echo ""; echo PWNED; echo " "; echo PWNED; echo "", and
    #   bash runs both echo PWNED as commands.
    on:
      workflow_dispatch:
        inputs:
          x: {}
    jobs:
      j:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - run: echo "${{ inputs.x }} ${{ github.event.inputs.x }}"
    ```
- input-call: an input of a reusable workflow or a composite action (inputs), which the caller gives
  - disposition: todo (needs: repo-file, fact)
  - example: input-call.yml (workflow, inconclusive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the workflow is a reusable workflow (workflow_call) with the
    #   input x, and a step writes inputs.x into its run script by ${{ }}.
    # reason: the value of inputs.x is what the caller gives, and no file read
    #   here calls this workflow, so whether an attacker controls it is not
    #   known.
    # cause: the rule reads what each caller among the files read gives
    #   inputs.x, and decides only when those are every caller: the files read
    #   are the whole repository and every call to this workflow is resolved.
    #   Here no file read calls it; a caller in another repository is never
    #   read.
    # attack-value: inputs.x = "\"; echo PWNED; echo \""
    # attack-run-behavior: when a caller gives the value as x, for example the
    #   title of an issue on issues, the script becomes echo ""; echo PWNED;
    #   echo "", and bash runs the second echo as a command, which prints PWNED.
    on:
      workflow_call:
        inputs:
          x:
            type: string
    jobs:
      j:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - run: echo "${{ inputs.x }}"
    ```
  - example: input-call.ghsa-rg3q-prf8-qxmp.action.yml (action-metadata, inconclusive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: a composite action with no caller among the files that the linter
    #   reads, whose input title takes the title of the pull request as its
    #   default, and whose step writes the input into run by ${{ }}. The action is
    #   action.yml of embano1/wip (commit e83c03c8f4696b0cef273d83115521b26ebb8bec,
    #   the parent of the fix c25450f77ed02c20d00b76ee3b33ff43838739a2, lines
    #   6-35); the branding and the comments are left out.
    #   action.yml of fish-shop/syntax-check (commit
    #   c7ed2fdeaee680fed281d7e86fb76c8c6e53734e, the parent of the fix
    #   91e6817c48ad475542fe4e78139029b036a53b03, GHSA-xj87-mqvh-88w2) writes its
    #   input pattern into the run of a composite step the same way (for file in
    #   ${{ inputs.pattern }}, line 20).
    # reason: the rule does not read the default of an input, so it does not know
    #   that inputs.title is the title of the pull request when the caller passes
    #   no title, and the caller is not among the files that the linter reads.
    #   The advisory is the form where the caller passes no title, and the author
    #   of a pull request writes its title.
    # attack-value: inputs.title = "x' == x ]]; echo PWNED; [[ 'x"
    # attack-run-behavior: the runner puts the title into the script before bash
    #   reads the script; the quote in the title ends the string, and bash runs
    #   echo PWNED in the step, with the token of the job.
    # advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rg3q-prf8-qxmp
    # advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xj87-mqvh-88w2
    name: Check WIP
    description: Checks for WIP patterns in Titles
    inputs:
      title:
        description: Text to perform pattern match against
        required: true
        default: "${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"
      regex:
        description: Regex pattern to match in title
        required: true
        default: "^[[:space:]]*(WIP)+(:)*"
    runs:
      using: composite
      steps:
        - shell: bash
          run: |
            set -ex
            shopt -s nocasematch
            if [[ '${{ inputs.title }}' =~ ${{ inputs.regex }} ]]; then
              echo "::error::Title marked as work in progress"
              exit 1
            else
              echo "::debug::Title not marked as work in progress"
            fi
            shopt -u nocasematch
    ```
- matrix: a value of a matrix that is not written out in the workflow
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: matrix.yml (workflow, inconclusive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the matrix value v is ${{ vars.V }}, not written out in the
    #   workflow, and a step writes matrix.v into its run script by ${{ }}.
    # reason: what the value holds is not known from the workflow, so whether an
    #   attacker controls it is not known.
    # attack-value: matrix.v = "\"; echo PWNED; echo \""
    # attack-run-behavior: when vars.V holds the value, the script becomes echo
    #   ""; echo PWNED; echo "", and bash runs the second echo as a command,
    #   which prints PWNED.
    on: issues
    jobs:
      j:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        strategy:
          matrix:
            include:
              - v: ${{ vars.V }}
        steps:
          - run: echo "${{ matrix.v }}"
    ```
- env-unset: an env the workflow does not set, which a step before may set at run time (\$GITHUB_ENV)
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file, fact)
  - example: env-unset.yml (workflow, inconclusive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: a step writes env.NOWHERE into its run script by ${{ }}, an env
    #   the workflow does not set.
    # reason: a step before may set it at run time through $GITHUB_ENV, so what
    #   it holds, and whether an attacker controls it, is not known.
    # attack-value: env.NOWHERE = "\"; echo PWNED; echo \""
    # attack-run-behavior: when a step before writes NOWHERE with the value to
    #   $GITHUB_ENV, the script becomes echo ""; echo PWNED; echo "", and bash
    #   runs the second echo as a command, which prints PWNED.
    on: issues
    jobs:
      j:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - run: echo "${{ env.NOWHERE }}"
    ```
  - example: env-unset.ghsl-2024-205.yml (workflow, inconclusive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on pull_request_target, a step lists the files that the pull
    #   request changes with gh pr view and writes them to $GITHUB_ENV as
    #   CHANGED_FILES, and a later step writes env.CHANGED_FILES into its run by
    #   ${{ }}. This is check_properties.yml of Stirling-Tools/Stirling-PDF (commit
    #   93e51e47ffa55fa3f62339258fbaef96d2d14c3f, lines 1-19 and the steps Fetch PR
    #   changed files and Determine reference file); the checkout of the pull
    #   request, the trigger push (lines 8-10), the lines cd pr-branch, gh repo
    #   set-default and cd .., the echo lines, BRANCH_PATH, the else branch and
    #   the steps after
    #   them (where line 79, GHSL-2024-206, writes env.CHANGED_FILES again) are
    #   left out. tests_results.yml of espressif/arduino-esp32 (commit
    #   690bdb511d9f001e2066da2dda2c631a3eee270f, GHSL-2024-169) has the same
    #   kind of value: a step reads files of an artifact of the triggering
    #   workflow_run into variables of the script and writes them to $GITHUB_ENV,
    #   and steps of actions/github-script write env.original_ref and others into
    #   their scripts (lines 39-48, 74, 77, 107 and 112).
    #   test_build_deploy.yml of wireapp/wire-webapp (commit
    #   5bdd49291b278d6d3d5fe89f1e656a556bd6db8e, GHSL-2020-232) writes the
    #   first line of the message of the commit github.event.after to $GITHUB_ENV
    #   as PR_LAST_COMMIT_MESSAGE, and a later step writes
    #   env.PR_LAST_COMMIT_MESSAGE into its run (line 43).
    # reason: env.CHANGED_FILES is what an earlier step writes to $GITHUB_ENV, the
    #   names of the files of the pull request, which its author names; the rule
    #   does not follow a variable of $GITHUB_ENV back to the step that writes it.
    # cause: the rule does not read what a run step writes to $GITHUB_ENV.
    # attack-value: env.CHANGED_FILES = "a\"$(echo${IFS}PWNED>/proc/$$/fd/1)\"b"
    # attack-run-behavior: the author of a pull request from a fork adds a file
    #   whose name holds the value; the script of Determine reference file becomes
    #   if echo "a"$(echo PWNED>/proc/$$/fd/1)"b" | grep …, and bash runs the
    #   command substitution, which prints PWNED, with the token of contents:
    #   write.
    # advisory: https://securitylab.github.com/advisories/GHSL-2024-205_GHSL-2024-206_Stirling_PDF/
    # advisory: https://securitylab.github.com/advisories/GHSL-2024-169_Arduino-ESP32/
    # advisory: https://securitylab.github.com/advisories/GHSL-2020-232-wireapp-wire-webapp-workflow/
    on:
      pull_request_target:
        types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]
        paths:
          - "src/main/resources/messages_*.properties"
    permissions:
      contents: write
      pull-requests: write
    jobs:
      check-files:
        if: github.event_name == 'pull_request_target'
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - name: Fetch PR changed files
            id: fetch-pr-changes
            env:
              GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
            run: |
              gh pr view ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }} --json files -q ".files[].path" > changed_files.txt
              CHANGED_FILES=$(cat changed_files.txt | tr '\n' ' ')
              echo "CHANGED_FILES=${CHANGED_FILES}" >> $GITHUB_ENV
          - name: Determine reference file
            id: determine-file
            run: |
              if echo "${{ env.CHANGED_FILES }}" | grep -q 'src/main/resources/messages_en_GB.properties'; then
                  echo "REFERENCE_FILE=pr-branch/src/main/resources/messages_en_GB.properties" >> $GITHUB_ENV
              fi
    ```
- env-dynamic: a variable of the env of the workflow, a job or a step, where the whole env of the workflow, the job or the step is one \${{ }}
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: env-dynamic.yml (workflow, inconclusive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the env of the job is the whole ${{ fromJSON(vars.E) }}, and a
    #   step writes env.X into its run script by ${{ }}.
    # reason: which names that env sets, and their values, are known only at run
    #   time, so whether an attacker controls env.X is not known.
    # attack-value: env.X = "\"; echo PWNED; echo \""
    # attack-run-behavior: when the JSON in vars.E sets X to the value, the
    #   script becomes echo ""; echo PWNED; echo "", and bash runs the second
    #   echo as a command, which prints PWNED.
    on: issues
    jobs:
      j:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        env: ${{ fromJSON(vars.E) }}
        steps:
          - run: echo "${{ env.X }}"
    ```
- env-whole: the whole env (toJSON(env)), or an env whose name is not known, which has what steps set at run time
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file, fact)
  - example: env-whole.yml (workflow, inconclusive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: a step writes toJSON(env) into its run script by ${{ }}, the
    #   whole env.
    # reason: the whole env has what steps set at run time, so whether an
    #   attacker controls a part of it is not known.
    # attack-value: a variable of env that a step before sets through $GITHUB_ENV = "'; echo PWNED; echo '"
    # attack-run-behavior: when a step before sets a variable to the value,
    #   toJSON(env) writes it inside a JSON string, where a single quote stays
    #   as it is, so the script becomes echo '{ ... "<name>": "'; echo PWNED;
    #   echo '" ... }': the single quote ends echo's string, and bash runs echo
    #   PWNED as a command, which prints PWNED.
    on: issues
    jobs:
      j:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - run: echo '${{ toJSON(env) }}'
    ```
- call-body-unknown: a call of a function after the rule has read the bodies of the functions at 4,096 calls in the script, such as a call after a chain of functions in which each function calls the next function twice (f1() { f0; f0; }; ... f13() { f12; f12; }; f13; w): the rule does not read the bodies of the functions at the calls past the 4,096 calls, so the rule does not decide the assignments, the writes, the prints and the requests in the bodies of the functions at the calls past the 4,096 calls
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: call-body-unknown.yml (workflow, inconclusive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on issues opened, a step passes the issue's title in the
    #   environment variable TITLE, defines a function w that sets TITLE to a
    #   fixed command when SAFE_MODE is set (the step does not set SAFE_MODE),
    #   runs a chain of functions f0 to f13 in which each function calls the
    #   function before it twice (16,383 calls), calls w, and runs
    #   TITLE with eval.
    # reason: the call of w comes after the 4,096 calls of functions that the
    #   rule follows, so the rule does not read the body of w, and does not
    #   decide whether TITLE holds the title of the issue when eval runs.
    # attack-value: github.event.issue.title = "echo PWNED"
    # attack-run-behavior: w sets nothing, and eval runs the title, which
    #   prints PWNED.
    on:
      issues:
        types: [opened]
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - env:
              TITLE: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
            run: |
              w() { if [ -n "$SAFE_MODE" ]; then TITLE="echo safe"; fi; }
              f0() { :; }
              f1() { f0; f0; }
              f2() { f1; f1; }
              f3() { f2; f2; }
              f4() { f3; f3; }
              f5() { f4; f4; }
              f6() { f5; f5; }
              f7() { f6; f6; }
              f8() { f7; f7; }
              f9() { f8; f8; }
              f10() { f9; f9; }
              f11() { f10; f10; }
              f12() { f11; f11; }
              f13() { f12; f12; }
              f13
              w
              eval "$TITLE"
    ```
- remote-callee-unknown: a job that calls a reusable workflow of another repository, when the linter asked the fact workflow.definition for the reusable workflow and got no answer (the token that the linter uses cannot read the file, the file is larger than the limit, or the linter has used up the requests it may send to the GitHub API), or when the call is deeper than the 3 levels of reusable workflows that the linter reads, for which the linter does not ask the fact: the rule does not read the jobs and the steps of the reusable workflow
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: remote-callee-unknown.yml (workflow, inconclusive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: a job calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/w.yml of
    #   the repository example-org/code-injection-unknown, whose content is the
    #   workflow of the true positive controlled (controlled.parallel.yml) of
    #   the rule, with on: workflow_call in place of the on of
    #   controlled.parallel.yml. The linter asked the fact workflow.definition
    #   for the reusable workflow and got no answer.
    # reason: what the jobs of the reusable workflow do is in the file that the
    #   linter could not read; whoever changes the uses, such as the author of a
    #   pull request, can name a reusable workflow that the token that the
    #   linter uses cannot read.
    # attack-value: github.event.issue.title = "\"; echo PWNED; echo \""
    # attack-run-behavior: the script becomes echo ""; echo PWNED; echo "", and
    #   the shell runs the second echo as a command, which prints PWNED.
    on:
      issues:
        types: [opened]
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      c:
        uses: example-org/code-injection-unknown/.github/workflows/w.yml@eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee
    ```

### false positive forms

- wiki-closed: gollum in a repository whose wiki is off or that only collaborators may edit
  - finding kinds: code-injection.wiki, code-injection.env-variable-wiki
  - fact kinds:
    - repo.wiki-open (provider: repo-setting, answer that removes the finding: false)
  - example: wiki-closed.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the job runs on gollum and reads the title of a wiki page.
    # reason: the wiki is off, or only collaborators may edit it (GitHub's
    #   default), so no outsider writes the title of a page.
    # cause: unless a file of facts or --fact says that not anyone may edit the
    #   wiki (repo.wiki-open false), the rule reports the finding. When no source
    #   answers repo.wiki-open, the finding is conditional.
    # attack-value: github.event.pages[0].title = "$(echo PWNED)"
    # attack-run-behavior: with the wiki off or edited only by collaborators,
    #   the title is one a collaborator wrote; were it the value, the script
    #   would become echo "$(echo PWNED)", and bash would run the command
    #   substitution, so echo would print PWNED.
    on: gollum
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - run: echo "${{ github.event.pages[0].title }}"
    ```
- writer-string: a string only those who can write to the repository, or moderate or administer its organization, set, which the webhook schema leaves free and the table reads as arbitrary, such as the name of a label (https://docs.github.com/en/issues/using-labels-and-milestones-to-track-work/managing-labels), the reason a comment is hidden (https://docs.github.com/en/communities/moderating-comments-and-conversations/managing-disruptive-comments), the name of an issue field or of its option (https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/managing-issue-fields-in-your-organization)
  - finding kinds: code-injection.controlled, code-injection.env-variable
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: writer-string.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on issues labeled, a run writes the label's name by ${{ }}.
    # reason: only those who can write to the repository create a label, so its
    #   name is no attacker's.
    # cause: the webhook schema gives the name no enum, and the table reads a
    #   free string as arbitrary.
    # attack-value: github.event.label.name = "\"; echo PWNED; echo \""
    # attack-run-behavior: no attacker can name a label; were the name the
    #   value, the script would become echo ""; echo PWNED; echo "", and bash
    #   would run the second echo as a command.
    on: {issues: {types: [labeled]}}
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - run: echo "${{ github.event.label.name }}"
    ```
- if-unnarrowed: a value that an if compares with strings that the workflow writes in the if (strings compared by == with the value and joined by ||, or the strings of contains(fromJSON('&#91;...]'), value)), where each string has only ASCII letters, digits, spaces, -, \_, . and /, does not start with -, and has no - right after a space, where the rule reports the value although the if limits the value to those strings, because the rule does not read the if in one of three forms. (1) A reusable workflow or a composite action gets the value through an input, and the if of the calling job or the calling step compares the value. The rule reports the value in the file of the reusable workflow or the composite action. The value is harmless when the if of every caller of that file, inside and outside the repository, compares the value. (2) The if compares the value under one name, and the script writes the value under another name: for example, the if compares env.BODY, which the env of the step sets to \${{ github.event.comment.body }}, and the script writes \${{ github.event.comment.body }}; or the if compares \${{ github.head_ref }}, and the script writes \${{ github.event.pull_request.head.ref }}. The value is harmless when the two names hold the same value in the step; the rule does not check that the two names hold the same value. (3) The if of a step that uses an action compares a value that the with or the env of the same step holds. At the start of the job, the runner runs the pre step of each action from another repository whose action.yml has runs.pre, under the condition runs.pre-if of that action.yml and not under the if of the step. For the pre step, the runner evaluates the with and the env of the step, and the code of the pre step may read the inputs. The runner runs no pre step of a local action (./). The value is harmless when the action has no pre step, or when the code of the pre step does not read the value. In each form, the value is harmless only where the case of the letters does not change what the value names (the undetected form if-compared)
  - finding kinds: code-injection.controlled, code-injection.env-variable
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: if-unnarrowed.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on issue_comment created, a step that has the comment's body in
    #   env.BODY runs only when env.BODY is deploy, and the step writes
    #   ${{ github.event.comment.body }} into its run: script.
    # reason: the step's if compares env.BODY, which holds the comment's body,
    #   with deploy, so in the step the body is deploy, ignoring the case of its
    #   letters: the body has no character that the shell reads as code, no
    #   line break, no word that starts with - and no workflow command.
    # cause: the rule limits a value by an if only under the name that the if
    #   compares: the if compares env.BODY, and the script writes
    #   ${{ github.event.comment.body }}; the rule does not check that env.BODY
    #   holds the comment's body.
    # attack-value: github.event.comment.body = "\"; echo PWNED; echo \""
    # attack-run-behavior: on GitHub, the step's if is false for such a body,
    #   and the runner skips the step.
    on:
      issue_comment:
        types: [created]
    jobs:
      j:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - if: env.BODY == 'deploy'
            env:
              BODY: ${{ github.event.comment.body }}
            run: echo "${{ github.event.comment.body }}"
    ```
- fork-flag-review: a job on pull_request_review or pull_request_review_comment whose if: condition lets the job run only when the head repository of the pull request is a fork, such as a job whose if: condition is github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork: on a pull request from a branch of the repository, the head repository is the repository itself, so in a repository that is not a fork the job runs only for a review of a pull request from a fork. The run of a review of a pull request from a fork has the secrets of the repository or a token that writes only where a private repository gives secrets or a token that writes to the runs of pull requests from forks (the undetected form fork-review). The rule does not read whether the repository that runs the workflow (not the head repository of the pull request) is a fork, and reports the job as if the job ran for a review of a pull request from a branch of the repository
  - finding kinds: code-injection.controlled, code-injection.env-variable
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: fork-flag-review.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on comments on the diff, a step writes the comment's body
    #   into the run: script with ${{ }}, in a job that runs only when the
    #   head repository of the pull request is a fork.
    # reason: the job runs only when the head repository of the pull request
    #   is a fork. On a pull request from a branch of the repository, the head
    #   repository is the repository itself, so in a repository that is not a
    #   fork the job runs only for a review of a pull request from a fork. In
    #   a public repository, the run of such a review has no secrets and a
    #   token that only reads; in a private repository, the run has neither
    #   secrets nor a token that writes unless the repository gives secrets or
    #   a token that writes to the runs of pull requests from forks (the
    #   undetected form fork-review).
    # cause: the rule does not read whether the repository that runs the
    #   workflow (not the head repository of the pull request) is a fork, and
    #   reads the job as if the job ran for a review of a pull request from a
    #   branch of the repository.
    # attack-value: github.event.comment.body = "\"; echo PWNED; echo \""
    # attack-run-behavior: in a public repository that is not a fork, a review
    #   of a pull request from a branch of the repository does not start the
    #   job, as the head repository of such a pull request is the repository
    #   itself; a review of a pull request from a fork starts the job with no
    #   secrets and a token that only reads, so the value reaches no secret
    #   and no token that writes.
    on: pull_request_review_comment
    jobs:
      a:
        if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - run: echo "${{ github.event.comment.body }}"
    ```
- lastpipe-not-literal: a variable of the env of the step that the script sets again in the last command of a pipeline after a shopt -s lastpipe whose option name the script does not write as a literal word (shopt -s "\$o"): bash runs the last command of the pipeline in the shell that runs the pipeline, so after the pipeline the variable holds the value that the script sets, and the rule reads the variable as holding the value of the env
  - finding kinds: code-injection.env-variable
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: lastpipe-not-literal.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on issues opened, a step passes the issue's title in the
    #   environment variable TITLE, turns lastpipe on with shopt -s and the
    #   option name in a variable, sets TITLE to a fixed command in the last
    #   command of a pipeline, and runs TITLE with eval.
    # reason: with lastpipe, bash runs the last command of the pipeline in the
    #   shell that runs the pipeline, so TITLE holds the fixed command when eval
    #   runs, and the title of the issue does not run.
    # cause: the rule follows lastpipe only after shopt -s lastpipe written as
    #   literal words, so the rule reads TITLE as the value of the env.
    # attack-value: github.event.issue.title = "echo PWNED"
    # attack-run-behavior: eval runs the fixed command, which prints "safe".
    on:
      issues:
        types: [opened]
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - env:
              TITLE: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
            run: |
              o=lastpipe
              shopt -s "$o"
              true | TITLE="echo safe"
              eval "$TITLE"
    ```
- name-not-literal: a variable of the env of the step that the script sets again by an assignment whose variable name the script does not write as a literal word (n=TITLE; declare "\$n=echo safe"): bash assigns the word after = to the variable whose name is the value of n, so after the assignment the variable of the env holds the word that the script assigns, and the rule still reads the variable as holding the value of the env of the step
  - finding kinds: code-injection.env-variable
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: name-not-literal.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on issues opened, a step passes the issue's title in the
    #   environment variable TITLE, sets n to the name TITLE, assigns a fixed
    #   command to the variable that n names with declare, and runs TITLE with
    #   eval.
    # reason: bash assigns the fixed command to TITLE, so TITLE holds the fixed
    #   command when eval runs, and the title of the issue does not run.
    # cause: the variable name of the assignment is not a literal word, so the
    #   rule reads TITLE as holding the value of the env.
    # attack-value: github.event.issue.title = "echo PWNED"
    # attack-run-behavior: eval runs the fixed command, which prints "safe".
    on:
      issues:
        types: [opened]
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - env:
              TITLE: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
            run: |
              n=TITLE
              declare "$n=echo safe"
              eval "$TITLE"
    ```
- git-config-value: a variable inside quotes given to git -c as the value of a configuration key that git keeps as data but that the rule's list of data keys (user.name, user.email and the like) does not name, such as git -c merge.conflictStyle="\$X" merge: the rule reads the value of every key outside that list as code, as git runs the value of core.sshCommand, init.templateDir or imap.tunnel. Without the quotes, the shell splits the value of the variable into words, and a word of the value can add another -c with a key that names a program, so that form is not a false positive
  - finding kinds: code-injection.env-variable
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: git-config-value.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on an opened issue, a step passes the issue's title in the
    #   environment variable ISSUE_TITLE and gives the variable to git -c as the
    #   value of the configuration key merge.conflictStyle.
    # reason: git reads the value of merge.conflictStyle as the name of a style
    #   of conflict markers, and does not run the value as a program.
    # cause: the rule reads the value of every configuration key outside its
    #   list of data keys as code, as git does for the value of core.sshCommand.
    # attack-value: github.event.issue.title = "$(echo PWNED)"
    # attack-run-behavior: git status rejects the style $(echo PWNED) or
    #   ignores it, and nothing prints PWNED.
    on:
      issues:
        types: [opened]
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - env:
              ISSUE_TITLE: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
            run: git -c merge.conflictStyle="$ISSUE_TITLE" status
    ```
- associative-key-not-literal: a key of an associative array that a declare, typeset or local command declares with an initial value written as a list in parentheses (declare -A m=(&#91;k]=v); echo "\${m&#91;\$KEY]}"), where a variable of env is in the key: the rule reads the subscript as arithmetic, which bash does only for an indexed array, as the rule does not read which names such a command declares associative
  - finding kinds: code-injection.env-variable
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: associative-key-not-literal.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on issues opened, a step passes the issue's title in the
    #   environment variable KEY, declares the associative array m with declare
    #   -A and an initial value in the same word, and prints the element of m
    #   whose key is KEY.
    # reason: the subscript of an associative array is a key, and bash does not
    #   read the key as arithmetic, so the title of the issue does not run.
    # cause: the word that declares m holds an initial value, so the word is
    #   not literal, and the rule does not read m as an associative array and
    #   reads the subscript as arithmetic.
    # attack-value: github.event.issue.title = "a[$(echo PWNED >/proc/$$/fd/1)]"
    # attack-run-behavior: echo prints an empty line, and nothing prints PWNED.
    on:
      issues:
        types: [opened]
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - env:
              KEY: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
            run: |
              declare -A m=([k]=v)
              echo "${m[$KEY]}"
    ```
- sha-suffix: a SHA whose name the table's \*\*.sha does not match, such as merge_commit_sha, read as arbitrary
  - finding kinds: code-injection.controlled, code-injection.env-variable
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: sha-suffix.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the job writes merge_commit_sha in a run.
    # reason: merge_commit_sha is the SHA of a commit GitHub makes, 40 hex
    #   digits, which no attacker shapes into code.
    # cause: the table's **.sha does not match its name, so it is read as
    #   arbitrary.
    # attack-value: github.event.pull_request.merge_commit_sha = "\"; echo PWNED; echo \""
    # attack-run-behavior: GitHub sets merge_commit_sha to the 40 hex digits of
    #   the SHA of the merge commit it makes, so the script is echo "<40 hex
    #   digits>"; were it the value, the script would become echo ""; echo
    #   PWNED; echo "", and bash would run the second echo as a command.
    on: pull_request_target
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - run: echo "${{ github.event.pull_request.merge_commit_sha }}"
    ```
- repository-name: the name of a repository, as the name by itself (github.event.pull_request.head.repo.name), as owner/name (github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name) or inside a URL that GitHub builds from owner/name (github.event.pull_request.head.repo.html_url), written inside quotes or as an argument, not as the name of a command. GitHub allows only ASCII letters, digits, ., - and \_ in the name of a repository, and no shell or JavaScript reads these characters as code in those positions. The rule reports the value because the rule's table of the contexts an attacker controls puts the name of a repository, and a URL built from the name, in the class named structured, the class that the table also gives the name of a branch. The name of a branch can contain the characters \$( ); the name of a repository cannot contain them
  - finding kinds: code-injection.controlled, code-injection.env-variable
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: repository-name.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on pull_request_target, the job writes the name of the
    #   repository of the pull request's head, owner/name, in a run, and the URL
    #   GitHub builds from owner/name in another.
    # reason: GitHub allows only ASCII letters, digits, ., - and _ in the name
    #   of a repository, and a login in front of it, so the value holds no $, no
    #   quote and no white space that a shell reads as code.
    # cause: the table reads a repository's name as structured, as a branch's
    #   name, which can hold $( ), and code-injection reports structured values.
    # attack-value: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name = "\"; echo PWNED; echo \""
    # attack-run-behavior: GitHub turns each character it does not allow in the
    #   name into -, so the script is echo "<login>/<name>"; were it the value,
    #   the script would become echo ""; echo PWNED; echo "", and bash would run
    #   the second echo as a command.
    on: pull_request_target
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - run: echo "${{ github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name }}"
          - run: echo "${{ github.event.pull_request.head.repo.html_url }}"
    ```
- callee: a reusable workflow or a composite action when all of the following are true: the rule does not know all of the callers of the reusable workflow or the composite action; every workflow that runs the reusable workflow or the composite action (directly, or through another reusable workflow or composite action) is a workflow in the same repository; and the rule would report no finding of the finding kind if the rule read the reusable workflow or the composite action only on the events on which the workflows in the same repository run the reusable workflow or the composite action (for example, every workflow that runs the reusable workflow or the composite action runs only on push). When the rule does not know all of the callers, the rule can read the reusable workflow or the composite action on every event (the worst case). For example, the rule does not know all of the callers when no caller is among the inputs; when the inputs are not the whole repository; for a composite action, when an input is excluded or cannot be read; when a caller names the reusable workflow or the composite action by a name of the form owner/repo/path@ref instead of by a ./ path, in which owner/repo is the repository that the --repo flag names, or is any repository when no --repo flag is given; when a step names the composite action by a ./ path, and either no checkout step runs before that step or the last checkout step before that step is not a plain checkout step (a plain checkout step has no ref input, no repository input and no path input); when a step inside a composite action names another composite action by a ./ path; or when the rule does not know all of the callers of a caller
  - finding kinds: code-injection.controlled, code-injection.env-variable, code-injection.env-variable-wiki, code-injection.wiki
  - disposition: todo (needs: repo-file)
  - example: callee.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: a reusable workflow that reads the title of an issue, and that
    #   only the repository's own workflows call, all of them on push.
    # reason: the issue it reads is never an outsider's.
    # cause: a callee is read in the worst case, as if a caller ran on issues.
    # attack-value: github.event.issue.title = "\"; echo PWNED; echo \""
    # attack-run-behavior: the callers in the repository run on push, whose
    #   payload has no issue, so the expression is empty and the script is echo
    #   ""; were the title the value, the script would become echo ""; echo
    #   PWNED; echo "", and bash would run the second echo as a command.
    on: workflow_call
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - run: echo "${{ github.event.issue.title }}"
    ```
  - example: .github/workflows/called.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: ci.yml of the repository o/r calls this reusable workflow on
    #   push only, by the name o/r/.github/workflows/called.yml@main, not by the
    #   path ./.github/workflows/called.yml.
    # reason: when the run of the linter names the repository (--repo o/r), the
    #   call by the name is a call of this file, and the only caller runs on
    #   push, which no attacker of the finding kind triggers. A run without
    #   --repo reads the call by the name o/r/.github/workflows/called.yml@main
    #   as a call that may name a file of the repository, because the run does
    #   not know which repository the inputs are; the rule does not resolve the
    #   call to this file, so the rule reads this file on every event and reports
    #   the same finding.
    # cause: the rule does not resolve a call by the name of the repository to
    #   the file, so the rule reads this workflow on every event.
    # attack-value: github.event.issue.title = "\"; echo PWNED; echo \""
    # attack-run-behavior: only a push to the repository runs ci.yml, which
    #   calls this workflow on push; the run of the push reads no value of the
    #   attacker's issue, pull request or comment.
    on:
      workflow_call:
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - run: echo "${{ github.event.issue.title }}"
    ```
    - finding on: .github/workflows/called.yml
    - .github/workflows/ci.yml (workflow)
      ```yaml
      on: push
      jobs:
        call:
          uses: o/r/.github/workflows/called.yml@main
          secrets: inherit
      ```
- pull-request-target-blocked: a workflow whose on has pull_request_target and no other event (no workflow_call event either), in a repository whose Actions policies block the runs of the workflow on pull_request_target (repo.pull-request-target-allowed false): an event policy that an administrator sets without pull_request_target among the allowed events, or the default policy that GitHub adds to a public repository without an applicable event policy, from the time when GitHub enforces the default policy on the repository. GitHub's documents say that GitHub evaluates the policies before a run, and that a run that a policy does not allow fails with an error. The documents do not say whether a job of such a run starts before the run fails; the rule assumes that no job of such a run starts
  - finding kinds: code-injection.controlled, code-injection.env-variable
  - fact kinds:
    - repo.pull-request-target-allowed (provider: repo-setting, answer that removes the finding: false)
  - example: pull-request-target-blocked.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on pull_request_target opened, a run step echoes the title of
    #   the pull request, written in by ${{ }}.
    # reason: the Actions policies of the repository block the runs of the
    #   workflow on pull_request_target: the default policy that GitHub adds to a
    #   public repository without an applicable event policy, from the time when
    #   GitHub enforces the default policy on the repository, or an event policy
    #   whose list of allowed events does not have pull_request_target. GitHub's
    #   documents say that GitHub evaluates the policies before a run, and that a
    #   run that a policy does not allow fails with an error; the documents do not
    #   say whether a job of such a run starts before the run fails, and the rule
    #   assumes that no job starts.
    # cause: unless a file of facts or --fact says that the Actions policies block
    #   runs on pull_request_target (repo.pull-request-target-allowed false), the
    #   rule reports the finding. When no file of facts and no --fact answers
    #   repo.pull-request-target-allowed, the finding is conditional.
    # attack-value: github.event.pull_request.title = "\"; echo PWNED; echo \""
    # attack-run-behavior: the pull request of the attacker triggers
    #   pull_request_target, and the run fails with an error, and no job of the
    #   run starts (the assumption of the reason), so the echo never runs.
    on:
      pull_request_target:
        types: [opened]
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - run: echo "${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"
    ```
- actions-policy: a run that the Actions policies of the repository block, in four cases where the rule does not take the policies into account. First, an event policy that blocks an event of the attackers other than pull_request_target (such as issue_comment) in a workflow whose on has that event: the rules ask a fact only for pull_request_target. Second, an actor rule that does not allow the account of the attacker (for example, an actor rule that allows only the repository roles with write access): repo.pull-request-target-allowed is one value for all the runs of a workflow file on pull_request_target, and an actor rule blocks a run by the account that starts the run, so the fact cannot tell what an actor rule blocks. Third, a workflow whose on has pull_request_target and another event: the rule does not ask repo.pull-request-target-allowed for such a workflow, because a run on the other event can reach the job. When the if of the job is false on the other event, so that the job runs only on pull_request_target, and a policy blocks pull_request_target, the finding is a false positive. Fourth, a reusable workflow (on workflow_call) or an action that only workflows on pull_request_target call: the rule asks repo.pull-request-target-allowed only of a workflow whose on has pull_request_target, not of the reusable workflow or the action, so a finding in the reusable workflow or the action is still reported when the policies block the runs of every caller
  - finding kinds: code-injection.controlled, code-injection.env-variable
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: .github/workflows/called.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the called workflow writes inputs.t into a run by ${{ }}; the
    #   caller ci.yml runs on pull_request_target alone and gives the title of
    #   the pull request as t, and no other workflow calls the called workflow.
    # reason: the Actions policies of the repository block the runs of ci.yml on
    #   pull_request_target (the default policy that GitHub adds to a public
    #   repository without an applicable event policy, from the time when GitHub
    #   enforces the default policy on the repository, or an event policy that
    #   an administrator sets without pull_request_target among the allowed
    #   events), so no run calls the called workflow. GitHub's documents say that
    #   GitHub evaluates the policies before a run, and that a run that a policy
    #   does not allow fails with an error; the documents do not say whether a
    #   job of such a run starts before the run fails, and the rule assumes that
    #   no job starts.
    # cause: the rule asks repo.pull-request-target-allowed only of a workflow
    #   whose on has pull_request_target, and the on of the called workflow has
    #   workflow_call, so the finding in the called workflow is still reported
    #   when the policies block the runs of the caller.
    # attack-value: inputs.t = "\"; echo PWNED; echo \""
    # attack-run-behavior: the pull request of the attacker triggers
    #   pull_request_target, and the run of ci.yml fails with an error, and no job
    #   of the run starts (the assumption of the reason), so the job of ci.yml
    #   never calls the called workflow, and the echo never runs.
    on:
      workflow_call:
        inputs:
          t: {type: string}
    jobs:
      j:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - run: echo "${{ inputs.t }}"
    ```
    - finding on: .github/workflows/called.yml
    - .github/workflows/ci.yml (workflow)
      ```yaml
      on: pull_request_target
      jobs:
        c:
          uses: ./.github/workflows/called.yml
          with:
            t: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
      ```
- app-checks-unasked: a run of status, check_suite or check_run in a repository where no app outside GitHub Actions makes a commit status or a check run for a commit that the attacker of the finding writes: the facts that the finding kind asks are false (repo.fork-pr-app-checks for a commit of a pull request from a fork, repo.merge-commit-app-checks for a commit that the merge of a pull request puts in a branch of the repository). In two cases, the rule does not ask these facts, and reports the finding whatever the values of the facts are. First, a workflow whose on has an event other than status, check_suite and check_run: the rule decides whether to ask the facts from the events of on alone, and does not read the if of the job, so the rule does not ask the facts even when the if of the job lets the job run only on status, check_suite or check_run. Second, a reusable workflow (on workflow_call) or an action (an action has no on) that only workflows on status, check_suite or check_run call: the rule asks the facts only of a workflow whose on has only events among these three, not of the reusable workflow or the action, so the rule reports a finding in the reusable workflow or the action whatever the values of the facts are
  - finding kinds: code-injection.controlled, code-injection.env-variable
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file, repo-file)
  - example: app-checks-unasked.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on status and push, the job runs only on status (its if), and
    #   writes the message of the commit of the status
    #   (github.event.commit.commit.message) where the rule reads it.
    # reason: no app outside GitHub Actions makes a commit status or a check run
    #   for a commit whose message an attacker writes in the repository: no app
    #   makes one for a commit of a pull request from a fork
    #   (repo.fork-pr-app-checks false), and no app makes one for a commit that
    #   the merge of a pull request puts in a branch
    #   (repo.merge-commit-app-checks false), so no run of status has such a
    #   commit, and the job does not run on push.
    # cause: the rule asks repo.fork-pr-app-checks and
    #   repo.merge-commit-app-checks only of a workflow whose on has no event
    #   other than status, check_suite and check_run, and the on of this
    #   workflow has push.
    # attack-value: github.event.commit.commit.message = "$(echo PWNED)"
    # attack-run-behavior: the author of a pull request from a fork writes the
    #   value in the message of a commit; no app makes a status for the commit,
    #   so no run of status starts with the value, and a push by one who can
    #   write runs no job.
    on: [status, push]
    jobs:
      j:
        if: github.event_name == 'status'
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - run: echo "${{ github.event.commit.commit.message }}"
    ```
- actions-not-allowed: a workflow whose run GitHub does not start, or a job that GitHub fails in the step "Set up job", because of the setting of allowed actions of GitHub (the fact repo.allowed-actions, which the quality rule allowed-actions reads): GitHub does not start a run of a workflow that has a uses, or that calls a reusable workflow that has a uses, that the setting does not allow, and fails a job before any step of the job runs when a step of a composite action that the job runs has a uses that the setting does not allow, or when the setting requires a full commit SHA and a step names an action by a tag or a branch. The harm that the finding reports happens only when GitHub runs the workflow or the job, and the rule does not read repo.allowed-actions
  - finding kinds: code-injection.controlled, code-injection.env-variable, code-injection.env-variable-wiki, code-injection.wiki
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: actions-not-allowed.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the workflow of the true positive controlled (controlled.yml)
    #   of the rule, with a job added whose step uses
    #   example-org/not-allowed-action, which the setting of allowed actions of
    #   GitHub (repo.allowed-actions) blocks with
    #   !example-org/not-allowed-action@*. In the true positive, on issues
    #   opened, a run step echoes the issue's title, written in by ${{ }}.
    # reason: GitHub checks each uses of the workflow before the run starts, and
    #   does not start the run because of the uses of
    #   example-org/not-allowed-action: no job of the run runs, so what the
    #   reason of the true positive says does not happen (in runs that the
    #   authors of the rule made on GitHub, such runs ended as startup_failure).
    # cause: the rule does not read repo.allowed-actions.
    # attack-value: github.event.issue.title = "\"; echo PWNED; echo \""
    # attack-run-behavior: GitHub does not start the run, so no step of the run
    #   runs, and the attack does nothing.
    on:
      issues:
        types: [opened]
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - run: echo "${{ github.event.issue.title }}"
      not-allowed:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - uses: example-org/not-allowed-action@eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee
    ```
- fork-pull-request: a job that runs only for a pull request from a fork (pull_request, pull_request_review or pull_request_review_comment, with an if that compares github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork with true, or github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name with github.repository), in a repository that is not a fork, in a run of the linter that adds variables-writer or secrets-writer: the rule reads each value of vars and secrets as a value that the attacker writes in every workflow run of the event; the workflow run for a pull request from a fork has no secret except GITHUB_TOKEN and a GITHUB_TOKEN that only reads, unless the settings of a private repository send secrets or a GITHUB_TOKEN that writes to such workflow runs (the facts repo.fork-pr-secrets and repo.fork-pr-write-tokens), and the attacker who writes a variable or a secret gets nothing from the job that the author of the pull request does not get from the code of the pull request. A job with no such if, in a repository where every pull request comes from a fork, is a false positive in the same way. The linter does not tell a workflow run for a pull request from a fork from a workflow run for a pull request from a branch of the repository. A fix: the linter splits the workflow runs of the three events into the runs for a pull request from a fork and the runs for a pull request from a branch of the repository, reads the comparisons of the if with the fork in each, and counts a run for a pull request from a fork only when the facts repo.fork-pr-secrets or repo.fork-pr-write-tokens say that the run gets secrets or a GITHUB_TOKEN that writes. A job with no such if keeps the runs for a pull request from a branch of the repository, and the finding stays. A fact of the rulesets of the repository (a ruleset with the rule Restrict creations on every branch and no actor that may bypass the ruleset) could say that no new branch, and so no pull request from a new branch, can be made, and remove a part of the false positives of a job with no such if; the actors that may bypass a ruleset, the branches made before the ruleset and the names of branches outside the patterns of the ruleset remain. The fix is not observed on GitHub
  - finding kinds: code-injection.controlled, code-injection.env-variable, code-injection.env-variable-wiki, code-injection.wiki
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file, fact)
  - added attackers: variables-writer, secrets-writer
  - example: fork-pull-request.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on pull_request, a job that runs only when the head repository
    #   of the pull request is a fork writes values of vars and secrets where
    #   the rule reads a value that the attacker writes.
    # reason: in a run of the linter that adds variables-writer or
    #   secrets-writer, the rule reads each value of vars and secrets as a
    #   value that the attacker writes. In a repository that is not a fork,
    #   the job runs only for a pull request from a fork, and such a workflow
    #   run has no secret except GITHUB_TOKEN and a GITHUB_TOKEN that only
    #   reads, unless the settings of a private repository send secrets or a
    #   GITHUB_TOKEN that writes to the workflow runs for pull requests from
    #   forks (the facts repo.fork-pr-secrets and repo.fork-pr-write-tokens).
    #   The attacker who writes a variable or a secret gets nothing from the
    #   job that the author of the pull request does not get from the code of
    #   the pull request.
    # cause: the rule counts every workflow run of the event pull_request, and
    #   does not tell a workflow run for a pull request from a fork from a
    #   workflow run for a pull request from a branch of the repository.
    # attack-value: vars.NAME = "\"; echo PWNED; echo \""
    # attack-run-behavior: a pull request from a branch of the repository does
    #   not start the job, as the head repository of such a pull request is the
    #   repository itself; a pull request from a fork starts the job with no
    #   secret and a GITHUB_TOKEN that only reads, so the value reaches no
    #   secret and no token that writes.
    on: pull_request
    jobs:
      j:
        if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - run: echo "${{ secrets.TOKEN }} ${{ vars.NAME }} ${{ runner.os }} ${{ steps.s.outcome }} ${{ needs.a.result }}"
    ```

### threat

- precondition runner-writes: the runner writes the value of \${{ }} into the script before the shell or JavaScript reads it
  - observed: 2026-09-25, runner 2.337.0: a commit message with a quote and a command, written into run by \${{ }}, ran the command; an author name written into the script of actions/github-script ran as JavaScript
  - cites:
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/script-injections>
- precondition value-read-as-code: bash expands a variable after bash parses the script, so the value of the variable is not code to the bash that runs the script; the value becomes code where bash, or a program that bash gives the value to, reads the value again: an operand of eval, the code that a shell or an interpreter takes after -c, a program that git runs (git -c core.fsmonitor=...), a variable outside quotes as the command name at the start of a command (bash splits the value into words, and the first word names the program that runs), the input of a command that runs the input as code, and arithmetic (a value such as a&#91;\$(...)] holds an array subscript whose command substitution runs)
  - observed: 2026-10-31: a test ran a script for each of those places with GNU bash 5.3.15, with the variable V set to a value that held a command that creates a file, and the file appeared; where the script reads the value as data (echo "\$V", echo \$V, A=\$V, the body of a heredoc that cat reads), none of the values created the file
  - cites:
    - <https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Shell-Operation.html>
    - <https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Bourne-Shell-Builtins.html>
- precondition attacker-writes: the value is one an attacker writes: a title, a body, a comment, a commit message, a branch name
  - observed: 2026-09-25, runner 2.337.0: GitHub accepted a branch named with \$( ) and \${IFS}; written into run as github.head_ref, the command in it ran
  - cites:
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/script-injections>
- precondition attacker-event: the job runs on an event whose payload has what an attacker wrote, with the token and the secrets of the repository: the attacker starts the run by an act of the attacker, or the act of another person or a schedule starts the run (run starters); not pull_request, whose run takes the workflow from the branch of the pull request: the author of the pull request can change the workflow of the pull request, so the author gets what the run has (read-only from a fork, or what a private repository sends to the runs of pull requests from forks) without the flaw of the rule
  - observed: 2026-09-25, runner 2.337.0: a pull_request run took its workflow from the pull request's branch
  - cites:
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/securely-using-pull_request_target>
- precondition app-status-check: an app outside GitHub Actions, such as an outside CI, makes a commit status or a check run for a commit whose message an attacker writes (a commit of a pull request from a fork, or a commit that merges a pull request; the message of a commit that merges a pull request can have the title of the pull request), and the commit status or the check run starts a run of status, check_suite or check_run, which runs the workflow of the default branch, whatever branch the commit is on. The payload of a run of any of the three events has the SHA of the commit, and the payload of a run of status or check_suite also has the message, the author name and the committer name of the commit. A finding of a workflow whose on has only events among status, check_suite and check_run (one, two or all three) holds only when the fact of the commit is true: repo.fork-pr-app-checks for a commit of a pull request from a fork, and repo.merge-commit-app-checks for a commit that the merge of a pull request puts in a branch of the repository or that a merge queue of the repository makes. A finding kind asks the fact of each kind of commit that its attackers write; the finding of a finding kind that asks both facts holds when at least one of the two facts is true. The rule does not ask these facts of a workflow whose on has another event too, and reports the finding of such a workflow whatever the values of the facts are. The finding is conditional when no file of facts and no --fact answers the facts
  - observed: 2026-11-05, runner 2.338.2: a GitHub App made a commit status and a check run for a commit of a pull request from a fork: runs of status, check_suite and check_run started on the default branch, and the message of the commit, with \$( ) in it, was in commit.commit.message of status and in check_suite.head_commit.message of check_suite
  - observed: 2026-11-06, runner 2.338.2: the same again: the SHA of the commit of the pull request was in sha and commit.sha of status, check_suite.head_sha and check_suite.head_commit.id of check_suite, and check_run.head_sha and check_run.check_suite.head_sha of check_run; check_suite.after and check_suite.before were null; the author name and the committer name of the commit, with \$( ) in each, were in the payloads of status and check_suite
  - cites:
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#status>
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#check_suite>
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#check_run>
- precondition callers-events: a reusable workflow or a composite action that is among the inputs runs on the events of the callers of the workflow or the action, whoever the callers are; when the inputs are the whole repository and hold every caller of the workflow or the action, the rule reads the workflow or the action on the events of the callers, with the values that the callers give under with
  - cites:
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#workflow_call>
    - <https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7x29-qqmq-v6qc>
- precondition wiki-open: on gollum, an account with no role in the repository can edit the wiki only in a public repository whose settings let anyone with an account edit the wiki (the fact repo.wiki-open). The finding holds only when repo.wiki-open is true, and the finding is conditional when no source answers repo.wiki-open
  - observed: 2026-09-25, runner 2.337.0: a wiki page titled with \$( ) and backticks, written into run as github.event.pages&#91;0].title, ran the commands; GitHub kept \$, (, ), backticks and ;
  - observed: 2026-10-30, runner 2.338.0: in a public repository whose settings let anyone with an account edit the wiki, an account with no role in the repository created a wiki page on the web interface of GitHub and edited the page; the creation and the edit each started a run of gollum, and each run had the repository's secret, and a step of each run created a ref with the token of the run, which the workflow asked for with contents: write
  - cites:
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/communities/documenting-your-project-with-wikis/changing-access-permissions-for-wikis>

  - run starters: pull_request_target: attacker, workflow_run: attacker, status: attacker, check_suite: attacker, check_run: attacker
