## permissions

- problem: a job's GITHUB_TOKEN may write more than the job needs, write-all or the repository's default when no permissions are written; every action, reusable workflow and package the job runs holds it, and one whose maintainer turns or is taken over writes to the repository with it
- expected: permissions written on the workflow or the job with only the scopes the job needs
- severity: high (the worst of its kinds)
- targets: workflow
- facets:
  - weakness: excessive-privilege
  - attack-means: none
- default run: always: in a run without --rule, the rule runs unless --skip-rule names the rule

### finding kinds

- permissions.write-all
  - detected: the permissions of {write_all} are write-all: the job's GITHUB_TOKEN may write every scope
  - arguments:
    - {write_all}: Where write-all holds for a job's GITHUB_TOKEN.
  - consequence: code of others that the job runs, an action, a reusable workflow or a package a script installs, writes to the repository with the token if its maintainer turns it or loses it to an attacker: pushes, releases, packages
  - remedy: write permissions on the job with only the scopes it needs
  - severity: high (found from the CVSS metrics below by the table)
  - attackers: maintainer-of-called
  - preconditions: others-code, malicious-code
  - incidents: agentkit-2025
  - true positives:
    - write-all.remote-callee.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: a job calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/w.yml of
      #   the repository example-org/permissions-remote, which the fact
      #   workflow.definition answers with the workflow of the true positive
      #   write-all (write-all.yml) of the rule, with on: workflow_call in place
      #   of the on of write-all.yml. The job passes its secrets with secrets:
      #   inherit. In the true positive, permissions: write-all is written at the
      #   top of the workflow, and the job runs actions/checkout,
      #   actions/setup-node and npm ci.
      # reason: the jobs of a reusable workflow run on the event that started the
      #   run of the calling job, so the reason of the true positive holds:
      #   write-all gives the job's token write on every scope; both actions take
      #   it as the default of their token input, and actions/checkout leaves it
      #   in .git/config, where the install scripts of the packages npm ci
      #   installs can read it.
      # attack: the maintainer of a package npm ci installs, or whoever takes over
      #   their account, publishes a version whose install script reads the token
      #   and sends it out.
      # attack-run-behavior: actions/checkout writes the token into .git/config as
      #   an extraheader; npm ci runs the package's install script, which reads it
      #   there, and the token it sends writes every scope until the job ends.
      on: push
      permissions: write-all
      jobs:
        c:
          uses: example-org/permissions-remote/.github/workflows/w.yml@v1
          secrets: inherit
      ```
    - write-all.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: permissions: write-all is written at the top of the workflow,
      #   and the job runs actions/checkout, actions/setup-node and npm ci.
      # reason: write-all gives the job's token write on every scope; both actions
      #   take it as the default of their token input, and actions/checkout leaves
      #   it in .git/config, where the install scripts of the packages npm ci
      #   installs can read it.
      # attack: the maintainer of a package npm ci installs, or whoever takes over
      #   their account, publishes a version whose install script reads the token
      #   and sends it out.
      # attack-run-behavior: actions/checkout writes the token into .git/config
      #   as an extraheader; npm ci runs the package's install script, which reads
      #   it there, and the token it sends writes every scope until the job ends.
      on: push
      permissions: write-all
      jobs:
        build:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - uses: actions/checkout@v4
            - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
            - run: npm ci && npm test
      ```
  - true negatives:
    - write-all.yml (workflow, true-negative)
      ```yaml
      # situation: the workflow gives the token only contents: read, and the job
      #   runs actions/checkout, actions/setup-node and npm ci && npm test.
      # reason: in place of write-all, the token may only read contents, so the
      #   actions of other repositories and the npm scripts the job runs get a
      #   token that writes no scope.
      # attack: the maintainer of a package npm ci installs, or whoever takes over
      #   their account, publishes a version whose install script reads the token
      #   and sends it out.
      # attack-run-behavior: actions/checkout writes the token into .git/config
      #   as an extraheader; npm ci runs the package's install script, which reads
      #   it there, but the token it sends has contents: read and no other scope,
      #   so GitHub refuses a push, a release or any other write made with it.
      on: push
      permissions:
        contents: read
      jobs:
        build:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - uses: actions/checkout@v4
            - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
            - run: npm ci && npm test
      ```
- permissions.unwritten
  - detected: neither the job nor the workflow writes permissions: the job's GITHUB_TOKEN has the repository's default, which may write
  - consequence: code of others that the job runs, an action, a reusable workflow or a package a script installs, writes to the repository with the token if its maintainer turns it or loses it to an attacker: pushes, releases, packages
  - remedy: write permissions on the workflow or the job with only the scopes it needs, permissions: {} when it needs none
  - severity: high (found from the CVSS metrics below by the table)
  - fact kinds: repo.default-token-write (provider: repo-setting)
  - attackers: maintainer-of-called
  - preconditions: others-code, malicious-code, token-writes
  - incidents: agentkit-2025
  - true positives:
    - unwritten.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: neither the workflow nor the job writes permissions, and the
      #   job runs actions/checkout, actions/setup-node and npm ci.
      # reason: without permissions, the token has the repository's default, which
      #   may write (repo.default-token-write true); both actions take it as the
      #   default of their token input, and actions/checkout leaves it in
      #   .git/config, where the install scripts of the packages npm ci installs can
      #   read it.
      # attack: the maintainer of a package npm ci installs, or whoever takes over
      #   their account, publishes a version whose install script reads the token
      #   and sends it out.
      # attack-run-behavior: actions/checkout writes the token into .git/config
      #   as an extraheader; npm ci runs the package's install script, which reads
      #   it there, and the token it sends has the repository's default
      #   permissions, which write (repo.default-token-write is true), until the
      #   job ends.
      on: push
      jobs:
        build:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - uses: actions/checkout@v4
            - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
            - run: npm ci && npm test
      ```
  - true negatives:
    - unwritten.never-runs.yml (workflow, true-negative)
      ```yaml
      # situation: on push, the job whose id is disabled has if: false, and the job
      #   whose id is on-failure needs the job build and has if: needs.build.result
      #   == 'failure'; each of the two jobs writes no permissions, in a repository
      #   whose default GITHUB_TOKEN may write, and runs actions/checkout,
      #   actions/setup-node and npm ci.
      # reason: GitHub skips the job disabled because the if of the job disabled is
      #   false. The if of the job on-failure calls no status function, so GitHub
      #   evaluates the if of the job on-failure only when the job build succeeded;
      #   needs.build.result is then success, and the if is false. When the job
      #   build fails or is skipped, GitHub skips the job on-failure without
      #   evaluating the if. So neither job runs
      #   (https://github.com/github/docs/blob/404a5f4de6cd5311e3ce2d5c076571291e0107d6/data/reusables/actions/jobs/section-using-conditions-to-control-job-execution.md).
      # attack: the maintainer of a package that npm ci installs, or whoever takes
      #   over the account of the maintainer, publishes a version whose install
      #   script reads the GITHUB_TOKEN and sends the GITHUB_TOKEN out.
      # attack-run-behavior: GitHub skips the job disabled and the job on-failure,
      #   so no code runs with the GITHUB_TOKEN of the job disabled or of the job
      #   on-failure.
      on: push
      jobs:
        build:
          permissions: {}
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - run: echo built
        disabled:
          if: false
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - uses: actions/checkout@v4
            - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
            - run: npm ci && npm test
        on-failure:
          needs: build
          if: needs.build.result == 'failure'
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - uses: actions/checkout@v4
            - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
            - run: npm ci && npm test
      ```
    - unwritten.yml (workflow, true-negative)
      ```yaml
      # situation: a reusable workflow (on: workflow_call) writes no permissions,
      #   and checks out, sets up Node and runs npm ci && npm test.
      # reason: unlike a workflow on push, which gets the repository's default
      #   token, a called workflow gets the caller's token, whose permissions it
      #   can only lower, so it may write no more than the caller chose.
      # attack: the maintainer of a package npm ci installs, or whoever takes over
      #   their account, publishes a version whose install script reads the token
      #   and sends it out.
      # attack-run-behavior: the job runs only when another workflow calls it,
      #   with the caller's token, whose permissions this file does not raise; the
      #   install script reads that token from .git/config, and it writes only the
      #   scopes the caller's job gave it.
      on: workflow_call
      jobs:
        build:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - uses: actions/checkout@v4
            - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
            - run: npm ci && npm test
      ```

### undetected forms

- id-token: a job that writes id-token write and no other scope: the rule does not report written scopes, yet code there takes an OIDC token for the clouds that trust the repository
  - finding kinds: permissions.write-all, permissions.unwritten
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: id-token.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on push, a job writes id-token write and nothing else, and
    #   assumes a role of AWS.
    # reason: a todo (the same file): code there takes an OIDC token for the
    #   clouds that trust the repository.
    # cause: the rule does not report id-token write as a written scope.
    # attack: the maintainer of aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials, or
    #   whoever takes over their account or moves its tag v4, makes the action
    #   send out what it gets.
    # attack-run-behavior: id-token: write puts ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL and
    #   ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN in the job's environment; the action
    #   requests an OIDC token for the repository with them, assumes
    #   arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/deploy with it and holds that role's AWS
    #   credentials, which it can send out.
    on: push
    permissions:
      id-token: write
    jobs:
      deploy:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
            with:
              role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/deploy
              aws-region: us-east-1
    ```
- written-scopes: a job whose written permissions give write on scopes it does not need: what it needs is what the code it runs calls with the token, which the workflow does not say; the rule reports only write-all and permissions not written
  - finding kinds: permissions.write-all, permissions.unwritten
  - disposition: limitation (decided by: run-time)
  - example: written-scopes.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on push, a job writes contents write and packages write, and
    #   only checks out and builds.
    # reason: a limitation (run time): the job needs to read contents only, but
    #   what it needs is what the code it runs calls with the token.
    # cause: the rule reports write-all and permissions not written, not the
    #   scopes written.
    # attack: the maintainer of actions/setup-node, or whoever takes over their
    #   account or moves its tag v4, makes the action push with the token.
    # attack-run-behavior: the job's GITHUB_TOKEN may write contents and
    #   packages; the action reads it from the github context and pushes a
    #   commit or publishes a package with it, though the build needed neither.
    on: push
    permissions:
      contents: write
      packages: write
    jobs:
      build:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - uses: actions/checkout@v4
          - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
          - run: npm ci && npm run build
    ```
- remote-callee: a job or a step inside a reusable workflow of another repository (uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/&lt;file>@&lt;ref>) whose content the fact workflow.definition does not give. For every rule: a run that does not ask the fact (a run without --online and without the answer in --facts). For a quality rule, also: a run where the linter asked the fact and got no answer (an answer of unknown: the GitHub API did not give the file), and a call deeper than the 3 levels of reusable workflows that the linter reads, for which the linter does not ask the fact. The rule reads a reusable workflow of another repository only from the answer of workflow.definition. For a rule that is not a quality rule (a rule with a threat), the last two forms are the inconclusive kind remote-callee-unknown, not this form
  - finding kinds: permissions.write-all, permissions.unwritten
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: remote-callee.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: a job calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/w.yml of
    #   the repository example-org/permissions-unanswered, whose content is the
    #   workflow of the true positive write-all (write-all.yml) of the rule,
    #   with on: workflow_call in place of the on of write-all.yml. The linter
    #   has no answer of the fact workflow.definition for the reusable workflow.
    # reason: a todo (a fact): the jobs of a reusable workflow run on the event
    #   that started the run of the calling job, and the linter does not read
    #   the reusable workflow.
    # cause: the rule reads a reusable workflow of another repository only from
    #   the answer of workflow.definition.
    # attack: the maintainer of a package npm ci installs, or whoever takes over
    #   their account, publishes a version whose install script reads the token
    #   and sends it out.
    # attack-run-behavior: actions/checkout writes the token into .git/config as
    #   an extraheader; npm ci runs the package's install script, which reads it
    #   there, and the token it sends writes every scope until the job ends.
    on: push
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      c:
        uses: example-org/permissions-unanswered/.github/workflows/w.yml@eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee
    ```

### inconclusive

- remote-callee-unknown: a job that calls a reusable workflow of another repository, when the linter asked the fact workflow.definition for the reusable workflow and got no answer (the token that the linter uses cannot read the file, the file is larger than the limit, or the linter has used up the requests it may send to the GitHub API), or when the call is deeper than the 3 levels of reusable workflows that the linter reads, for which the linter does not ask the fact: the rule does not read the jobs and the steps of the reusable workflow
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: remote-callee-unknown.yml (workflow, inconclusive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: a job calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/w.yml of
    #   the repository example-org/permissions-unknown, whose content is the
    #   workflow of the true positive write-all (write-all.yml) of the rule,
    #   with on: workflow_call in place of the on of write-all.yml. The linter
    #   asked the fact workflow.definition for the reusable workflow and got no
    #   answer.
    # reason: what the jobs of the reusable workflow do is in the file that the
    #   linter could not read; whoever changes the uses, such as the author of a
    #   pull request, can name a reusable workflow that the token that the
    #   linter uses cannot read.
    # attack: the maintainer of a package npm ci installs, or whoever takes over
    #   their account, publishes a version whose install script reads the token
    #   and sends it out.
    # attack-run-behavior: actions/checkout writes the token into .git/config as
    #   an extraheader; npm ci runs the package's install script, which reads it
    #   there, and the token it sends writes every scope until the job ends.
    on: push
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      c:
        uses: example-org/permissions-unknown/.github/workflows/w.yml@eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee
    ```

### false positive forms

- job-never-runs: a job that GitHub never runs because the if of the job is false in every run, and the if is false because of a value other than github.event_name and github.event.action (for example, if: github.event.pull_request.merged == true in a workflow that runs only on pull_request with types: &#91;opened]). No code runs with the GITHUB_TOKEN of a job that GitHub never runs. In the if of a job, and in the if of each job that the job needs, the rule reads only github.event_name, github.event.action and needs.&lt;job_id>.result.
  - finding kinds: permissions.unwritten, permissions.write-all
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: job-never-runs.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the workflow runs only on pull_request with types: [opened]; the
    #   job deploy has if: github.event.pull_request.merged == true, writes no
    #   permissions, and runs the action some/action.
    # reason: a pull request is not merged when the pull request is opened, so
    #   github.event.pull_request.merged is false in every run of the workflow,
    #   the if of the job deploy is false in every run, and GitHub never runs the
    #   job deploy
    #   (https://github.com/github/docs/blob/404a5f4de6cd5311e3ce2d5c076571291e0107d6/data/reusables/actions/jobs/section-using-conditions-to-control-job-execution.md).
    # cause: the rule reads only github.event_name and github.event.action in the
    #   if of a job, and reads the if of the job deploy as an if that may be true.
    # attack: the attacker publishes the code of the action some/action, which the
    #   job deploy runs.
    # attack-run-behavior: GitHub never runs the job deploy, so no code runs with
    #   the GITHUB_TOKEN of the job deploy.
    on:
      pull_request:
        types: [opened]
    jobs:
      deploy:
        if: github.event.pull_request.merged == true
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - uses: some/action@0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567
    ```
- no-third-party-code: a job that runs no code of others, only commands of the runner: no one else holds the token, which the rule does not tell apart
  - finding kinds: permissions.write-all, permissions.unwritten
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: no-third-party-code.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the job writes no permissions and runs nothing but a command of
    #   the runner.
    # reason: no code of others holds the token.
    # cause: the rule does not tell a job that runs no code of others apart.
    # attack: the maintainer of an action or a package, or whoever takes over
    #   their account, turns its code malicious, as in the true positive.
    # attack-run-behavior: the job runs echo hello, a builtin of bash, and uses
    #   no action and installs no package, so no code of others runs in it to
    #   read the token.
    on: push
    jobs:
      hello:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - run: echo hello
    ```
- called-narrows: a job that only calls a reusable workflow of the same repository, which writes permissions that narrow the token before any code of others runs: the called workflow can only downgrade the caller's token, and the rule does not read it
  - finding kinds: permissions.write-all, permissions.unwritten
  - disposition: todo (needs: repo-file)
  - example: called-narrows.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the job writes no permissions and only calls a reusable
    #   workflow of the same repository, which writes permissions: {}.
    # reason: the called workflow downgrades the token before any code of others
    #   runs.
    # cause: the rule does not read the called workflow.
    # attack: the maintainer of an action or a package that build.yml runs, or
    #   whoever takes over their account, makes it read the token and send it
    #   out.
    # attack-run-behavior: the job call runs build.yml, whose permissions: {}
    #   lowers the token its jobs get to no scope, so the code there reads a
    #   token with which GitHub refuses every write.
    on: push
    jobs:
      call:
        uses: ./.github/workflows/build.yml
    ```
- default-token-read: a job that writes no permissions, in a repository whose default token is read
  - finding kinds: permissions.unwritten
  - fact kinds:
    - repo.default-token-write (provider: repo-setting, answer that removes the finding: false)
  - example: default-token-read.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the job writes no permissions and runs actions and npm.
    # reason: the repository's default token is read, so the token writes
    #   nothing.
    # cause: unless a file of facts or --fact says that the default token is read
    #   (repo.default-token-write false), the rule treats the default token as a
    #   token that may write and reports the finding. When no source answers
    #   repo.default-token-write, the finding is conditional.
    # attack: the maintainer of a package npm ci installs, or whoever takes over
    #   their account, publishes a version whose install script reads the token
    #   and sends it out.
    # attack-run-behavior: actions/checkout writes the token into .git/config
    #   as an extraheader; npm ci runs the package's install script, which reads
    #   it there, but the token it sends has the repository's default, which is
    #   read (repo.default-token-write is false here), so GitHub refuses a write
    #   made with it.
    on: push
    jobs:
      build:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - uses: actions/checkout@v4
          - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
          - run: npm ci && npm test
    ```
- actions-not-allowed: a workflow whose run GitHub does not start, or a job that GitHub fails in the step "Set up job", because of the setting of allowed actions of GitHub (the fact repo.allowed-actions, which the quality rule allowed-actions reads): GitHub does not start a run of a workflow that has a uses, or that calls a reusable workflow that has a uses, that the setting does not allow, and fails a job before any step of the job runs when a step of a composite action that the job runs has a uses that the setting does not allow, or when the setting requires a full commit SHA and a step names an action by a tag or a branch. The harm that the finding reports happens only when GitHub runs the workflow or the job, and the rule does not read repo.allowed-actions
  - finding kinds: permissions.write-all, permissions.unwritten
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: actions-not-allowed.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the workflow of the true positive write-all (write-all.yml) of
    #   the rule, with a job added whose step uses
    #   example-org/not-allowed-action, which the setting of allowed actions of
    #   GitHub (repo.allowed-actions) blocks with
    #   !example-org/not-allowed-action@*. In the true positive, permissions:
    #   write-all is written at the top of the workflow, and the job runs
    #   actions/checkout, actions/setup-node and npm ci.
    # reason: GitHub checks each uses of the workflow before the run starts, and
    #   does not start the run because of the uses of
    #   example-org/not-allowed-action: no job of the run runs, so what the
    #   reason of the true positive says does not happen (in runs that the
    #   authors of the rule made on GitHub, such runs ended as startup_failure).
    # cause: the rule does not read repo.allowed-actions.
    # attack: the maintainer of a package npm ci installs, or whoever takes over
    #   their account, publishes a version whose install script reads the token
    #   and sends it out.
    # attack-run-behavior: GitHub does not start the run, so no step of the run
    #   runs, and the attack does nothing.
    on: push
    permissions: write-all
    jobs:
      build:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - uses: actions/checkout@v4
          - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
          - run: npm ci && npm test
      not-allowed:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - uses: example-org/not-allowed-action@eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee
    ```

### threat

- precondition others-code: the job runs code of others: an action or a reusable workflow of another repository, or a package a script installs; an action reads the token from the github context with nothing written in with
  - cites:
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use#using-third-party-actions>
- precondition malicious-code: that code turns malicious: its maintainer's doing, or that of an attacker who took over their account or moved its tag
  - cites:
    - <https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mrrh-fwg8-r2c3>
    - <https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qmg3-hpqr-gqvc>
- precondition token-writes: neither the job nor the workflow declares permissions, and the default GITHUB_TOKEN of the repository may write (repo.default-token-write true; without an answer, the finding is conditional. The permissive default is the default of the repositories made before 2023-02-02, and those repositories keep the permissive default until someone changes the setting)
  - cites:
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/github_token>
- actor: maintainer-of-called
  - via: turns the action, the reusable workflow or the package the job runs, or takes over an account that maintains it, and the code reads github.token
  - gains: write-with-token
- incident agentkit-2025: 2025-03-14, CVE-2025-30066: the attacker pointed a tag of tj-actions/changed-files to a malicious commit made in a fork and aimed at coinbase/agentkit; its pull_request workflow, which named tj-actions/changed-files@v39 and wrote no permissions, ran it and leaked a GITHUB_TOKEN that could write (15:10 UTC), before the attacker moved every tag of tj-actions/changed-files (16:57 UTC); Coinbase found no damage
  - advisory: <https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/github-actions-supply-chain-attack/>
  - compromised: tj-actions/changed-files
  - downstream: coinbase/agentkit
