## self-hosted-runner

- problem: a repository has a self-hosted runner, which the code of a pull request from a fork reaches, of anyone in a public repository, of whoever may read it in a private or internal one that runs the workflows of such pull requests, and whose state persists for the jobs after it
- expected: the jobs on GitHub-hosted runners, or on self-hosted runners that no pull request from a fork reaches; or a private or internal repository that does not run the workflows of pull requests from its forks. The rule reads the labels of runs-on only: the rule does not distinguish an ephemeral runner from another runner, and does not read the settings of a runner group. An ephemeral runner removes the files and the processes that a job leaves on the machine of the runner before the next job, and the code of a pull request still reaches the network of the runner while the job runs
- severity: high (the worst of its kinds)
- targets: workflow
- facets:
  - weakness: untrusted-code-execution
  - attack-means: code
- default run: always: in a run without --rule, the rule runs unless --skip-rule names the rule

### finding kinds

- self-hosted-runner.private
  - detected: the job runs on a self-hosted runner ({label}) of a private or internal repository that runs the workflows of pull requests from its forks
  - arguments:
    - {label}: The label that names the self-hosted runner, as written or as the matrix gives the label.
  - consequence: one who may read the repository and fork it, which every member of the enterprise reads for an internal one, can open a pull request that runs their code on the runner, whose state persists for the jobs after it: their secrets, their tokens and the runner's network
  - remedy: turn off Run workflows from fork pull requests, which the rule reads as the fact repo.fork-pr-run-workflows (with the fact false, the rule reports nothing), or run the jobs on GitHub-hosted runners: with a label of a GitHub-hosted runner in runs-on, the rule reports nothing. On self-hosted runners that no pull request from a fork reaches, the rule still reports the job, as the rule reads the labels of runs-on only. An ephemeral runner removes the files and the processes that a job leaves on the machine of the runner before the next job, and the code of a pull request still reaches the network of the runner while the job runs.
  - severity: high (found from the CVSS metrics below by the table)
  - fact kinds: repo.public (provider: repo-setting), repo.allow-forking (provider: repo-setting), repo.fork-pr-run-workflows (provider: repo-setting)
  - attackers: fork-pr-author
  - preconditions: reader-fork, pr-workflow, runner-persists
  - true positives:
    - private.remote-callee.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: a job calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/w.yml of
      #   the repository example-org/self-hosted-runner-remote, which the fact
      #   workflow.definition answers with the workflow of the true positive
      #   private (private.yml) of the rule, with on: workflow_call in place of
      #   the on of private.yml. The job passes its secrets with secrets: inherit.
      #   In the true positive, on pull_request, a job runs make on a runner
      #   labelled self-hosted and linux, in a private or internal repository that
      #   lets those who may read it fork it and runs the workflows of pull
      #   requests from its forks (repo.public false, repo.allow-forking true,
      #   repo.fork-pr-run-workflows true).
      # reason: the jobs of a reusable workflow run on the event that started the
      #   run of the calling job, so the reason of the true positive holds: on
      #   pull_request, GitHub runs the workflow file as the pull request has it,
      #   so one who may read the repository and fork it (every member of the
      #   enterprise reads an internal one) can rewrite the steps, and runs-on:
      #   [self-hosted, linux] sends them to the repository's own runner.
      # attack: one who may read the repository forks it and opens a pull request
      #   whose copy of this workflow runs a step of their own in place of make.
      # attack-run-behavior: the setting Run workflows from fork pull requests is
      #   on, so the pull request's run starts; the job a runs the attacker's step
      #   on a runner of the repository with both labels, where what it leaves
      #   stays for the jobs that run there after it, with their secrets and
      #   tokens.
      on: pull_request
      jobs:
        c:
          uses: example-org/self-hosted-runner-remote/.github/workflows/w.yml@v1
          secrets: inherit
      ```
    - private.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: on pull_request, a job runs make on a runner labelled
      #   self-hosted and linux, in a private or internal repository that lets
      #   those who may read it fork it and runs the workflows of pull requests
      #   from its forks (repo.public false, repo.allow-forking true,
      #   repo.fork-pr-run-workflows true).
      # reason: on pull_request, GitHub runs the workflow file as the pull request
      #   has it, so one who may read the repository and fork it (every member of
      #   the enterprise reads an internal one) can rewrite the steps, and
      #   runs-on: [self-hosted, linux] sends them to the repository's own runner.
      # attack: one who may read the repository forks it and opens a pull request
      #   whose copy of this workflow runs a step of their own in place of make.
      # attack-run-behavior: the setting Run workflows from fork pull requests is
      #   on, so the pull request's run starts; the job a runs the attacker's step
      #   on a runner of the repository with both labels, where what it leaves
      #   stays for the jobs that run there after it, with their secrets and
      #   tokens.
      on: pull_request
      jobs:
        a:
          runs-on: [self-hosted, linux]
          steps:
            - run: make
      ```
  - true negatives:
    - private+public.yml (workflow, true-negative)
      ```yaml
      # situation: on pull_request, in a public repository or in a private or
      #   internal one that runs the workflows of pull requests from its forks,
      #   the job runs make on ubuntu-latest.
      # reason: ubuntu-latest is a runner GitHub hosts, which GitHub makes new for
      #   each job and discards after it, unlike a self-hosted runner whose state
      #   persists, so a pull request from a fork leaves nothing on the runner for the
      #   later jobs.
      # attack: one who may fork the repository opens a pull request whose copy of
      #   this workflow runs a step of their own in place of make: in a public
      #   repository, anyone who may open a pull request (in pytorch-2023, the
      #   attacker first became a contributor by a typo fix that was merged); in a
      #   private or internal one, one who may read the repository.
      # attack-run-behavior: the job a runs the attacker's step on ubuntu-latest,
      #   a machine GitHub makes for the job and discards after it, so nothing the
      #   step leaves reaches a later job.
      on: pull_request
      jobs:
        a:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - run: make
      ```
- self-hosted-runner.public
  - detected: the job runs on a self-hosted runner ({label}) of a public repository
  - arguments:
    - {label}: The label that names the self-hosted runner, as written or as the matrix gives the label.
  - consequence: anyone who opens a pull request can run their code on the runner, whose state persists for the jobs after it: their secrets, their tokens and the runner's network
  - remedy: run the jobs of a public repository on GitHub-hosted runners: with a label of a GitHub-hosted runner in runs-on, the rule reports nothing. An owner of the organization can instead put the self-hosted runners in a runner group that does not allow public repositories: no job of the repository reaches those runners, though the rule still reports the job, as the rule reads the labels of runs-on only (the false positive form group-access). An ephemeral runner removes the files and the processes that a job leaves on the machine of the runner before the next job, and the code of a pull request still reaches the network of the runner while the job runs.
  - severity: high (found from the CVSS metrics below by the table)
  - fact kinds: repo.public (provider: repo-setting)
  - attackers: fork-pr-author
  - preconditions: public-repo, pr-workflow, runner-persists
  - incidents: pytorch-2023
  - true positives:
    - public.remote-callee.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: on push, a job calls
      #   example-org/self-hosted-workflow/.github/workflows/build.yml@v1, a
      #   reusable workflow of another repository whose job runs on a runner
      #   labelled self-hosted and linux, in a public repository (repo.public true).
      # reason: the jobs of a called workflow run on the runners of the
      #   repository that calls it, so the repository has a self-hosted runner
      #   with both labels; workflow.definition answers the file of the called
      #   workflow.
      # attack: the attacker, once a contributor, opens a pull request from a
      #   fork whose workflow runs a step of their own on runs-on: [self-hosted,
      #   linux].
      # attack-run-behavior: a self-hosted runner of the repository picks up the
      #   attacker's job, and the step runs on that machine, where what it leaves
      #   stays for the jobs after it, those of the called workflow among them.
      on: push
      jobs:
        a:
          uses: example-org/self-hosted-workflow/.github/workflows/build.yml@v1
      ```
    - public.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: on pull_request, a job runs make on a runner labelled self-hosted
      #   and linux, in a public repository (repo.public true).
      # reason: on pull_request, GitHub runs the workflow file as the pull request
      #   has it, so the author of a pull request from a fork can rewrite the
      #   steps, and runs-on: [self-hosted, linux] sends them to the repository's
      #   own runner, not a fresh GitHub-hosted one; whether the run waits for
      #   approval depends on the author and the repository's setting.
      # attack: the attacker becomes a contributor (in pytorch-2023, by a typo fix
      #   that was merged), then opens a pull request from a fork whose copy of
      #   this workflow runs a step of their own in place of make.
      # attack-run-behavior: pull_request runs the workflow as the pull request
      #   has it, so the job a runs the attacker's step; runs-on: [self-hosted,
      #   linux] sends it to a runner of the repository with both labels, and the
      #   step runs on that machine, where what it leaves stays for the jobs that
      #   run there after it. If the repository's setting makes the run wait for
      #   approval, the run starts once someone approves the run: a maintainer, or
      #   the attacker with a credential whose only write access is to the
      #   permission Actions.
      on: pull_request
      jobs:
        a:
          runs-on: [self-hosted, linux]
          steps:
            - run: make
      ```
  - true negatives:
    - private+public.yml (workflow, true-negative)
      ```yaml
      # situation: on pull_request, in a public repository or in a private or
      #   internal one that runs the workflows of pull requests from its forks,
      #   the job runs make on ubuntu-latest.
      # reason: ubuntu-latest is a runner GitHub hosts, which GitHub makes new for
      #   each job and discards after it, unlike a self-hosted runner whose state
      #   persists, so a pull request from a fork leaves nothing on the runner for the
      #   later jobs.
      # attack: one who may fork the repository opens a pull request whose copy of
      #   this workflow runs a step of their own in place of make: in a public
      #   repository, anyone who may open a pull request (in pytorch-2023, the
      #   attacker first became a contributor by a typo fix that was merged); in a
      #   private or internal one, one who may read the repository.
      # attack-run-behavior: the job a runs the attacker's step on ubuntu-latest,
      #   a machine GitHub makes for the job and discards after it, so nothing the
      #   step leaves reaches a later job.
      on: pull_request
      jobs:
        a:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - run: make
      ```

### undetected forms

- group: a runs-on of a runner group: the group may be of self-hosted runners or of GitHub's larger runners, and public repositories cannot use a group's runners by default
  - finding kinds: self-hosted-runner.private, self-hosted-runner.public
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: group.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on push, a job runs on a runner group.
    # reason: a todo (a fact): the group may be of self-hosted runners or of
    #   larger runners.
    # cause: a group is not a label, and the rule reads the label self-hosted
    #   only.
    # attack: the attacker, once a contributor, opens a pull request from a fork
    #   whose workflow runs a step of their own on runs-on: group: big-runners.
    # attack-run-behavior: where big-runners is a group of self-hosted runners
    #   that the repository's pull requests may use, a runner of it picks up the
    #   job of the pull request, and the step runs on its machine, where what it
    #   leaves stays for the jobs after it, the push's job a among them.
    on: push
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on:
          group: big-runners
        steps:
          - run: echo
    ```
- custom-label: a runs-on of labels of its own without self-hosted, such as linux.2xlarge: a runner may be made without the default labels, and whether a self-hosted runner has them is not known
  - finding kinds: self-hosted-runner.private, self-hosted-runner.public
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: custom-label.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on push, a job runs on labels of its own without self-hosted.
    # reason: a todo (a fact): a runner may be made without the default labels,
    #   so whether these name a self-hosted runner is not known. pytorch/pytorch
    #   c913f3857fb6a8ff8a32174db1da1b4f808f178f
    #   .github/workflows/generated-linux-binary-libtorch-cxx11-abi-nightly.yml:805
    #   ran on "runs-on: linux.rocm.gpu"; the runner the researchers took in
    #   2023 was "labeled jenkins-worker-rocm-amd-34" (John Stawinski, "Playing
    #   with Fire", 2024-01-11).
    # cause: the rule reports a runs-on with the label self-hosted only.
    # attack: as in pytorch-2023, the attacker becomes a contributor by a typo
    #   fix that is merged, then opens a pull request from a fork whose workflow
    #   runs a step of their own on runs-on: linux.rocm.gpu.
    # attack-run-behavior: where linux.rocm.gpu is a label of a self-hosted
    #   runner of the repository, that runner picks up the job of the pull
    #   request, and the step runs on its machine, where what it leaves stays
    #   for the jobs after it, the push's job a among them.
    on: push
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: linux.rocm.gpu
        steps:
          - run: echo
    ```
- remote-callee: a job or a step inside a reusable workflow of another repository (uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/&lt;file>@&lt;ref>) whose content the fact workflow.definition does not give. For every rule: a run that does not ask the fact (a run without --online and without the answer in --facts). For a quality rule, also: a run where the linter asked the fact and got no answer (an answer of unknown: the GitHub API did not give the file), and a call deeper than the 3 levels of reusable workflows that the linter reads, for which the linter does not ask the fact. The rule reads a reusable workflow of another repository only from the answer of workflow.definition. For a rule that is not a quality rule (a rule with a threat), the last two forms are the inconclusive kind remote-callee-unknown, not this form
  - finding kinds: self-hosted-runner.private, self-hosted-runner.public
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: remote-callee.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: a job calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/w.yml of
    #   the repository example-org/self-hosted-runner-unanswered, whose content
    #   is the workflow of the true positive private (private.yml) of the rule,
    #   with on: workflow_call in place of the on of private.yml. The linter has
    #   no answer of the fact workflow.definition for the reusable workflow.
    # reason: a todo (a fact): the jobs of a reusable workflow run on the event
    #   that started the run of the calling job, and the linter does not read
    #   the reusable workflow.
    # cause: the rule reads a reusable workflow of another repository only from
    #   the answer of workflow.definition.
    # attack: one who may read the repository forks it and opens a pull request
    #   whose copy of this workflow runs a step of their own in place of make.
    # attack-run-behavior: the setting Run workflows from fork pull requests is
    #   on, so the pull request's run starts; the job a runs the attacker's step
    #   on a runner of the repository with both labels, where what it leaves
    #   stays for the jobs that run there after it, with their secrets and
    #   tokens.
    on: pull_request
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      c:
        uses: example-org/self-hosted-runner-unanswered/.github/workflows/w.yml@eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee
    ```

### inconclusive

- input-dispatch: a label of runs-on with a \${{ }} that refers to an input of workflow_dispatch (inputs, github.event.inputs), alone or in a string with other text: whoever dispatches the workflow chooses the value of the input. A credential whose only write access is to the permission Actions can dispatch the workflow, and the credential premise keeps the holder of such a credential as a possible attacker; the linter does not know whether such a credential exists or who holds it. The rule reports the value in a job with an environment that has required reviewers too, where a required reviewer of the environment can stop the run
  - disposition: limitation (decided by: dispatcher)
  - example: input-dispatch.yml (workflow, inconclusive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on workflow_dispatch, runs-on is ${{ inputs.runner }}.
    # reason: the one who dispatches the workflow chooses the value of the input
    #   runner, and the workflow does not tell who dispatches, so whether an
    #   attacker chooses the label is not known; nothing that the rule could
    #   read is expected to tell who dispatches.
    # attack: the attacker of this attack is the author of a pull request from a
    #   fork, not the one who dispatches the workflow. When a dispatch gives the
    #   input runner the label of a self-hosted runner of the repository, such
    #   as self-hosted, the attacker opens a pull request from a fork whose
    #   workflow runs a step of their own on runs-on: self-hosted.
    # attack-run-behavior: a dispatch with runner set to self-hosted runs the
    #   job a on that runner; the attacker's pull_request run, from the workflow
    #   their pull request writes, is picked up by a runner with that label too,
    #   and their step runs on that machine, where what it leaves stays for the
    #   jobs after it, such as this one when dispatched again. With a label of a
    #   runner GitHub hosts, such as ubuntu-latest, the job runs on a machine
    #   discarded after it.
    on:
      workflow_dispatch:
        inputs:
          runner: {type: string}
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: ${{ inputs.runner }}
        steps:
          - run: echo
    ```
- runs-on-expr: a label of runs-on with a \${{ }} that refers to no input of workflow_dispatch and that the rule does not read as values written in the matrix, such as an input of workflow_call, fromJSON, or a value of the matrix in a string with other text (the rule reads the values of the matrix only for a label that is a \${{ matrix.&lt;name> }} alone)
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: runs-on-expr.yml (workflow, inconclusive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on push, runs-on is ${{ matrix.prefix }}-hosted, and the matrix
    #   gives prefix the value self.
    # reason: the label mixes a value of the matrix with the text -hosted, and
    #   the rule reads the values of the matrix only for a label that is a ${{
    #   matrix.<name> }} alone, so the rule does not determine the runner that
    #   the label names; reading the matrix of the same file would determine the
    #   label.
    # attack: the label is self-hosted, so the repository has a self-hosted
    #   runner; the attacker opens a pull request from a fork whose workflow
    #   runs a step of their own on runs-on: self-hosted.
    # attack-run-behavior: the job a runs on a runner with the label
    #   self-hosted; the attacker's pull_request run, from the workflow their
    #   pull request writes, is picked up by a runner with that label too, and
    #   their step runs on that machine, where what it leaves stays for the jobs
    #   after it, such as this one.
    on: push
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: ${{ matrix.prefix }}-hosted
        strategy:
          matrix:
            prefix: [self]
        steps:
          - run: echo
    ```
- remote-callee-unknown: a job that calls a reusable workflow of another repository, when the linter asked the fact workflow.definition for the reusable workflow and got no answer (the token that the linter uses cannot read the file, the file is larger than the limit, or the linter has used up the requests it may send to the GitHub API), or when the call is deeper than the 3 levels of reusable workflows that the linter reads, for which the linter does not ask the fact: the rule does not read the jobs and the steps of the reusable workflow
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: remote-callee-unknown.yml (workflow, inconclusive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: a job calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/w.yml of
    #   the repository example-org/self-hosted-runner-unknown, whose content is
    #   the workflow of the true positive private (private.yml) of the rule,
    #   with on: workflow_call in place of the on of private.yml. The linter
    #   asked the fact workflow.definition for the reusable workflow and got no
    #   answer.
    # reason: what the jobs of the reusable workflow do is in the file that the
    #   linter could not read; whoever changes the uses, such as the author of a
    #   pull request, can name a reusable workflow that the token that the
    #   linter uses cannot read.
    # attack: one who may read the repository forks it and opens a pull request
    #   whose copy of this workflow runs a step of their own in place of make.
    # attack-run-behavior: the setting Run workflows from fork pull requests is
    #   on, so the pull request's run starts; the job a runs the attacker's step
    #   on a runner of the repository with both labels, where what it leaves
    #   stays for the jobs that run there after it, with their secrets and
    #   tokens.
    on: pull_request
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      c:
        uses: example-org/self-hosted-runner-unknown/.github/workflows/w.yml@eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee
    ```

### false positive forms

- group-access: a job whose labels only self-hosted runners of the organization have, where all those runners are in runner groups that do not allow public repositories: GitHub does not let a public repository use any runner of such a runner group, and a runner group does not allow public repositories by default
  - finding kinds: self-hosted-runner.public
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: group-access.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: a public repository runs a job of pull_request on
    #   [self-hosted, linux], and the only runners with those labels are
    #   runners of the organization in a runner group that does not allow
    #   public repositories.
    # reason: GitHub does not let a public repository use any runner of a
    #   runner group that does not allow public repositories, and a runner
    #   group does not allow public repositories by default
    #   (https://github.com/github/docs/blob/5815d11586b0796688963a98c889680e60d72dc4/data/reusables/actions/self-hosted-runner-public-repo-access.md),
    #   so the job of a pull request from a fork reaches no such runner.
    # cause: the rule reads the labels of runs-on only, and does not ask which
    #   runners have them, or the settings of their runner groups.
    # attack: the attacker opens a pull request from a fork whose workflow runs
    #   their code on [self-hosted, linux].
    # attack-run-behavior: the repository can use no runner that has the
    #   labels, so no self-hosted runner takes the job of the pull request, and
    #   the code of the attacker runs on no self-hosted runner.
    on: pull_request
    jobs:
      build:
        runs-on: [self-hosted, linux]
        steps:
          - run: make
    ```
- matrix-exclude: a self-hosted label of a matrix that its exclude takes out, so no job runs on it
  - finding kinds: self-hosted-runner.public, self-hosted-runner.private
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: matrix-exclude.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: runs-on is a value of a matrix of self-hosted and
    #   ubuntu-latest.
    # reason: exclude takes out the self-hosted value, so every job runs on
    #   ubuntu-latest.
    # cause: the rule does not read exclude.
    # attack: the attacker becomes a contributor (in pytorch-2023, by a typo fix
    #   that was merged), then opens a pull request from a fork whose copy of
    #   this workflow runs a step of their own in place of make.
    # attack-run-behavior: exclude leaves the matrix only os: ubuntu-latest, so
    #   the one job runs the attacker's step on ubuntu-latest, a machine GitHub
    #   discards after the job.
    on: pull_request
    jobs:
      a:
        strategy:
          matrix:
            os: [self-hosted, ubuntu-latest]
            exclude:
              - os: self-hosted
        runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
        steps:
          - run: make
    ```
- matrix-no-label: a matrix whose labels are none that can be read, or an empty one, so that no job runs
  - finding kinds: self-hosted-runner.public, self-hosted-runner.private
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: matrix-no-label.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: runs-on is self-hosted and a value of a matrix, whose only
    #   value has a space before it.
    # reason: no runner label has a space before it, so no job runs.
    # cause: a label written as a literal that no runner has makes the rule
    #   take the job as running on none, but a value of the matrix that no
    #   runner has drops only that value; when every value is dropped, the
    #   self-hosted label is still left and is reported.
    # attack: the attacker becomes a contributor (in pytorch-2023, by a typo fix
    #   that was merged), then opens a pull request from a fork whose copy of
    #   this workflow runs a step of their own in place of make.
    # attack-run-behavior: with runs-on as this file writes it, the one job asks
    #   for a runner with the labels self-hosted and " x", which no runner has,
    #   so no runner picks it up and the attacker's step does not run.
    on: pull_request
    jobs:
      a:
        strategy:
          matrix:
            os: [" x"]
        runs-on: [self-hosted, "${{ matrix.os }}"]
        steps:
          - run: make
    ```
- private-repository: a private or internal repository, which not anyone forks: one who may read it and fork it is self-hosted-runner.private
  - finding kinds: self-hosted-runner.public
  - fact kinds:
    - repo.public (provider: repo-setting, answer that removes the finding: false)
  - example: private-repository.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: a pull request runs the job on a self-hosted runner.
    # reason: the repository is private or internal, so not anyone forks it and
    #   opens a pull request: one who may read it and fork it is
    #   self-hosted-runner.private.
    # cause: unless a file of facts or --fact says that the repository is not
    #   public (repo.public false), the rule reports the finding. When no source
    #   answers repo.public, the finding is conditional.
    # attack: the attacker becomes a contributor (in pytorch-2023, by a typo fix
    #   that was merged), then opens a pull request from a fork whose copy of
    #   this workflow runs a step of their own in place of make.
    # attack-run-behavior: the repository is private or internal, so only those
    #   who may read it, every member of the enterprise for an internal one, fork
    #   it and open a pull request; an outsider cannot, and the job a runs on the
    #   self-hosted runner only the steps of those people's pull requests.
    on: pull_request
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: [self-hosted, linux]
        steps:
          - run: make
    ```
- readers-write: a private repository whose readers all may write to it, as every collaborator of a repository of a personal account: they reach the runner by pushing a branch, which the rule does not count
  - finding kinds: self-hosted-runner.private
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: readers-write.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on pull_request, a job runs make on a runner labelled
    #   self-hosted and linux, in a private repository of a personal account
    #   that lets its collaborators fork it and runs the workflows of pull
    #   requests from forks.
    # reason: every collaborator of a private repository of a personal account
    #   has write access, so one who forks it can also push a branch of the
    #   repository and reach the runner that way; the rule does not count those
    #   who may write as attackers, and no one reads the repository without
    #   writing to it.
    # cause: no fact says whether a reader of the repository lacks write
    #   access.
    # attack: one who may read the repository forks it and opens a pull request
    #   whose copy of this workflow runs a step of their own in place of make.
    # attack-run-behavior: the pull request's run starts and runs the step on
    #   the runner, but its author is a collaborator with write access, who
    #   could push the same step to a branch of the repository.
    on: pull_request
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: [self-hosted, linux]
        steps:
          - run: make
    ```
- owner-policy: a private or internal repository whose organization or enterprise forbids forking it, or running the workflows of pull requests from forks, where whether the settings of the repository the facts read show the policy was not checked
  - finding kinds: self-hosted-runner.private
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: owner-policy.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on pull_request, a job runs make on a runner labelled
    #   self-hosted and linux, in a private or internal repository whose own
    #   settings let its readers fork it and run the workflows of pull requests
    #   from forks, while its organization or enterprise forbids forking it.
    # reason: no one forks the repository, so no pull request comes from a
    #   fork, and the step of a reader never reaches the runner.
    # cause: the facts read the settings of the repository; whether they show
    #   the policy of its organization or enterprise was not checked.
    # attack: one who may read the repository tries to fork it to open a pull
    #   request whose copy of this workflow runs a step of their own in place
    #   of make.
    # attack-run-behavior: the policy keeps them from forking the repository,
    #   so there is no pull request of theirs, and the job a runs no step of
    #   theirs.
    on: pull_request
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: [self-hosted, linux]
        steps:
          - run: make
    ```
- actions-not-allowed: a workflow whose run GitHub does not start, or a job that GitHub fails in the step "Set up job", because of the setting of allowed actions of GitHub (the fact repo.allowed-actions, which the quality rule allowed-actions reads): GitHub does not start a run of a workflow that has a uses, or that calls a reusable workflow that has a uses, that the setting does not allow, and fails a job before any step of the job runs when a step of a composite action that the job runs has a uses that the setting does not allow, or when the setting requires a full commit SHA and a step names an action by a tag or a branch. The harm that the finding reports happens only when GitHub runs the workflow or the job, and the rule does not read repo.allowed-actions
  - finding kinds: self-hosted-runner.private, self-hosted-runner.public
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: actions-not-allowed.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the workflow of the true positive private (private.yml) of the
    #   rule, with a job added whose step uses example-org/not-allowed-action,
    #   which the setting of allowed actions of GitHub (repo.allowed-actions)
    #   blocks with !example-org/not-allowed-action@*. In the true positive, on
    #   pull_request, a job runs make on a runner labelled self-hosted and
    #   linux, in a private or internal repository that lets those who may read
    #   it fork it and runs the workflows of pull requests from its forks
    #   (repo.public false, repo.allow-forking true, repo.fork-pr-run-workflows
    #   true).
    # reason: GitHub checks each uses of the workflow before the run starts, and
    #   does not start the run because of the uses of
    #   example-org/not-allowed-action: no job of the run runs, so what the
    #   reason of the true positive says does not happen (in runs that the
    #   authors of the rule made on GitHub, such runs ended as startup_failure).
    # cause: the rule does not read repo.allowed-actions.
    # attack: one who may read the repository forks it and opens a pull request
    #   whose copy of this workflow runs a step of their own in place of make.
    # attack-run-behavior: GitHub does not start the run, so no step of the run
    #   runs, and the attack does nothing.
    on: pull_request
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: [self-hosted, linux]
        steps:
          - run: make
      not-allowed:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - uses: example-org/not-allowed-action@eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee
    ```

### threat

- precondition reader-fork: the repository is private or internal, lets those who may read it fork it (repo.allow-forking) and runs the workflows of pull requests from its forks (repo.fork-pr-run-workflows), a setting of private and internal repositories: those who may read it and fork it, generally those with read access, open such a pull request and compromise the runner; every member of the enterprise reads an internal repository, and the policies of the repository, the organization and the enterprise decide who forks it
  - cites:
    - <https://github.com/github/docs/blob/8b39dc44a066dda794bfacdd25653ff86324ef21/content/actions/reference/security/secure-use.md>
    - <https://github.com/github/docs/blob/8b39dc44a066dda794bfacdd25653ff86324ef21/content/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/about-repositories.md>
    - <https://github.com/github/docs/blob/8b39dc44a066dda794bfacdd25653ff86324ef21/data/reusables/actions/private-repository-forks-overview.md>
    - <https://github.com/github/docs/blob/8b39dc44a066dda794bfacdd25653ff86324ef21/content/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/about-repositories.md#about-internal-repositories>
- precondition public-repo: the repository is public, so anyone forks it and opens a pull request (repo.public true); by default, the run of a first-time contributor's pull request waits for approval, a contributor's does not; a credential whose only write access is to the permission Actions can approve the run (the endpoint POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs/{run_id}/approve), and the credential premise keeps the holder of such a credential as a possible attacker
  - cites:
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use#hardening-for-self-hosted-runners>
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/manage-workflow-runs/approve-runs-from-forks>
- precondition pr-workflow: a pull request from a fork proposes changes to the repository's workflows, and its pull_request run uses them: its author writes the runs-on
  - cites:
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/manage-workflow-runs/approve-runs-from-forks>
- precondition runner-persists: a self-hosted runner does not run each job in a clean virtual machine: what a job leaves stays for the jobs after it
  - cites:
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use#hardening-for-self-hosted-runners>
- actor: fork-pr-author
  - via: opens a pull request whose workflow, which the pull request writes, runs their code on the self-hosted runner
  - events: pull_request
  - run starters: pull_request: attacker
  - gains: run-code, persist-on-runner
- incident pytorch-2023: 2023-08-09: researchers became contributors by a typo fix, then a pull request whose workflow they wrote ran on the self-hosted runners of pytorch/pytorch, where they took secrets and tokens; the repository had jobs on runs-on &#91;self-hosted, linux.2xlarge], and the runner they used had labels of its own
  - advisory: <https://johnstawinski.com/2024/01/11/playing-with-fire-how-we-executed-a-critical-supply-chain-attack-on-pytorch/>
  - compromised: pytorch/pytorch
